knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scenario in a finite-horizon dynamic system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scenario is a complete realization path of the period-indexed uncertainty vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_t^s\) be a realization of \(\widetilde{\xi}_t\) at each index \(t=0,\ldots,T\). The tuple \[s=\left(\xi_0^s,\xi_1^s,\ldots,\xi_T^s\right)\] is called a scenario and represents one possible future.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario is the sequence of realized uncertainty vectors indexed from 0 through T, representing one possible future.
assumptions_latex: \xi_t^s\text{ is a realization of }\widetilde{\xi}_t\quad(t=0,\ldots,T)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s=(\xi_0^s,\ldots,\xi_T^s)\text{ is a scenario representing one possible future.}

source_evidence.locator: Dynamic Systems / 2.6. Scenario Aggregation / Definition 2.6-extra-1

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario in a finite-horizon dynamic system

children.title: Scenario Catalog Design
children.top_down_role: Selection, indexing, coverage, plus organization of scenarios in a finite catalog.

assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) is finite and positive.
\(\Xi\) is the measurable uncertainty space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=(I,\xi)\) is a finite scenario catalog.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite indexed catalogs; repeated scenario values are permitted because indices may encode distinct information paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and let \(\xi:I\to\Xi\) map each index to a realization of the uncertain data. A finite scenario catalog is the pair \(C=(I,\xi)\), with entries \(\xi_i=\xi(i)\). Distinct indices may have equal values in \(\Xi\); hence catalog identity is indexed, while its set of distinct realized values is \(\xi(I)=\{\xi_i:i\in I\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario catalog is a finite indexed collection of uncertainty realizations; different indices may represent the same realized value.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Catalog Design

children.title: Scenario Probability Weights
children.top_down_role: Probability mass assignments for cataloged scenarios.

assumptions_latex: \(I=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) indexes a finite scenario catalog.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\Delta_m\) defines a probability mass function on \(I\).

notation.meaning: probability weight of scenario index i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconditional probability weights for a finite scenario catalog.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scenario-probability vector is an element \(p=(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\) of the simplex \[\Delta_m=\left\{q\in\mathbb{R}^m:q_i\ge 0\ \text{for every }i\in I,\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}q_i=1\right\}.\] For each \(i\in I\), \(p_i\) is the probability assigned to catalog index \(i\). Its active index set is \(I_+=\{i\in I:p_i>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario weights are nonnegative numbers summing to one; positive-weight indices form the active catalog.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Probability Weights

children.title: Catalog-Weight Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Structural compatibility between scenario support coverage plus assigned probability mass.

knowledge_statements.title: Catalog-Weight Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of an indexed catalog with unconditional probability masses, including duplicate-point aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(I,\xi)\) be a finite scenario catalog in a measurable space \((\Xi,\mathcal{F})\), and let \(p=(p_i)_{i\in I}\) be indexed by the same set. The pair \((C,p)\) is catalog-weight compatible if and only if \(p_i\ge 0\) for every \(i\in I\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}p_i=1\). It then induces the probability measure \[P_{C,p}=\sum_{i\in I}p_i\delta_{\xi_i}.\] Its support within the finite represented point set is \[\operatorname{supp}(P_{C,p})=\left\{x\in\xi(I):\sum_{i\in I:\,\xi_i=x}p_i>0\right\}.\] Thus duplicate points are combined by adding their weights. If an irredundant one-to-one listing of the support is required, the points \(\xi_i\) must be distinct and every \(p_i\) must be positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A catalog and its weights are compatible when they share an index set and the weights form a probability distribution. Duplicate points receive their aggregate mass; distinct points with positive weights are required only for an irredundant support listing.
assumptions_latex: \((\Xi,\mathcal{F})\) is a measurable space.
\(C=(I,\xi)\) is a finite scenario catalog with \(\xi_i=\xi(i)\in\Xi\).
\(p=(p_i)_{i\in I}\in\mathbb{R}^{|I|}\) is indexed by the same finite set \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility holds exactly when \(p_i\ge 0\) for all \(i\in I\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}p_i=1\), producing \(P_{C,p}=\sum_{i\in I}p_i\delta_{\xi_i}\).

notation.meaning: atomic law induced by the catalog and weights
support of the induced atomic law within the represented point set

children.title: Scenario Partitions
children.top_down_role: Disjoint scenario classes used to organize finite uncertainty models.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic partitions of a finite scenario index set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive. A scenario partition is a family \(\Pi=\{B_1,\ldots,B_K\}\) of subsets of \(I\) such that \(B_k\ne\varnothing\) for every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), \(B_k\cap B_\ell=\varnothing\) whenever \(k\ne\ell\), and \(\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}B_k=I\). Equivalently, each scenario index belongs to exactly one block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario partition divides all scenario indices into nonempty, pairwise-disjoint blocks, with each index belonging to exactly one block.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite, nonempty scenario index set.
\(K\in\mathbb{N}\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi\) is a partition of \(I\) precisely when its blocks are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and cover \(I\).

children.title: Scenario Bundles
children.top_down_role: Scenario groups formed for coordinated approximation or decomposition.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite scenario index set.
\(p_i\ge 0\) are scenario weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bundle \(B\) is a nonempty scenario subset treated as one computational group, with mass \(p(B)\).

notation.meaning: aggregate probability mass of the bundle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational grouping sense; whether bundles must form a partition requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scenario bundle is a nonempty subset \(B\subseteq I\) selected for joint processing in a scenario-decomposition operation. Its aggregate probability is \[p(B)=\sum_{i\in B}p_i.\] A bundle family \(\mathcal{B}=\{B_1,\ldots,B_K\}\) is partitioning when its members are pairwise disjoint and their union is \(I\). The term bundle alone imposes no additional equivalence relation unless the governing algorithm explicitly requires \(\mathcal{B}\) to be a partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario bundle is a nonempty group processed jointly; a bundle family becomes partitioning only when its groups are disjoint and exhaustive.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Bundles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set and mass formulas are coherent, but whether “bundle” denotes any jointly processed subset or necessarily belongs to a partition is terminology-dependent and unsupported here.

children.title: Scenario Bunches
children.top_down_role: Aggregated collections used in scenario compression or computational organization.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite scenario index set.
\(p_i\ge 0\) are scenario weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bunch family is modeled as a finite cover \(\mathcal{H}\) of \(I\), allowing overlap unless excluded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provisional cover-based sense distinguishing bunches from partition blocks and algorithmic bundles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the provisional cover convention, a scenario bunch family is a finite collection \(\mathcal{H}=\{H_1,\ldots,H_R\}\) of nonempty subsets of \(I\) satisfying \(\bigcup_{r=1}^{R}H_r=I\). Distinct bunches may overlap, so an index can occur in several members. Each bunch has mass \(p(H_r)=\sum_{i\in H_r}p_i\); consequently, \(\sum_{r=1}^{R}p(H_r)\) need not equal one when overlap occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Provisionally, scenario bunches form a finite cover whose groups may overlap; overlap can make the sum of group masses exceed one.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Bunches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed cover-based, overlap-permitting meaning of “scenario bunch” is not a standard convention that can be accepted without an authoritative source.

children.title: Grouping-Structure Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Differences in coverage, overlap, granularity, plus computational role across grouping structures.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and nonempty.
\(\Pi\), \(\mathcal{B}\), and \(\mathcal{H}\) use the local partition, bundle, and bunch conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Partitions are disjoint covers; partitioning bundles coincide structurally with partitions; bunch covers may overlap.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison under provisional local conventions for bundles and bunches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every partition \(\Pi\) is a disjoint cover of \(I\). A bundle family \(\mathcal{B}\) has the same set-theoretic structure as a partition exactly when it is partitioning. A bunch family \(\mathcal{H}\) is only required provisionally to cover \(I\), so it is a partition exactly when its distinct members are pairwise disjoint. Thus partitioning bundles permit unique group assignment, whereas overlapping bunches permit multiple group assignments for one scenario index.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partitions uniquely assign scenarios; partitioning bundles have the same structure, while provisional bunch covers may assign one scenario to several groups.
knowledge_statements.title: Grouping-Structure Comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-theoretic comparison is valid under the stated local conventions, but its substantive distinction between bundles and bunches depends on two unsupported terminology choices.

children.title: Support-Point Representations
children.top_down_role: Locations chosen to represent a discrete approximation of uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Point Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite ordered support-point representation, separated from its probability weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite support-point representation is an ordered tuple \(\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m)\in\Xi^m\). Its represented point set is \[S(\boldsymbol{\xi})=\{x\in\Xi:x=\xi_i\ \text{for some }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\}.\] The tuple retains scenario labels and may contain repeated points. It specifies potential support locations only; without a compatible probability vector it does not determine a probability measure on \((\Xi,\mathcal{F})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support-point representation is an ordered finite tuple of uncertainty realizations; it records potential support locations and labels but does not by itself specify probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \((\Xi,\mathcal{F})\) is a measurable space.
\(m\in\mathbb{N}\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordered tuple \((\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m)\in\Xi^m\) represents potential support locations for an atomic distribution but does not determine that distribution without weights.

children.title: Weight Representations
children.top_down_role: Mass allocations attached to discrete support locations.

assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite weight representation is a vector \(p\in\Delta_m\), interpreted relative to an ordered support tuple.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex-vector representation of masses paired positionally with finite support points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite weight representation is a vector \(p=(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\in\Delta_m\), where \[\Delta_m=\left\{q\in\mathbb{R}_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^{m}q_i=1\right\}.\] Coordinate \(p_i\) is interpreted as the mass paired with the support point in position \(i\). The active coordinates are \(I_+(p)=\{i:p_i>0\}\). The vector alone specifies a distribution on the index set, not on an uncertainty space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weight representation is a simplex vector whose coordinates are paired positionally with support points; alone it distributes mass only over indices.
knowledge_statements.title: Weight Representations

children.title: Support-Weight Coupling
children.top_down_role: Joint structural choices linking support placement to mass allocation.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Weight Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positional coupling of finite support points and probability masses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Xi,\mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space. Coupling the support tuple \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) and weight vector \(p\) by their common index produces the atomic probability measure \[P=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i\delta_{\xi_i}.\] For every measurable, real-valued, \(P\)-integrable function \(f:\Xi\to\mathbb{R}\), \[\int_{\Xi}f(\xi)\,P(d\xi)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i f(\xi_i).\] Simultaneously permuting both tuples leaves \(P\) unchanged; permuting only one generally changes the coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positionally pairing support points with weights defines an atomic probability law and expresses every integrable expectation as a weighted finite sum.
assumptions_latex: \((\Xi,\mathcal{F})\) is a measurable space.
\(m\in\mathbb{N}\) is positive.
\(\boldsymbol{\xi}=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m)\in\Xi^m\).
\(p=(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\in\Delta_m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled pair determines \(P=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i\delta_{\xi_i}\), and every measurable, real-valued, \(P\)-integrable function has expectation \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i f(\xi_i)\).

children.title: Scenario-Tree Nodes
children.top_down_role: Stage-indexed decision or uncertainty locations within scenario trees.

assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb{N}\) is the finite planning horizon.
\(G=(V,E)\) is a finite rooted directed tree with root \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each node represents one stage-specific information history and has a unique ancestral history.

notation.meaning: information history represented by node v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite rooted scenario trees with one-stage edges and history-labeled nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scenario-tree node is a vertex \(v\in V\) equipped with a stage \(\tau(v)\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), where \(\tau(r)=0\) and \(\tau(v)=\tau(a(v))+1\) for every nonroot node \(v\). Because \(G\) is rooted and acyclic, each \(v\) has a unique ancestor chain from \(r\). The label \(h(v)\) denotes the information history shared by all complete scenarios whose root-to-leaf paths pass through \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario-tree node is a staged vertex with a unique ancestor chain, representing the information history shared by scenarios passing through it.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Tree Nodes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decision and Chance Nodes in a Stochastic Decision Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded representation illustrated by a two-period investment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the illustrated stochastic decision tree, square decision nodes represent points at which account \(A\) or \(B\) is selected, and circular chance nodes represent points at which an uncertain interest rate becomes known. A second-period decision following investment in \(A\) may depend on the first-period interest rate that was experienced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the illustrated stochastic decision tree, square nodes represent choices between accounts A and B, while circular nodes represent revelation of an uncertain interest rate. After choosing A, the second-period decision may depend on the observed first-period interest rate.
assumptions_latex: \text{The return on account }B\text{ is known with certainty.}
\text{The return on account }A\text{ is random.}
R_{A,1}\perp R_{A,2}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The second-period decision after choosing }A\text{ may depend on the observed first-period return.}

children.title: Scenario-Tree Paths
children.top_down_role: Root-to-stage or root-to-leaf trajectories through scenario trees.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Tree Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root-to-leaf paths in a stagewise finite scenario tree whose leaves all occur at the terminal stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complete scenario-tree path is a sequence \(\pi=(v_0,\ldots,v_T)\) with \(v_0=r\), \((v_{t-1},v_t)\in E\), and \(\tau(v_t)=t\) for every \(t\in\{0,ldots,T\}\). Because every leaf is at stage \(T\), each leaf determines exactly one complete path, and the ordered node or edge labels along it determine one complete scenario history. Under the conditional edge probabilities, the path probability is \[P(\pi)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q_{v_{t-1}v_t}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every leaf is at the terminal stage, each complete scenario is represented by a unique root-to-leaf path, and its probability is the product of the conditional probabilities on that path.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb{N}\) is the finite terminal stage.
\(G=(V,E)\) is a finite rooted directed tree with root \(r\).
\(\tau:V\to\{0,\ldots,T\}\) satisfies \(\tau(r)=0\) and increases by one along every edge.
Every leaf \(v\) satisfies \(\tau(v)=T\).
For every edge \((v,w)\in E\), \(q_{vw}\ge 0\), and \(\sum_{w:(v,w)\in E}q_{vw}=1\) at every nonleaf node \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every leaf determines a unique root-to-leaf path \(\pi\), whose probability is \(P(\pi)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q_{v_{t-1}v_t}\).

notation.meaning: conditional probability of the edge from v to w

children.title: Information Histories
children.top_down_role: Observed histories associated with staged decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Information Histories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon histories generated by sequentially revealed exogenous information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\mathbb N\), let \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\) be a measurable space, and let \(\xi_t:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(\Xi_t,\mathcal X_t)\) be measurable for \(t=1,\ldots,T\). The information history through stage \(t\) is \(H_t(\omega)=(\xi_1(\omega),\ldots,\xi_t(\omega))\), and its generated information field is \(\mathcal F_t=\sigma(H_t)=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\), with \(\mathcal F_0=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\). Thus \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) is a filtration. If \((X_t,\mathcal A_t)\) is a measurable decision space, a decision map \(x_t:\Omega\to X_t\) depends only on the stage-\(t\) history precisely when it is \(\mathcal F_t/\mathcal A_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An information history records all observations available through a stage. The sigma-fields generated by successive histories form a filtration, and a history-dependent decision is measurable with respect to the corresponding stage sigma-field.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
Each \(\xi_t:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(\Xi_t,\mathcal X_t)\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_0\subseteq\mathcal F_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal F_T\), and a history-dependent \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t/\mathcal A_t\)-measurable.

notation.meaning: realized information history through stage t
sigma-field generated by the stage-t history

children.title: Node-Path-History Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Mappings among tree locations, trajectories, plus available information.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Path-History Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence for a finite, nonrecombining scenario tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\mathbb N\) and let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite rooted tree with stage map \(\tau:V\to\{0,\ldots,T\}\), root \(v_0\) satisfying \(\tau(v_0)=0\), and \(\tau(w)=\tau(v)+1\) for every edge \((v,w)\in E\). Label each nonroot node \(v\) by an observation \(\ell(v)\). For every \(v\in V_t:=\tau^{-1}(\{t\})\), the unique root-to-\(v\) path \((v_0,\ldots,v_t)\) determines the represented history \(H(v)=(\ell(v_1),\ldots,\ell(v_t))\). If distinct children of every node have distinct labels, then \(v\mapsto H(v)\) is injective on each \(V_t\). Hence the stage-\(t\) nodes, root-to-stage-\(t\) paths, and represented histories of length \(t\) are in bijection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite labeled nonrecombining scenario tree, every stage-t node has one ancestral path and therefore one represented history. Distinct labels among siblings make stage-t nodes, their root paths, and represented histories correspond bijectively.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite rooted tree whose edges join consecutive stages.
Distinct children of each node have distinct observation labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_t\cong\{\text{represented histories of length }t\}\cong\{\text{root-to-stage-}t\text{ paths}\}\).

notation.meaning: history along the unique path to v

children.title: Branching-Tree Representations
children.top_down_role: Expanding scenario structures with distinct descendant histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Tree Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite discrete scenario representation without recombination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A branching-tree representation of a horizon-\(T\) discrete process is a rooted directed tree \(G=(V,E)\) with stage partition \(V=\bigsqcup_{t=0}^T V_t\), node probabilities \(p_v>0\), and observation labels \(\xi_v\). Every \(w\in V_{t+1}\) has exactly one parent \(v\in V_t\), and \(p_v=\sum_{w\in\operatorname{ch}(v)}p_w\). Each leaf \(s\in V_T\) represents the scenario formed by its unique ancestral label sequence, with probability \(p_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching scenario tree assigns observations and consistent probability mass to nodes; every terminal scenario is the label sequence along one unique root-to-leaf path.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\) and every node has finitely many children.
The root has probability one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{s\in V_T}p_s=1\), and every leaf represents one complete scenario.

children.title: Recombining-Tree Representations
children.top_down_role: Scenario structures whose compatible histories merge into shared states.

knowledge_statements.title: Recombining-Tree Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Layered directed-acyclic representation merging equivalent histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A recombining-tree representation is a rooted layered directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), with edges from \(V_t\) to \(V_{t+1}\), in which a node may have multiple parents. Each edge \((v,w)\) has transition probability \(q_{vw}\ge0\), with \(\sum_{w:(v,w)\in E}q_{vw}=1\). A root-to-leaf path represents a complete scenario, while all paths reaching the same node \(w\) are identified with one information state whose admissible continuation law and decision data are identical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recombining representation merges histories into a shared node only when they have identical continuation laws and decision-relevant data.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, rooted, layered, and acyclic.
Outgoing transition probabilities sum to one at every nonterminal node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Multiple scenario paths may reach one node without changing their common conditional continuation model.

notation.meaning: transition probability on edge from v to w

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the asserted exact criterion that all paths reaching a shared node have identical continuation laws and decision data. An authoritative locator is needed to distinguish this layered DAG notion from other uses of recombining tree.

children.title: Lattice Representations
children.top_down_role: Layered state structures with repeated transitions or shared state locations.

knowledge_statements.title: Lattice Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recombining representation with coordinates and prescribed local increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lattice representation is a recombining layered graph whose stage-\(t\) nodes are indexed by points \(z\in L_t\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\). From \((t,z)\), transitions are permitted only to \((t+1,z+\delta)\) for \(\delta\) in a finite increment set \(D_t(z)\), with probabilities \(q_t(z,delta)\) summing to one. Distinct increment sequences that yield the same coordinate share the same node, conditional continuation law, and stagewise decision data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario lattice indexes recombining states by integer coordinates, so different increment sequences reaching the same coordinate share one continuation model.
assumptions_latex: \(L_t\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\) and \(D_t(z)\) are finite.
\(q_t(z,\delta)\ge0\) and \(\sum_{\delta\in D_t(z)}q_t(z,\delta)=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((t,z)\) represents every admissible path whose accumulated increments reach \(z\) at stage \(t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed integer-coordinate lattice is plausible but is only one possible lattice convention and has no citation. The statement also writes delta as an undeclared literal in one probability expression. A source must establish the intended scope before revision.

children.title: Recombination Eligibility
children.top_down_role: Information or state conditions governing when histories may share a representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Recombination Eligibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion for merging decision-relevant information histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h,h'\) be stage-\(t\) histories. They are eligible for exact recombination when there exists one common information-state label \(s\) such that \(s(h)=s(h')\), their feasible decision correspondences agree, \(X_t(h)=X_t(h')\), their stage costs agree on that set, \(c_t(x,h)=c_t(x,h')\), and their conditional kernels for the next state agree, \(Q_t(\cdot\mid h,x)=Q_t(\cdot\mid h',x)\), for every \(x\in X_t(h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two histories may be merged exactly only when they have identical feasible actions, current costs, and controlled conditional continuation laws.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) and \(h'\) occur at the same stage.
The conditional kernels are defined on a common measurable next-state space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\sim_t h'\) is an exact recombination relation under the displayed equalities.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equalities are plausible sufficient conditions for controlled recombination, but the claim of exact eligibility and the induced equivalence relation require sourced conditions on future costs, terminal data, kernels, and recursive compatibility.

children.title: Nested-Distribution Representations
children.top_down_role: Stage-consistent families of probability laws for multistage uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Distribution Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon law represented recursively by conditional probability kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\mathbb N\) and let \((\Xi_t,\mathcal X_t)\) be standard Borel spaces for \(t=1,\ldots,T\). A nested-distribution representation consists of an initial probability law \(K_1\) on \((\Xi_1,\mathcal X_1)\) and measurable probability kernels \(K_t(\cdot\mid\xi_{1:t-1})\) on \((\Xi_t,\mathcal X_t)\) for \(t=2,\ldots,T\). These kernels determine the unique joint law \(P\) satisfying \[P(d\xi_{1:T})=K_1(d\xi_1)\prod_{t=2}^T K_t(d\xi_t\mid\xi_{1:t-1}).\] Each \(K_t\) is a version of the conditional law of \(\xi_t\) given \(\xi_{1:t-1}\) under \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested distribution specifies an initial law and successive measurable history-conditioned kernels. Their chronological composition uniquely determines the complete scenario law.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
\((\Xi_t,\mathcal X_t)\) is standard Borel for every \(t\).
Each \(K_t\) is a measurable probability kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The kernels determine a unique probability measure \(P\) on \(\prod_{t=1}^T(\Xi_t,\mathcal X_t)\).

children.title: Conditional Scenario Systems
children.top_down_role: Finite successor scenarios conditioned on observed histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Scenario Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite conditional scenario families indexed by represented histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\mathbb N\), let \(\mathcal H_t\) be the set of represented histories through stage \(t\), and let \((\Xi_{t+1},\mathcal X_{t+1})\) be the next-observation space. A conditional scenario system is a family \(\{S_t(h):0\le t<T,\ h\in\mathcal H_t\}\), where \(S_t(h)=\{(\xi_{t+1}^j,p_{t+1}^j(h)):j\in J_t(h)\}\), each \(J_t(h)\) is finite, \(\xi_{t+1}^j\in\Xi_{t+1}\), \(p_{t+1}^j(h)>0\), and \(\sum_{j\in J_t(h)}p_{t+1}^j(h)=1\). Thus \(S_t(h)\) defines the discrete conditional law \(K_{t+1}(\cdot\mid h)=\sum_{j\in J_t(h)}p_{t+1}^j(h)\delta_{\xi_{t+1}^j}(\cdot)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditional scenario system assigns each represented history a finite probability distribution over its possible next observations.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
Each successor index set \(J_t(h)\) is finite.
Each support point \(\xi_{t+1}^j\) belongs to \(\Xi_{t+1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(S_t(h)\) defines a discrete conditional probability law \(K_{t+1}(\cdot\mid h)\) on \((\Xi_{t+1},\mathcal X_{t+1})\).

notation.meaning: conditional successor scenarios after history h

children.title: Conditional-Law Consistency
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of local conditional scenarios across stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional-Law Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of local conditional laws with one joint scenario law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_1,ldots,K_T\) be normalized measurable kernels and let \(P\) be a probability law on \(\Xi_1\times\cdots\times\Xi_T\). The system is conditionally law-consistent with \(P\) when, for every \(t<T\), every \(A\in\mathcal X_{t+1}\), and \(P\)-almost every history \(\xi_{1:t}\), \[K_{t+1}(A\mid xi_{1:t})=P(\xi_{t+1}\in A\mid sigma(\xi_{1:t})).\] Equivalently, the joint law obtained by recursively composing the kernels equals \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local scenario kernels are consistent when they are versions of one joint law's conditional distributions, equivalently when their recursive product reconstructs that law.
assumptions_latex: All stage spaces are standard Borel.
The kernels are measurable and normalized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=K_1\otimes K_2\otimes\cdots\otimes K_T\) in chronological kernel composition.

notation.meaning: sigma-field on the stage-t observation space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for the disintegration and reconstruction equivalence. The displayed equality also compares a scalar kernel value with conditional expectation notation relative to a sigma-field without evaluating a history, so the mathematical formulation requires authoritative correction.

children.title: Nested-Law Scenario Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural translation between nested probability laws plus finite conditional systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested-Law Scenario Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between finite-support nested kernels and weighted scenario trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T<\infty\), and suppose that each conditional kernel \(K_{t+1}(\cdot\mid h)\) has finite support for every positive-probability history \(h\) at stage \(t\), where \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\). Construct a node for every positive-probability history \(h\), connect \(h\) to each extended history \((h,\xi)\) satisfying \(K_{t+1}(\{\xi\}\mid h)>0\), and assign the edge probability \(K_{t+1}(\{\xi\}\mid h)\). Conversely, a weighted scenario tree defines at every nonterminal node the discrete conditional kernel supported on its children, with masses equal to the outgoing conditional edge probabilities. These constructions preserve the joint probability of every root-to-leaf scenario and are inverse up to a stage-preserving, probability-preserving relabeling of nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-support nested conditional laws and weighted scenario trees encode the same histories, scenarios, and probabilities, up to a probability-preserving relabeling of nodes.
assumptions_latex: The horizon is finite.
Every conditional support is finite.
Only positive-probability histories are represented.
Outgoing edge weights at each nonterminal node are normalized conditional probabilities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{K_t\}_{t=1}^T\longleftrightarrow\{\text{weighted scenario trees}\}\) up to stage-preserving, probability-preserving node isomorphism.

notation.meaning: conditional successor law at history h
history h extended by observation xi

children.title: Scenario-Tree Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Criteria for treating different tree structures as the same stochastic model.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Tree Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence relative to probability, information, and decision data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two finite scenario trees are equivalent for a multistage model when there is a stage-preserving bijection between their positive-probability information classes such that corresponding classes have equal reach probabilities, isomorphic conditional successor kernels, identical feasible-decision correspondences and stage costs, and corresponding terminal paths carry the same terminal data. Equivalently, after identifying matched information classes, both trees induce the same filtered finite probability space and the same adapted optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario trees are equivalent when they encode the same filtered probability model and identical decision-relevant data, despite different node labels or redundant nodes.
assumptions_latex: Both trees have the same finite horizon.
Zero-probability nodes are discarded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two trees induce identical feasible adapted policies and identical objective values for corresponding policies.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed equivalence combines probability-space, information, kernel, cost, feasibility, and terminal-data requirements without defining information classes or citing an established equivalence notion. A source is needed to determine the intended exact scope.

children.title: Minimal Scenario Trees
children.top_down_role: Irreducible tree representations preserving relevant information structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Scenario Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal representative under exact decision-relevant history equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite-support multistage model and its history equivalence relation \(\sim_t\), where histories are equivalent exactly when their reach-stage decision data and conditional continuation models coincide. A scenario tree is minimal when its stage-\(t\) nodes are precisely the positive-probability equivalence classes \(\mathcal H_t/\!\sim_t\) and no two distinct nodes at the same stage can be merged while preserving the model. The quotient construction is unique up to stage-preserving, probability- and data-preserving node isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal scenario tree has one node per decision-relevant history class and admits no further exact merge; its quotient form is unique up to isomorphism.
assumptions_latex: The horizon and represented history set are finite.
\(\sim_t\) is an equivalence relation compatible with successor kernels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_t=\mathcal H_t/\!\sim_t\), and every equivalent tree has at least \(|V_t|\) stage-\(t\) information nodes.

notation.meaning: nodes of the minimal tree at stage t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The first part is a plausible definition, but the record also asserts uniqueness of the quotient and a stagewise lower-bound theorem. Those nontrivial conclusions are not generic definition content and require a source establishing compatibility assumptions and theorem scope.

children.title: Equivalent-Tree Transformations
children.top_down_role: Structure-preserving changes among alternative scenario-tree representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent-Tree Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformations preserving the finite-tree information structure, probabilities, and optimization data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) and \(T'\) be finite scenario trees with leaf sets \(L\) and \(L'\), leaf probabilities \(p\) and \(p'\), and stagewise history maps \(h_t:L\to\mathcal H_t\) and \(h'_t:L'\to\mathcal H_t\). An equivalent-tree transformation is a bijection \(\phi:L\to L'\) such that \(p'_{\phi(\ell)}=p_\ell\) and \(h'_t(\phi(\ell))=h_t(\ell)\) for every \(\ell\in L\) and every stage \(t\), up to consistent node relabeling, and such that the decision domains, objective data, and constraint data attached to corresponding histories agree. Pullback by \(\phi\) then bijects the adapted feasible policies and preserves every policy's expected objective value. Consequently, the two deterministic equivalents have the same optimal value and corresponding optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A leaf bijection preserving probabilities, observed histories, decision domains, and model data yields corresponding adapted policies, objective values, and optima, up to node relabeling.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) and \(T'\) are finite scenario trees whose leaves have strictly positive probabilities.
Model coefficients and decision domains depend only on the represented stagewise histories.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(T)=v(T')\), with optimizers corresponding through pullback by \(\phi\).

notation.meaning: information history of leaf ell through stage t
optimal value represented by tree T

children.title: Minimality Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Information distinctions that prevent further tree compression.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimality Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when merging scenario-tree nodes ceases to preserve the represented stochastic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two nodes \(u\) and \(v\) at the same stage that share the same recorded past. Merging them is generally invalid if either their conditional continuation laws or their descendant objective and constraint data differ. Concretely, suppose the next disturbance is Bernoulli and \(\mathbb P(\xi_{t+1}=1\mid u)=q_u\) while \(\mathbb P(\xi_{t+1}=1\mid v)=q_v\neq q_u\). Replacing both nodes by one node with an averaged transition probability destroys at least one node-conditional distribution. For a continuation cost or constraint distinguishing the two outcomes, the merged tree can change conditional decisions, feasibility, or value; thus history equality alone does not justify reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nodes with identical recorded pasts cannot generally be merged when their conditional futures or descendant model data differ.
assumptions_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) occur at the same decision stage.
At least one continuation cost or constraint distinguishes the differing conditional futures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(q_u\neq q_v\), the proposed merge need not preserve the feasible adapted policies or optimal value.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Based Nonanticipativity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-indexed decisions encode equality across scenarios sharing an information history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a finite rooted scenario tree with stages \(t=0,\ldots,H\), node set \(N_t\) at stage \(t\), positive-probability leaf set \(S\), and map \(n_t:S\to N_t\) assigning to each leaf scenario its stage-\(t\) ancestor. For each \(n\in N_t\), let \(X_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_t}\) be its feasible decision domain. A node-based policy assigns one decision \(x_n\in X_n\) to every decision node \(n\). Its scenario realization is \(x_t^s=x_{n_t(s)}\). Consequently, \(n_t(s)=n_t(r)\) implies \(x_t^s=x_t^r\). Conversely, scenario-indexed decisions satisfying these equalities define a unique node-based policy when every retained node is reached by at least one leaf in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One decision is attached to each information node, forcing scenarios with the same observed history to use the same decision; the resulting equalities also characterize node-based policies.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a finite rooted tree.
Every retained node is reached by at least one positive-probability leaf.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n_t(s)=n_t(r)\Rightarrow x_t^s=x_t^r\), and these equalities characterize node-based policies.

notation.meaning: feasible decision domain at node n

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Copy Consensus Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-local decision copies coupled by consensus over common information histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite scenario set, let \(N_t\) be the information nodes at stage \(t\), and let \(n_t:S\to N_t\) map each scenario to its stage-\(t\) node. Define \(C_{t,n}=\{s\in S:n_t(s)=n\}\). For each stage \(t\), introduce a local copy \(x_t^s\in\mathbb R^{d_t}\) for every \(s\in S\) and a consensus variable \(z_{t,n}\in\mathbb R^{d_t}\) for every nonempty class \(C_{t,n}\). Nonanticipativity is represented by \(x_t^s=z_{t,n}\) for every \(s\in C_{t,n}\). Eliminating the consensus variables yields \(x_t^s=x_t^r\) whenever \(n_t(s)=n_t(r)\). Conversely, any family satisfying these pairwise equations admits a unique consensus value on each nonempty class, namely its common value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario-specific decision copies are nonanticipative exactly when all copies sharing an information node equal one consensus variable.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and the planning horizon are finite.
Each retained consensus class \(C_{t,n}\) is nonempty.
\(d_t\) is a positive integer for every decision stage \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The consensus and pairwise nonanticipativity representations define the same feasible decision set.

notation.meaning: stage-t decision copy for scenario s
stage-t information node of scenario s
scenarios sharing node n at stage t

children.title: Nonanticipativity Subspaces
children.top_down_role: Decision spaces compatible with prescribed information histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipativity Subspaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear subspace of scenario decisions constant on each information class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite scenario set, let the stages be \(t=0,\ldots,H\), let \(d_t\) be a positive integer, and let \(p_s>0\) for every \(s\in S\). Define the weighted product space \(\mathcal H=\prod_{t=0}^H\prod_{s\in S}\mathbb R^{d_t}\) with inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle_p=\sum_{t=0}^H\sum_{s\in S}p_s(x_t^s)^{\mathsf T}y_t^s\). For every stage \(t\), let \(\sim_t\) be the equivalence relation on \(S\) defined by equality of information histories through stage \(t\). The nonanticipativity subspace is \(\mathcal N=\{x\in\mathcal H:x_t^s=x_t^r\text{ whenever }s\sim_t r\}\). It is a closed linear subspace because it is the intersection of finitely many kernels of linear difference maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonanticipativity subspace consists of finite-horizon scenario decisions that are constant within every stagewise information class.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(\{0,\ldots,H\}\) are finite, and \(p_s>0\) for every \(s\in S\).
Each \(d_t\) is a positive integer.
Each relation \(\sim_t\) is induced by equality of stage-t information histories.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N\) is a closed linear subspace of \(\mathcal H\).

notation.meaning: equality of information histories through stage t
dimension of a stage-t decision copy

children.title: Nonanticipativity Projections
children.top_down_role: Mappings from scenario-copy decisions into information-compatible spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipativity Projections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted orthogonal projection obtained by conditional averaging within information classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be finite, let \(t=0,\ldots,H\), let \(d_t\) be a positive integer, and let \(p_s>0\) for every \(s\in S\). Equip \(\mathcal H=\prod_{t=0}^H\prod_{s\in S}\mathbb R^{d_t}\) with the inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle_p=\sum_{t=0}^H\sum_{s\in S}p_s(x_t^s)^{\mathsf T}y_t^s\). Let \(\sim_t\) denote equality of stage-\(t\) information histories, define \(C_t(s)=\{r\in S:r\sim_t s\}\), and let \(\mathcal N\) be the subspace of vectors constant on every class \(C_t(s)\). The orthogonal projection onto \(\mathcal N\) is \[(P_{\mathcal N}x)_t^s=\frac{\sum_{r\in C_t(s)}p_r x_t^r}{\sum_{r\in C_t(s)}p_r}.\] This formula is independent of the representative within a class and gives the unique minimizer of \(\min_{y\in\mathcal N}\sum_{t=0}^H\sum_{s\in S}p_s\lVert x_t^s-y_t^s\rVert_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting onto nonanticipativity replaces each scenario decision by the probability-weighted average over scenarios sharing its information history.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(\{0,\ldots,H\}\) are finite, and every \(p_s\) is positive.
Each \(d_t\) is a positive integer.
The product-space inner product is weighted by \(p_s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed conditional-average operator is the orthogonal projector \(P_{\mathcal N}\).

notation.meaning: stage-t information class containing scenario s
subspace of decisions constant on each information class
orthogonal projector onto the nonanticipativity subspace

children.title: Projection Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric relationships induced by norms, weights, plus scenario-copy structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal decomposition of scenario decisions into adapted and anticipative components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal N\) be the nonanticipativity subspace of a finite-dimensional weighted scenario space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(P_{\mathcal N}\) be its orthogonal projector. Every \(x\in\mathcal H\) has the unique decomposition \(x=P_{\mathcal N}x+(I-P_{\mathcal N})x\), where \(P_{\mathcal N}x\in\mathcal N\), \((I-P_{\mathcal N})x\in\mathcal N^\perp\), and the two terms are orthogonal. Consequently, \(\lVert x\rVert_p^2=\lVert P_{\mathcal N}x\rVert_p^2+\lVert(I-P_{\mathcal N})x\rVert_p^2\), while \(\operatorname{dist}_p(x,\mathcal N)=\lVert(I-P_{\mathcal N})x\rVert_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every scenario decision splits uniquely into a nonanticipative projection and an orthogonal disagreement component whose norm is the distance to feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a finite-dimensional weighted inner-product space.
\(\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal H\) is the nonanticipativity subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal H=\mathcal N\oplus\mathcal N^\perp\) with the stated Pythagorean identity and distance formula.

notation.meaning: orthogonal complement of the nonanticipativity subspace

children.title: Filtration Changes
children.top_down_role: Effects of refining, coarsening, or otherwise modifying staged information.

knowledge_statements.title: Filtration Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Policy-set monotonicity under coarsening or refinement of the decision filtration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), let \((\mathcal G_t)_{t=0}^H\) and \((\mathcal H_t)_{t=0}^H\) be filtrations with \(\mathcal G_t\subseteq\mathcal H_t\) for every \(t\). Every \(\mathcal G_t\)-measurable decision is also \(\mathcal H_t\)-measurable, so the adapted policy sets satisfy \(\mathcal X_{\mathcal G}\subseteq\mathcal X_{\mathcal H}\), provided their pointwise constraints coincide. Therefore refinement cannot increase the optimal value of a minimization problem, while coarsening cannot decrease it. Equality need not hold because added information may permit decisions unavailable under the coarser filtration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refining information enlarges the adapted policy set and cannot worsen a minimization optimum; coarsening has the reverse effect.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G_t\subseteq\mathcal H_t\subseteq\mathcal F\) for all \(t\).
Both models use identical objective functions and pointwise constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal X_{\mathcal G}\subseteq\mathcal X_{\mathcal H}\) and, for minimization, \(v_{\mathcal H}\leq v_{\mathcal G}\).

notation.meaning: coarser and finer stage-t information sigma-fields
policies adapted to the filtration G

children.title: Filtration Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Misalignment between modeled information availability plus the intended decision process.

knowledge_statements.title: Filtration Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by enforcing nonanticipativity for a filtration different from the intended one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)\) be the intended information filtration and \((\widehat{\mathcal F}_t)\) the filtration encoded by a scenario model. The encoding is filtration-compatible precisely when its admissible decisions coincide with the intended adapted decisions at every stage. If \(\widehat{\mathcal F}_t\subsetneq\mathcal F_t\), the formulation can impose spurious consensus and exclude legitimate policies; if \(\mathcal F_t\subsetneq\widehat{\mathcal F}_t\), it can admit decisions using unavailable information. When neither filtration contains the other, both defects may occur. Thus matching marginal scenario distributions does not by itself establish equivalence of stochastic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the wrong filtration either suppresses legitimate adaptation, permits unavailable information, or does both, even when scenario marginals match.
assumptions_latex: Both filtrations are defined on the same probability space and stages.
The intended policy class requires \(x_t\) to be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the encoded and intended adapted policy sets differ, the encoded stochastic program need not preserve feasibility or value.

notation.meaning: information encoded by the scenario representation

source_refs.locator: 5.9 A Measure-Theoretic View of Information** p. 211

source_witnesses.locator: 5.9 A Measure-Theoretic View of Information** p. 211

children.title: Anticipative Models
children.top_down_role: Models permitting decisions to depend on information unavailable at decision time.

knowledge_statements.title: Anticipative Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Models admitting decisions measurable with respect to information unavailable at their decision time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a finite probability space whose outcomes have positive probability, and let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^H\) be the operational filtration. A stochastic optimization model is anticipative if, for some decision stage \(t\), its feasible policy class contains a random decision \(x_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{d_t}\) that is not \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. On this finite space, this is equivalent to the existence of outcomes \(\omega,\omega'\in\Omega\) belonging to the same atom of \(\mathcal F_t\) for which the model permits \(x_t(\omega)\neq x_t(\omega')\). On a scenario tree, this occurs when decision copies associated with a common stage-\(t\) information node are not constrained to agree. Such a formulation uses future or otherwise unavailable information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite scenario space, a model is anticipative when it permits a current decision to vary across outcomes lying in the same current-information atom.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is finite and every \(\omega\in\Omega\) has positive probability.
\((\mathcal F_t)\) represents the information operationally available at each decision stage.
Each decision \(x_t\) takes values in \(\mathbb R^{d_t}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Anticipativity occurs exactly when some admissible \(x_t\) is not \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable; on the stated finite space, this is equivalent to variation within an atom of \(\mathcal F_t\).

notation.meaning: information available when the stage-t decision is made
finite-space outcomes compared at a decision stage

source_refs.locator: 5.9 A Measure-Theoretic View of Information** p. 211

children.title: Information-Leakage Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural boundaries separating admissible information use from anticipative dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Leakage Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp value distortion when a decision accesses even one unresolved future random variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) take values \(-1\) and \(1\) with equal probability, and require a decision \(x\in\mathbb R\) before \(\xi\) is observed. Under the trivial decision-time sigma-field, admissibility forces \(x\) to be constant, and \(\min_x\mathbb E[(x-\xi)^2]=1\), attained at \(x=0\). If the formulation leaks \(\sigma(\xi)\) into the decision information, it admits \(x=\xi\) and obtains objective value \(0\). Hence allowing distinctions between scenarios before those distinctions are observable can strictly and artificially improve the objective; nonanticipativity must identify exactly the scenarios indistinguishable at decision time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary example shows that revealing one future outcome can lower the modeled loss from one to zero, creating an artificial value improvement.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb P(\xi=-1)=\mathbb P(\xi=1)=1/2\).
The objective is to minimize expected squared error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adapted value is \(1\), whereas the leaked-information value is \(0\).

source_refs.locator: 5.9 A Measure-Theoretic View of Information** p. 211

source_witnesses.locator: 5.9 A Measure-Theoretic View of Information** p. 211

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Extensive Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario deterministic equivalent of a two-stage stochastic program with recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite scenario set with probabilities \(p_s>0\) satisfying \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\). Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) be the first-stage decision and \(y_s\in\mathbb R^{m_s}\) the recourse decision in scenario \(s\). Let \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^k\) be first-stage data. For each \(s\in S\), let \(q_s\in\mathbb R^{m_s}\), \(W_s\in\mathbb R^{\ell_s\times m_s}\), \(T_s\in\mathbb R^{\ell_s\times n}\), and \(h_s\in\mathbb R^{\ell_s}\) be recourse data. The two-stage linear stochastic program has the extensive form \[\min_{x,(y_s)_{s\in S}}\ c^{\mathsf T}x+\sum_{s\in S}p_s q_s^{\mathsf T}y_s\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\quad x\geq0,\quad W_s y_s=h_s-T_sx,\quad y_s\geq0\quad\text{for every }s\in S.\] The single shared variable \(x\) enforces first-stage nonanticipativity, while \(y_s\) may depend on the realized scenario. This finite deterministic program has the same feasible policies and expected objective as the corresponding two-stage model with these data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extensive form uses one common first-stage decision and separate probability-weighted recourse variables and constraints for each finite scenario.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(p_s>0\), and \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\).
The displayed matrices, vectors, and decision variables have the stated finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed deterministic program is equivalent to the finite-scenario two-stage linear stochastic program with the stated data.

notation.meaning: second-stage recourse decision in scenario s
scenario-s recourse constraint and objective data

knowledge_statements.title: Multistage Extensive Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-indexed deterministic equivalent on a finite scenario tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let stages be \(t=0,\ldots,T\), with scenario-tree node sets \(\mathcal N_t\), parent map \(a(n)\), and node probabilities \(p_n\). Assign decision \(x_n\in X_n\) to each node. The multistage extensive form is
\[
\min_{(x_n)}\ \sum_{t=0}^{T}\sum_{n\in\mathcal N_t}p_n c_n^{\mathsf T}x_n
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
W_nx_n+T_nx_{a(n)}\le h_n\quad(n\ne n_0),
\]
together with the root constraints. Because every node has one decision shared by all scenarios passing through it, node indexing enforces nonanticipativity. An equivalent leaf-scenario formulation duplicates decisions and imposes equality between copies having identical histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extensive form assigns one decision to each scenario-tree node, couples it only to its parent, and thereby enforces nonanticipativity across scenarios sharing the same history.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal N=\bigcup_{t=0}^{T}\mathcal N_t\) is a finite rooted scenario tree.
\(p_n\ge0\), with child probabilities conditionally consistent with their parent.
All decision sets and constraint dimensions are finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The stochastic program is represented by one finite deterministic optimization problem with node-shared decisions.}\)

children.title: Block-Angular Geometry
children.top_down_role: Scenario-separated deterministic-equivalent structure coupled through shared decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Angular Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage arrowhead sparsity after grouping variables by scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For first-stage variables \(x\) and scenario variables \(y_s\), order columns as \((x,y_1,\ldots,y_S)\). If scenario \(s\) has constraints \(T_sx+W_sy_s=h_s\) and no constraint contains both \(y_s\) and \(y_r\) for \(s\ne r\), then the coupling matrix has block-angular form
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
T_1&W_1&0&\cdots&0\\
T_2&0&W_2&\cdots&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
T_S&0&0&\cdots&W_S
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Deleting the shared \(x\)-columns separates \(A\) into independent diagonal scenario blocks; hence all cross-scenario dependence is mediated by the first-stage block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After scenario-wise ordering, recourse blocks are diagonal and interact only through shared first-stage columns; removing those columns separates the scenarios.
assumptions_latex: \(S<\infty\).
Each recourse variable \(y_s\) occurs only in scenario-\(s\) constraints.
The first-stage vector \(x\) is common to every scenario.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is block-angular, and removing its shared first-stage columns yields scenario-separable diagonal blocks.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical two-stage block-angular matrix structure
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property accurately describes two-stage block-angular sparsity, but the matrix characterization and separator interpretation lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Staircase Geometry
children.top_down_role: Stage-linked deterministic-equivalent structure induced by temporal dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Staircase Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parent-child sparsity of a node-ordered multistage extensive form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Order scenario-tree variables by nondecreasing stage and place each node constraint in the row block of that node. Suppose the row block for every nonroot node \(n\) contains only \(x_n\) and its parent decision \(x_{a(n)}\). Then its nonzero blocks satisfy
\[
A_{n,m}\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ m\in\{n,a(n)\}.
\]
Consequently the extensive-form matrix has a block lower-staircase pattern: diagonal blocks describe local node constraints, while off-diagonal blocks connect consecutive stages along tree arcs. Removing all blocks joining stages \(t-1\) and \(t\) separates the descendant subtrees rooted at stage \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stage ordering produces diagonal node blocks plus parent-child blocks below them. Cutting the blocks between two consecutive stages separates all descendant subtrees.
assumptions_latex: The scenario tree is finite and rooted.
Every dynamic constraint couples a node only to itself and its parent.
Variables and constraint rows are ordered by nondecreasing stage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) has tree-staircase sparsity, with separators formed by consecutive-stage coupling blocks.

notation.meaning: matrix block in node-n rows and node-m columns

children.title: Two-Stage Block Coupling
children.top_down_role: Coupling patterns connecting first-stage decisions to scenario-specific recourse blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Block Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario recourse blocks coupled through one common first-stage vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For scenarios \(s=1,\ldots,S\) with probabilities \(p_s\), the two-stage deterministic equivalent is
\[
\min_{x,y_1,\ldots,y_S}\ c^{\mathsf T}x+\sum_{s=1}^{S}p_s q_s^{\mathsf T}y_s
\]
subject to
\[
Ax=b,\qquad T_sx+W_sy_s=h_s\quad(s=1,\ldots,S),
\]
and the specified domains of \(x\) and \(y_s\). Conditional on a fixed \(x\), both the objective contribution and feasibility constraints separate by scenario. Thus \(x\) is the sole structural coupling block, while each \(y_s\) belongs to an independent recourse block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common first-stage decision enters every scenario constraint, while each recourse decision remains scenario-local and becomes independent once the first-stage decision is fixed.
assumptions_latex: \(S<\infty\) and \(p_s\ge0\) with \(\sum_{s=1}^{S}p_s=1\).
No recourse variable \(y_s\) occurs in another scenario's constraints.
All displayed products have compatible finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) couples the scenario blocks, and fixing \(x\) makes the recourse subproblems separable.

children.title: Multistage Staircase Coupling
children.top_down_role: Coupling patterns connecting decisions across successive information stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Multistage Staircase Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-arc coupling between consecutive stages in the deterministic equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_n\) be the decision at scenario-tree node \(n\), and let \(a(n)\) be its parent. A multistage staircase coupling is represented by constraints
\[
W_nx_n+T_nx_{a(n)}=h_n\qquad(n\ne n_0),
\]
with root constraints depending only on \(x_{n_0}\). Under stage ordering, every row block has a diagonal nonzero block \(W_n\) and at most one earlier-stage block \(T_n\). Distinct subtrees share no variables after their common ancestral decisions are fixed. Equivalently, ancestral decisions form separators whose removal decomposes the remaining extensive form into descendant-subtree problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each node constraint links its decision to its parent's decision. Fixing ancestral decisions separates distinct descendant subtrees.
assumptions_latex: The scenario tree has finitely many nodes.
Each constraint links only a node and its immediate parent.
One decision vector is shared by all paths passing through a node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic equivalent has consecutive-stage tree-staircase coupling and decomposes across subtrees after ancestral decisions are fixed.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scenario-tree extensive forms couple node rows to immediate ancestors
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is internally consistent and matches the leaf, but the tree-staircase and ancestral-separator claims have no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Extensive-Form Scaling Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage-size boundary induced by explicit scenario-tree enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a scenario tree with node set \(\mathcal N\), node decision dimensions \(d_n\), constraint counts \(m_n\), and local coupling blocks containing \(z_n\) nonzeros, an explicit node-indexed extensive form requires
\[
D=\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}d_n\quad\text{variables},\qquad
M=\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}m_n\quad\text{constraints},
\]
and \(O(\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}z_n)\) matrix storage. For a full \(b\)-ary tree through stage \(T\),
\[
|\mathcal N|=\sum_{t=0}^{T}b^t=\frac{b^{T+1}-1}{b-1}
\]
when \(b>1\). With uniformly bounded positive block dimensions, explicit formulation size is therefore \(\Theta(b^T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit extensive-form size is linear in the number of tree nodes, but a full branching tree has exponentially many nodes in its horizon.
assumptions_latex: The formulation stores every scenario-tree node and its local matrix blocks explicitly.
The branching factor is constant \(b>1\).
Node block dimensions are bounded above and below by positive constants for the asymptotic claim.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit full-tree storage and formulation size grow as \(\Theta(b^T)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-tree counting and sparse explicit-storage accounting
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counting argument and exponential full-tree scaling bound are precise under the stated assumptions, but no source supports the formulation-size and storage claims.

children.title: Finite-Distribution Approximation Method Family
children.top_down_role: Generation, bounding, compression, and refinement of finite uncertainty models.

knowledge_statements.title: Monte Carlo Scenario Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent sampling of an uncertainty distribution into an empirical measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a probability law \(P\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), sample size \(N\), and a random-number generator. Initialize an empty scenario list. For \(i=1,\ldots,N\), generate independent \(U_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^d)\), set \(\xi_i=G(U_i)\) for a measurable transform satisfying \(G_{\#}\lambda=P\), and assign weight \(p_i=1/N\). Output
\[
\widehat P_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\xi_i}.
\]
For every \(P\)-integrable function \(f\), the scenario estimate is \(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(\xi_i)\); repeated sampled values may either remain separate or be merged by summing their weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Draw independent samples from the uncertainty law, give them equal weights, and output their empirical distribution as the finite scenario approximation.
assumptions_latex: A measurable sampling transform \(G\) for \(P\) is available.
The generated uniforms are independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat P_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\xi_i}\) is the generated finite scenario distribution.

notation.meaning: pushforward of uniform measure under G

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Monte Carlo Scenario Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equal-weight scenarios obtained by transforming low-discrepancy points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a target law \(P\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), a deterministic low-discrepancy point set \(u_1,\ldots,u_N\in[0,1]^d\), and a measurable transport \(G\) satisfying \(G_{\#}\lambda=P\). For each \(i=1,
\ldots,N\), set \(\xi_i=G(u_i)\) and \(p_i=1/N\). Output
\[
P_N^{\mathrm{qmc}}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\xi_i}.
\]
If randomized quasi-Monte Carlo is requested, first apply a measure-preserving randomization to the entire point set, then use the same transformation and weighting. The approximation of \(\mathbb E_P[f(\xi)]\) is \(N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(\xi_i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transform a low-discrepancy point set into samples from the target law, assign equal weights, and use the resulting discrete measure as the scenario distribution.
assumptions_latex: The point set lies in \([0,1]^d\) and has a specified low-discrepancy construction.
A measurable transport \(G\) with \(G_{\#}\lambda=P\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_N^{\mathrm{qmc}}\) is an equal-weight finite approximation of \(P\) generated from structured points.

notation.meaning: transport from uniform measure to P

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard pushforward construction for quasi-Monte Carlo integration
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pushforward construction is coherent and appropriately classified as an algorithm, but no citation supports the low-discrepancy or randomized quasi-Monte Carlo procedure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasi-Monte Carlo sequences and star discrepancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines low-discrepancy sequences for uniform scenario generation, compares anchored and unrestricted rectangular discrepancy, and records the valid univariate Wasserstein bound and the absence of an unrestricted general comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\widetilde\xi_i\in[0,1]^m\), let \(\widetilde P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{\widetilde\xi_i}\). Its star discrepancy is \[D^*(\widetilde P_n,U)=\sup_{u\in[0,1]^m}\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1_{[0,u]}(\widetilde\xi_i)-\prod_{j=1}^m u_j\right|.\] The sequence is quasi-Monte Carlo when there is \(C>0\) such that \(D^*(\widetilde P_n,U)\le C(\log n)^m/n\) for every \(n\ge2\). If \(D\) denotes discrepancy over all axis-aligned rectangles, then \(D^*\le D\le2^mD^*\). No unrestricted general comparison with Wasserstein distance holds. In dimension one, \[d_1(\widetilde P_n,U[0,1])=\int_0^1|\widetilde G_n(u)-u|\,du\le D^*(\widetilde P_n,U[0,1]).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence in the unit cube is quasi-Monte Carlo when its anchored-rectangle discrepancy decays at most as C(log n)^m/n. Unrestricted rectangular discrepancy lies between the star discrepancy and 2^m times that discrepancy. Wasserstein distance is not generally controlled without additional hypotheses; in one dimension on the unit interval, W1 is at most the star discrepancy.
assumptions_latex: m\in\mathbb N
n\ge2
\widetilde\xi_i\in[0,1]^m
\widetilde P_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{\widetilde\xi_i}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^*(\widetilde P_n,U)\le C\frac{(\log n)^m}{n},\qquad D^*\le D\le2^mD^*,\qquad d_1(\widetilde P_n,U[0,1])\le D^*\ \text{when }m=1.
