children.title: Metric Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model features governing the suitability of each probability metric.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection principle for finite-distribution approximation; uniform observable-class control requires an explicit domination or regularity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose the probability metric according to the convergence and stability required of the model-relevant observables. If only convergence of \(\int_S f\,dP_n\) for each bounded continuous \(f:S\to\mathbb R\) is required, a Fortet–Mourier metric that metrizes weak convergence is sufficient. Uniform control over a class \(\mathcal F\) requires an additional bound relating \(\mathcal F\) to the metric's test-function class. If relevant continuous observables have growth controlled by \(1+d(\cdot,x_0)^p\) and their stability requires convergence of \(p\)-th moments, use \(W_p\) on \(\mathcal P_p(S)\). A weaker topology need not control the required model values, whereas a stronger topology imposes additional approximation requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use Fortet–Mourier distance for pointwise weak-law effects, require explicit test-class domination for uniform observable control, and use p-Wasserstein distance when model stability also requires p-th-moment control.
assumptions_latex: \((S,d)\) is Polish.
The approximation objective specifies whether observable convergence is pointwise over bounded continuous functions, uniform over a stated class, or dependent on \(p\)-th moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The required mode of observable stability determines whether weak convergence, explicit test-class domination, or \(W_p\)-convergence is appropriate.

notation.meaning: p-Wasserstein distance on probability measures with finite p-th moment
probability measures on S with finite p-th moment

children.title: Model-Induced Metrics
children.top_down_role: Probability metrics tailored to decision-model sensitivity.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a decision set and \(Q:X\times S\to\mathbb R\) is integrable under every law considered.
The displayed supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_Q\) measures exactly the largest distributional change visible through the model's decision-indexed costs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral probability pseudometric generated by a stochastic optimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For probability laws \(P\) and \(P'\) on \(S\), define
\[
d_Q(P,P'):=\sup_{x\in X}\left|\int_S Q(x,\xi)\,dP(\xi)-\int_S Q(x,\xi)\,dP'(\xi)\right|.
\]
This is a pseudometric on the laws for which all displayed expectations exist. It becomes a metric precisely when the family \(\{Q(x,\cdot):x\in X\}\) separates those laws. In all cases, \(d_Q(P,P')=0\) means that every fixed feasible decision has the same expected cost under \(P\) and \(P'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model-induced metric compares laws only through expected costs generated by feasible decisions; it is a true metric when those costs separate laws.
knowledge_statements.title: Model-Induced Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and model-induced pseudometric formula fit the leaf, but no source supports this precise construction or its separation characterization.

children.title: Minimal-Information Metrics
children.top_down_role: Probability comparisons based on restricted information classes.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is a nonempty class of measurable, integrable model-relevant functions on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathcal F}\) is the canonical integral probability pseudometric retaining exactly the distinctions observable through \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimality is relative to a prescribed information class and its induced observational equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
d_{\mathcal F}(P,P'):=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\int_S f\,dP-\int_S f\,dP'\right|,
\]
whenever this supremum is finite, and define \(P\sim_{\mathcal F}P'\) when all expectations indexed by \(\mathcal F\) agree. Then \(d_{\mathcal F}\) is a pseudometric on laws and a metric on the quotient by \(\sim_{\mathcal F}\). Any law approximation satisfying \(d_{\mathcal F}(P_n,P)\to0\) preserves every expectation in \(\mathcal F\) uniformly; distinctions inside one equivalence class are deliberately discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal-information metric distinguishes two laws only when some prescribed model-relevant observable has a different expectation.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Information Metrics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integral probability pseudometric and quotient interpretation are coherent, but the claimed canonical minimal-information role requires a specifically located source.

children.title: Decision-Relevance Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric distinctions weighted by their effect on stochastic-program behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(d_{\mathcal F}\) is finite on a class \(\mathcal P\) of probability laws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quotient \(\mathcal P/{\sim_{\mathcal F}}\), equipped with \(d_{\mathcal F}\), is the geometry of decision-relevant distributional information.

notation.meaning: quotient space of observationally equivalent laws

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient geometry induced by a specified class of decision-relevant observables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\sim_{\mathcal F}P'\) mean \(d_{\mathcal F}(P,P')=0\). The decision-relevance geometry is the quotient
\[
\mathcal G_{\mathcal F}:=\mathcal P/{\sim_{\mathcal F}},
\qquad
\bar d_{\mathcal F}([P]_{\mathcal F},[P']_{\mathcal F}):=d_{\mathcal F}(P,P').
\]
The quotient distance is well defined and is a metric. Hence two distributions occupy the same point exactly when no observable in \(\mathcal F\) distinguishes them, and metric neighborhoods consist of laws producing uniformly similar values for all observables in \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision-relevance geometry is the metric quotient obtained by identifying laws that agree on every model-relevant expected observable.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Relevance Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits and the metric quotient is mathematically coherent, but the decision-relevance interpretation has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Information-Class Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Changes in metric discrimination under richer or poorer observable information.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_1\subseteq a\mathcal F_2\) for some \(a>0\).
All defining expectations and suprema are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Enlarging or rescaling the information class strengthens the induced metric and its sensitivity to distributional perturbations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity and domination for integral probability metrics generated by nested information classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\mathcal F_1\subseteq a\mathcal F_2:=\{af:f\in\mathcal F_2\}\), then for every pair of admissible laws,
\[
d_{\mathcal F_1}(P,P')\le a\,d_{\mathcal F_2}(P,P').
\]
Consequently, convergence under \(d_{\mathcal F_2}\) implies convergence under \(d_{\mathcal F_1}\). If the inclusion is strict, the converse may fail because \(\mathcal F_2\) can distinguish distributional directions invisible to \(\mathcal F_1\). Thus sensitivity is determined jointly by the size, scaling, and separation power of the selected information class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger information class yields a stronger metric: it detects at least every distributional difference detected by a smaller class.
knowledge_statements.title: Information-Class Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The domination inequality and convergence implication are standard, and the property kind fits, but no source is cited for the information-class sensitivity claim.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are probability laws on finite rooted scenario trees with horizon \(T\).
The path cost \(c(x_{1:T},y_{1:T})\) is nonnegative and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nested distance is the minimum expected path cost over couplings that respect both scenario-tree filtrations.

notation.meaning: set of bicausal couplings of the two path laws
nested transport distance induced by cost c

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon, finite-scenario-tree primal formulation using bicausal couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A coupling \(\pi\) of \(P\) and \(Q\) is bicausal when, at every \(t<T\), the conditional law of \(Y_{1:t}\) given \(X_{1:T}\) depends only on \(X_{1:t}\), and symmetrically the conditional law of \(X_{1:t}\) given \(Y_{1:T}\) depends only on \(Y_{1:t}\). The nested distance associated with \(c\) is
\[
d_{\mathrm N,c}(P,Q):=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{bc}}(P,Q)}\int c(x_{1:T},y_{1:T})\,d\pi(x_{1:T},y_{1:T}).
\]
For finite trees the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested distance optimally couples two scenario trees while forbidding either tree's future from influencing the other's past.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Distance for Scenario Trees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but a generic nonnegative finite path cost yields a bicausal transport value, not necessarily a metric. A source must establish the intended nested-distance normalization and the conditions on the cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Backward Linear-Programming Computation of Nested Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic-programming algorithm for computing the nested distance and an associated leaf coupling of two finite scenario-tree processes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite rooted tree processes \(\mathbb P\) and \(\widetilde{\mathbb P}\) with horizon \(T\), initialize every leaf pair \((i,j)\) by
\[
\mathbb{dl}_T^r(i,j)=d\!\left((\xi_{i_0},\ldots,\xi_i),(\widetilde\xi_{j_0},\ldots,\widetilde\xi_j)\right)^r.
\]
For \(t=T-1,\ldots,0\) and every pair \((k,l)\) of stage-\(t\) nodes from the respective trees, solve
\[
\mathbb{dl}_t^r(k,l)=\min_{\pi\ge 0}\sum_{i'\in k^+,\,j'\in l^+}\pi(i',j'\mid k,l)\,\mathbb{dl}_{t+1}^r(i',j')
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{j'\in l^+}\pi(i',j'\mid k,l)=Q(i')\quad(i'\in k^+),\qquad
\sum_{i'\in k^+}\pi(i',j'\mid k,l)=\widetilde Q(j')\quad(j'\in l^+).
\]
Then
\[
\mathbb{dl}_r(\mathbb P,\widetilde{\mathbb P})^r=\mathbb{dl}_0^r(1,1),
\]
and composing the optimal conditional transport plans along each paired root-to-leaf history gives the associated leaf transport plan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each leaf pair the powered distance between its two complete histories. Proceed backward through the trees, solving at each pair of same-stage nodes a transportation linear program with the nodes' conditional successor distributions as marginals and the next-stage values as costs. The value at the root pair is the powered nested distance, and the optimal conditional couplings compose into a leaf transport plan.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb P\text{ and }\widetilde{\mathbb P}\text{ are finite rooted tree processes with stages }0,\ldots,T.
k\in\mathcal N_t\text{ and }l\in\widetilde{\mathcal N}_t\text{ are nodes of the respective trees, with successor sets }k^+\text{ and }l^+.
Q(i')\text{ and }\widetilde Q(j')\text{ are the respective conditional successor probabilities.
\mathbb{dl}_T^r(i,j)=d\!\left((\xi_{i_0},\ldots,\xi_i),(\widetilde\xi_{j_0},\ldots,\widetilde\xi_j)\right)^r\text{ is defined for every leaf pair.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb{dl}_r(\mathbb P,\widetilde{\mathbb P})^r=\mathbb{dl}_0^r(1,1),\quad\text{and the optimal stagewise conditional couplings compose into a leaf transport plan.}

children.title: Dual Representations of Nested Distance
children.top_down_role: Dual viewpoints for nested-distance comparison of multistage laws.

assumptions_latex: The two scenario trees and horizon are finite.
The bicausal transport problem is written as \(\min\{\langle c,\pi\rangle:A\pi=b,\ \pi\ge0\}\) with a nonempty feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nested-distance primal equals its finite-dimensional linear-programming dual.

notation.meaning: linear operator encoding marginals and bicausality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-tree linear-programming dual; normalization depends on the chosen constraint encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\pi=b\) encode the two marginal constraints and all finite-tree bicausality constraints. Then
\[
d_{\mathrm N,c}(P,Q)
=
\min_{\pi\ge0,\,A\pi=b}\langle c,\pi\rangle
=
\max_{z:\,A^*z\le c}\langle b,z\rangle.
\]
The components of \(z\) associated with marginal constraints act as path potentials, while those associated with conditional nonanticipativity constraints are adapted correction terms. Because the primal is a feasible finite linear program with finite objective, both optima are attained and there is no duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On finite scenario trees, nested distance is a linear program whose dual uses marginal potentials and adapted multipliers for bicausality constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Representations of Nested Distance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Finite-dimensional LP duality is plausible and the duality kind fits, but the abstract operator does not expose the exact bicausality constraints or justify the stated interpretation of its multipliers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Projection Operators for Nested-Distance Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise conditional-expectation operators used to formulate nested-distance dual constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(0\le t\le T\), define linear operators
\[
\operatorname{proj}_t:L^1(\mathcal F_T\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_T)\to L^1(\mathcal F_t\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_T),\qquad
\widetilde{\operatorname{proj}}_t:L^1(\mathcal F_T\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_T)\to L^1(\mathcal F_T\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t)
\]
by their action on integrable product-form functions:
\[
\operatorname{proj}_t\bigl(\lambda(\mathrm{id})\mu(\widetilde{\mathrm{id}})\bigr)
=\mathbb E[\lambda\mid\mathcal F_t](\mathrm{id})\mu(\widetilde{\mathrm{id}}),
\]
\[
\widetilde{\operatorname{proj}}_t\bigl(\lambda(\mathrm{id})\mu(\widetilde{\mathrm{id}})\bigr)
=\lambda(\mathrm{id})\mathbb E[\mu\mid\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t](\widetilde{\mathrm{id}}),
\]
and extend them linearly to the product-space \(L^1\) domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first projection conditionally averages only the first coordinate at stage t, while the second projection conditionally averages only the second coordinate. Each leaves the other coordinate unchanged and is extended linearly from product-form functions.
assumptions_latex: 0\le t\le T
\lambda(\mathrm{id})\mu(\widetilde{\mathrm{id}})\in L^1(\mathcal F_T\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_T)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_t(\lambda\mu)=\mathbb E[\lambda\mid\mathcal F_t]\mu,\qquad \widetilde{\operatorname{proj}}_t(\lambda\mu)=\lambda\mathbb E[\mu\mid\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of the One-Sided Projection Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a stagewise conditional marginal condition and expectation invariance under the first-coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\pi\) be a measure on \(\Omega\times\widetilde\Omega\). The conditional marginal condition
\[
\pi\bigl(A\times\widetilde\Omega\mid\mathcal F_t\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t\bigr)=P(A\mid\mathcal F_t)
\quad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal F_T
\]
holds if and only if
\[
\mathbb E_\pi[\lambda]=\mathbb E_\pi[\operatorname{proj}_t\lambda]
\]
for every integrable \(\mathcal F_T\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t\)-measurable function \(\lambda\). Moreover, if \(\pi\) has first marginal \(P\), then
\[
\operatorname{proj}_t(\lambda)=\mathbb E_\pi[\lambda\mid\mathcal F_t\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_T].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measure satisfies the stage-t conditional first-marginal condition exactly when expectations of all integrable functions with terminal first-coordinate and stage-t second-coordinate information are unchanged by the first-coordinate projection. If its first marginal is P, the proposition additionally identifies that projection with the stated conditional expectation under the measure.
assumptions_latex: \pi\text{ is a measure on }\Omega\times\widetilde\Omega
0\le t\le T
\lambda\in L^1(\pi)\text{ is }\mathcal F_T\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t\text{-measurable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi(A\times\widetilde\Omega\mid\mathcal F_t\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t)=P(A\mid\mathcal F_t)\ \forall A\in\mathcal F_T\iff \mathbb E_\pi\lambda=\mathbb E_\pi\operatorname{proj}_t\lambda\ \forall\lambda;\quad \pi_1=P\Rightarrow \operatorname{proj}_t\lambda=\mathbb E_\pi[\lambda\mid\mathcal F_t\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal F}_T].

children.title: Martingale Representations of Nested Distance
children.top_down_role: Martingale-based viewpoints for multistage transport geometry.

assumptions_latex: The scenario trees have finite node sets and strictly positive probabilities on retained nodes.
Conditional nonanticipativity constraints are expressed nodewise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual corrections for nodewise bicausality constraints admit a finite martingale-difference representation.

notation.meaning: natural filtration of a scenario tree

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-tree martingale-difference form of dual nonanticipativity corrections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each tree, nodewise dual multipliers for conditional nonanticipativity can be centered with respect to the parent-node conditional probabilities. The resulting increments satisfy
\[
\mathbb E[\Delta M_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0,
\qquad t=1,\ldots,T,
\]
and their dual contribution can be written as a finite sum of predictable martingale transforms
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T H_{t-1}\Delta M_t.
\]
Conversely, every such centered finite-tree increment array defines a linear functional that vanishes on the corresponding nonanticipative consistency subspace. Thus the adapted correction part of the nested-distance dual may be parameterized by martingale differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After nodewise centering, dual multipliers enforcing nonanticipativity become martingale differences, and their adapted transforms supply the dual correction terms.
knowledge_statements.title: Martingale Representations of Nested Distance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf, but the claimed equivalence between centered nodewise multipliers and predictable martingale transforms depends on the exact constraint spaces and normalization and cannot be verified from the record.

children.title: Dual-Martingale Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between dual potentials plus martingale viewpoints.

assumptions_latex: A fixed finite-tree linear encoding of the bicausality constraints is used.
Dual multipliers are identified when they induce the same functional on coupling arrays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constraint multipliers modulo redundant directions correspond to martingale corrections modulo null increments.

notation.meaning: dual multiplier space for bicausality constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear correspondence after quotienting redundant finite-tree dual parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Centering nodewise bicausality multipliers defines a linear map \(\Phi:Z_{\mathrm{bc}}\to\mathcal M_0\). Its kernel consists exactly of multiplier arrays whose adjoint contribution to every coupling variable is zero. Consequently,
\[
Z_{\mathrm{bc}}/\ker\Phi\ \cong\ \operatorname{ran}\Phi\subseteq\mathcal M_0.
\]
Under a complete, nonredundant nodewise encoding, \(\operatorname{ran}\Phi=\mathcal M_0\). Hence the multiplier and martingale dual formulations have the same feasible inequalities and objective values, although their parameters need not be unique before quotienting null directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual constraint multipliers and martingale corrections represent the same functionals once redundant multipliers and null increments are identified.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Martingale Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind is reasonable, but the kernel characterization, surjectivity under a nonredundant encoding, and equality of the resulting dual formulations require an exact theorem and a defined constraint encoding.

children.title: Representation Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model classes or information structures supporting each representation.

assumptions_latex: The primal nested-distance problem is feasible.
In the finite regime, both scenario trees have finitely many nodes and the cost is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite trees guarantee attained primal and dual representations; infinite models require additional topological and integrability hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-tree validity is definitive; the stated infinite-space requirements are necessary review boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite scenario trees, feasibility and finiteness of \(c\) suffice for primal attainment, linear-programming strong duality, and finite martingale reparameterization of the adapted dual terms. For general path spaces, the analogous representations require at least a closed or suitably compact bicausal feasible set, a lower-semicontinuous cost bounded below with adequate moment control, and integrable dual potentials and martingale corrections. Without closedness, uniform integrability, or the required moment bounds, minimizers may fail to exist and an unrestricted pointwise dual formula may exhibit a gap or undefined expectations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All representations are valid on finite trees; general path spaces additionally need closedness, lower semicontinuity, moment control, and integrable dual variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Validity Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits, and the finite-LP boundary is plausible, but the infinite-space claims use non-specific compactness, closedness, integrability, and moment hypotheses. Exact representation and duality theorems are required.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty decision set common to both probability laws.
For every \(x\in X\), the map \(\xi\mapsto F(x,\xi)\) is measurable and \(L\)-Lipschitz, with the same finite \(L\).
Both laws have finite first moments, and their objective infima are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert v(P)-v(Q)\rvert\le L W_1(P,Q)\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value under probability law P
First Wasserstein distance on the uncertainty space
Uniform Lipschitz modulus of the integrand in uncertainty

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform Lipschitz continuity and Kantorovich-Rubinstein control give the standard single-stage stability bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-stage expected-value model with first-Wasserstein perturbations and a common feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be probability laws on a Polish metric space \((\Xi,d)\). Define \(f_P(x):=\int F(x,\xi)\,P(d\xi)\) and \(v(P):=\inf_{x\in X}f_P(x)\). If \(\lvert F(x,\xi)-F(x,\zeta)\rvert\le Ld(\xi,\zeta)\) for every \(x\in X\) and all \(\xi,\zeta\in\Xi\), then \(\lvert f_P(x)-f_Q(x)\rvert\le L W_1(P,Q)\) uniformly in \(x\). Consequently,
\[
\lvert v(P)-v(Q)\rvert\le L W_1(P,Q).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform Lipschitz bound on scenario costs makes the single-stage optimal value Lipschitz continuous in the first Wasserstein distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Stage Probability-Metric Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-stage Wasserstein bound is mathematically precise and fits the stability-property container, but no inspectable authoritative citation supports it.

assumptions_latex: The horizon \(T\) is finite and admissible decisions are nonanticipative with respect to the canonical filtration.
The total policy cost is integrable and has a uniform adapted Lipschitz modulus \(L\).
The two process laws admit the same action and feasibility structure with relatively complete recourse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert v(P)-v(Q)\rvert\le L d_{\mathrm{nest}}(P,Q)\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value for the multistage process law P
Nested distance defined through bicausal couplings
Adapted Lipschitz modulus of total policy cost

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nested distance is designed to control multistage stochastic programs while respecting conditional information
exact adapted-Lipschitz and recourse hypotheses require an authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon process laws compared by nested distance under common nonanticipative recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be laws of processes \(\xi_{1:T}\) on a finite-horizon path space. Let \(d_{\mathrm{nest}}(P,Q)\) be the infimum, over bicausal couplings \(\pi\), of \(\int c(\xi_{1:T},\zeta_{1:T})\,d\pi\). Suppose feasible policies are nonanticipative, relatively complete recourse holds under both laws, and policy transfer along every bicausal coupling yields total-cost discrepancy at most \(L\int c\,d\pi\). Then the corresponding optimal values satisfy
\[
\lvert v(P)-v(Q)\rvert\le Ld_{\mathrm{nest}}(P,Q).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested distance controls multistage optimal values when cost and recourse are stable under bicausal, information-preserving transport.
knowledge_statements.title: Multistage Nested-Distance Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the multistage nested-distance container, but the policy-transfer and adapted-Lipschitz hypotheses are framework-dependent and require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Value Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic perturbation lemma underlying probability-metric optimal-value bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be nonempty and let \(f,g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) have finite infima. If \(\sup_{x\in X}\lvert f(x)-g(x)\rvert\le\varepsilon<\infty\), define \(v_f:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(v_g:=\inf_{x\in X}g(x)\). Then \(v_f\le v_g+\varepsilon\) and \(v_g\le v_f+\varepsilon\), and hence
\[
\lvert v_f-v_g\rvert\le\varepsilon.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two finite real-valued objectives on the same nonempty decision set, a uniform objective perturbation of at most epsilon changes the optimal value by at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty and common to the two optimization problems.
The functions \(f,g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) have finite infima.
Their uniform discrepancy satisfies \(\sup_{x\in X}\lvert f(x)-g(x)\rvert\le\varepsilon<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\inf_{x\in X}f(x)-\inf_{x\in X}g(x)\rvert\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Optimal values of f and g

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the infimum functional is nonexpansive under the uniform norm for finite real-valued objectives

assumptions_latex: The reference solution set \(S_f:=\operatorname{argmin}_X f\) is nonempty.
For some \(\alpha>0\) and \(p>0\), \(f(x)\ge v_f+\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S_f)^p\) on \(X\).
\(\sup_{x\in X}\lvert f(x)-g(x)\rvert\le\varepsilon\), and \(x_g\) is \(\delta\)-optimal for \(g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_g,S_f)\le((2\varepsilon+\delta)/\alpha)^{1/p}\).

notation.meaning: Minimizer set of the reference objective
Growth constants away from the reference solution set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform objective error combined with a growth condition yields quantitative solution-set stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer stability of approximate minimizers under uniform perturbation and polynomial growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_f:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\), let \(S_f:=\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\neq\varnothing\), and suppose \(f(x)\ge v_f+\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S_f)^p\) for every \(x\in X\), where \(\alpha,p>0\). If \(\sup_{x\in X}\lvert f(x)-g(x)\rvert\le\varepsilon\) and \(g(x_g)\le\inf_X g+\delta\), then
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x_g,S_f)\le\left(\frac{2\varepsilon+\delta}{\alpha}\right)^{1/p}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform objective error plus growth away from the reference minimizers bounds how far any approximate perturbed solution can move.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Set Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The growth condition and uniform-error calculation support the stated solution-set bound, and property is an appropriate kind, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Metric Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where probability-metric proximity fails to control model behavior.

assumptions_latex: Probability laws are defined on \(\mathbb{R}\) with its usual metric.
The tested stochastic objective contains the unbounded function \(h(\xi)=\xi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak convergence alone does not imply convergence of the tested expectations or optimal values.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit escaping-mass sequence separates weak convergence from first-moment convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of weak-metric stability for objectives sensitive to unbounded moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P_n:=(1-n^{-1})\delta_0+n^{-1}\delta_n\) and \(P:=\delta_0\), one has \(P_n\Rightarrow P\) because \(\int\varphi\,dP_n\to\varphi(0)\) for every bounded continuous \(\varphi\). Nevertheless, for \(h(\xi):=\xi\),
\[
\int h\,dP_n=1\quad\text{for every }n,
\qquad
\int h\,dP=0.
\]
Thus a metric that metrizes only weak convergence cannot control stochastic objectives with linear growth unless an additional moment or uniform-integrability condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vanishing amount of probability escaping to infinity preserves weak convergence but prevents convergence of an unbounded expected cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The escaping-mass example correctly identifies a weak-metric failure boundary, but the record supplies no cited source or locator.

children.title: Information-Structure Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where altered filtrations invalidate multistage stability conclusions.

assumptions_latex: The model has two stages, and the second-stage action may depend on the observed first-stage signal.
Path laws are compared by ordinary Wasserstein distance on \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary path-space convergence need not preserve conditional information or multistage values.

notation.meaning: Informative two-stage law with a vanishing first-stage signal
Limit law in which the first-stage signal is uninformative
Best squared prediction loss after observing the first coordinate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit signal-collapse family exhibits discontinuity of conditional information under ordinary transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage signal collapse under a metric that ignores filtration structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_\varepsilon:=\tfrac12\delta_{(-\varepsilon,-1)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(\varepsilon,1)}\) and \(P_0:=\tfrac12\delta_{(0,-1)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(0,1)}\). Then \(W_1(P_\varepsilon,P_0)\le\varepsilon\). For \(V(P):=\inf_a\mathbb{E}_P[(a(X)-Y)^2]\), where \(a\) is measurable in the observed first-stage signal \(X\), one has
\[
V(P_\varepsilon)=0\quad(\varepsilon>0),
\qquad V(P_0)=1.
\]
Hence ordinary path-space proximity does not preserve the decision-relevant filtration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vanishing signal can remain perfectly informative before the limit, so ordinary path distance converges while the multistage value jumps.
knowledge_statements.title: Information-Structure Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signal-collapse example and value discontinuity are correct and fit a failure-boundary container, but no inspectable citation is provided.

children.title: Metric-Information Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Alignment required between probability geometry plus staged information.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{P}\) is a class of process laws equipped with their canonical filtrations.
\(\mathcal{G}\) is the decision-relevant class of nonanticipative policy costs.
The metric \(d\) is defined on \(\mathcal{P}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility means \(d(P_n,P)\to0\) implies uniform convergence of expectations over \(\mathcal{G}\), with admissible information preserved.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a stability metric must control the objective test class and the information available to policies
the precise compatibility notion varies across stochastic-programming frameworks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-relative compatibility criterion for probability metrics on filtered process laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A metric \(d\) on a class \(\mathcal{P}\) of filtered process laws is compatible with a decision class \(\mathcal{G}\) if, whenever \(d(P_n,P)\to0\),
\[
\sup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\left\lvert\mathbb{E}_{P_n}[G]-\mathbb{E}_{P}[G]\right\rvert\to0,
\]
and the comparison identifies only policies having the same nonanticipative information pattern. Under this condition, taking infima over the common policy class preserves value convergence. Compatibility is therefore relative to both the growth and regularity of \(\mathcal{G}\) and the filtration encoded by \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability metric is decision-compatible only when it controls relevant policy costs and preserves the information available when decisions are made.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Information Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is a suitable content kind, but the proposed compatibility notion and its information-preservation clause are framework-dependent and need a precise authoritative source.

children.title: Single-Stage Transfer Failures
children.top_down_role: Failures arising when single-stage metric guarantees are transferred to multistage models.

assumptions_latex: The second-stage decision observes the first coordinate of a two-stage process.
A proposed transfer uses only ordinary Wasserstein proximity of complete paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A single-stage Wasserstein stability argument cannot generally be transferred to this multistage problem.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit two-stage family isolates why a single-stage transport estimate fails under endogenous information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to transferring ordinary single-stage Wasserstein bounds to nonanticipative multistage decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P_\varepsilon:=\tfrac12\delta_{(-\varepsilon,-1)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(\varepsilon,1)}\) and \(P_0:=\tfrac12\delta_{(0,-1)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(0,1)}\), ordinary path-space Wasserstein distance tends to zero. Yet, with measurable decisions \(a(X)\),
\[
\inf_a\mathbb{E}_{P_\varepsilon}[(a(X)-Y)^2]=0,
\qquad
\inf_a\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[(a(X)-Y)^2]=1.
\]
The pointwise integrand is regular in \(Y\), but the admissible optimizer depends discontinuously on the information carried by \(X\); therefore the single-stage transfer argument is invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary Wasserstein convergence of paths does not transfer a single-stage value bound when admissible decisions depend on changing conditional information.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Stage Transfer Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit counterexample correctly demonstrates failure of single-stage transfer and the selected content kind fits the leaf, but it lacks a cited source.

children.title: Marginal Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Accuracy of individual uncertainty-component distributions.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are probability laws on the product space \(\prod_{j=1}^m\Xi_j\).
Each coordinate space \(\Xi_j\) is equipped with a chosen probability metric \(d_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Marginal fidelity at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is the condition \(\max_j d_j(P_j,Q_j)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Coordinate marginals of P and Q

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: marginal fidelity is naturally defined by coordinatewise discrepancies between projected laws
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise distributional fidelity for a finite-dimensional scenario model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a target law and \(Q\) a scenario-model law on \(\Xi:=\prod_{j=1}^m\Xi_j\). For the coordinate projection \(\pi_j\), define \(P_j:=P\circ\pi_j^{-1}\) and \(Q_j:=Q\circ\pi_j^{-1}\). Given probability metrics \(d_j\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the model has marginal fidelity at level \(\varepsilon\) when
\[
\max_{1\le j\le m}d_j(P_j,Q_j)\le\varepsilon.
\]
Exact marginal fidelity is the case \(\varepsilon=0\). This condition alone imposes no restriction on dependence among coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginal fidelity measures how closely every coordinate distribution of a scenario model matches the corresponding target marginal.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Fidelity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinatewise definition is coherent and fits the marginal-fidelity container, but no authoritative source and locator are supplied.

children.title: Dependence Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Accuracy of cross-sectional or temporal dependence structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence Fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Copula-based dependence fidelity under continuous marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be probability laws on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) with continuous univariate marginal distribution functions. Write \(F_P,F_Q\) for their joint distribution functions and \(F_{P,j},F_{Q,j}\) for their marginal distribution functions. Their unique copulas \(C_P\) and \(C_Q\) satisfy
\[
F_P(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=C_P\bigl(F_{P,1}(x_1),\ldots,F_{P,m}(x_m)\bigr)
\]
and the analogous identity for \(Q\). For a metric \(d_C\) on copulas and \(\eta\ge0\), dependence fidelity at level \(\eta\) means
\[
d_C(C_P,C_Q)\le\eta.
\]
Exact dependence fidelity means \(C_P=C_Q\), independently of whether the marginal laws agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For laws with continuous marginals, dependence fidelity compares their unique copulas using a selected copula metric, independently of marginal agreement.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are probability laws on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) with continuous univariate marginal distribution functions.
Dependence is represented by the unique copulas supplied by Sklar's theorem.
A metric \(d_C\) is fixed on the relevant class of copulas.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dependence fidelity at tolerance \(\eta\ge0\) is the condition \(d_C(C_P,C_Q)\le\eta\).

notation.meaning: Joint distribution functions of P and Q
Univariate marginal distribution functions of P and Q
Unique copulas of P and Q under continuous marginals

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: copulas separate dependence from continuous marginal distributions
authoritative source for Sklar's theorem and the selected diagnostic metric is required

children.title: Joint-Distribution Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Combined preservation of marginal behavior plus dependence patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint-Distribution Fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-law fidelity on the product uncertainty space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a target probability law and \(Q\) a scenario-model probability law on the same measurable product space \(\Xi\). Let \(d\) be a metric on the relevant class of joint laws. For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), joint-distribution fidelity at level \(\varepsilon\) is the condition
\[
d(P,Q)\le\varepsilon.
\]
Exact joint-distribution fidelity is the case \(d(P,Q)=0\), equivalently \(P=Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint-distribution fidelity measures the discrepancy between the complete target and scenario laws using a selected probability metric.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are probability laws on a common measurable product space \(\Xi\).
The function \(d\) is a metric on the relevant class of joint laws.
The tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Joint-distribution fidelity at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is the condition \(d(P,Q)\le\varepsilon\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: joint fidelity is a metric discrepancy between full target and scenario laws
the operational metric must be selected according to the downstream objective class

children.title: Marginal-Dependence Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Cases where fitting one distributional aspect degrades another.

assumptions_latex: All displayed random vectors are two-dimensional.
Marginal and dependence diagnostics are evaluated separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact fidelity in either component does not imply fidelity in the other component.

notation.meaning: Independent Bernoulli target and comonotone Bernoulli approximation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit finite and comonotone examples demonstrate independence of marginal and dependence fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of marginal accuracy from dependence accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be uniform on \(\{0,1\}^2\), and let \(Q:=\tfrac12\delta_{(0,0)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(1,1)}\). Both coordinates have the same Bernoulli marginal under \(P\) and \(Q\), yet \(P\) is independent while \(Q\) is comonotone; indeed \(\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=\tfrac12\). Conversely, if \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), the vectors \((U,U)\) and \((2U,2U)\) have the same comonotone dependence structure but different marginals. Thus neither marginal fidelity nor dependence fidelity alone guarantees joint fidelity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact marginals can coexist with wrong dependence, while exact dependence structure can coexist with wrong marginals; joint diagnostics must balance both.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal-Dependence Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both examples correctly separate marginal from dependence fidelity, and counterexample is appropriate for the tradeoff leaf, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Tail Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Accuracy of distributional behavior in extreme regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail Fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exceedance-probability diagnostic for a finite scenario approximation of a loss distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the target law of \(\xi\), let \(Q=\sum_{i=1}^N w_i\delta_{\xi_i}\) with \(w_i\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^Nw_i=1\), and fix a decision \(x\). For the loss \(L(x,\xi)\), define \(\overline F_P(t)=P\{L(x,\xi)>t\}\) and \(\overline F_Q(t)=\sum_{i=1}^Nw_i\mathbf 1\{L(x,\xi_i)>t\}\). Given a tail threshold \(u\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the scenario model has \((u,\varepsilon)\)-tail fidelity at \(x\) when \[\sup_{t\ge u}\left|\overline F_Q(t)-\overline F_P(t)\right|\le\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail fidelity requires scenario-weighted exceedance probabilities to approximate the true exceedance probabilities uniformly above a specified threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(L(x,\xi)\) is measurable under both \(P\) and \(Q\).
\(Q\) is a probability measure with finite support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{t\ge u}|\overline F_Q(t)-\overline F_P(t)|\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Target and finite scenario probability laws.
True and scenario exceedance functions of the loss.
Tail threshold and permitted absolute error.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform tail-probability error is a standard distributional fidelity diagnostic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent and fits Tail Fidelity, but no inspectable source supports this specific uniform exceedance-error formulation.

children.title: Rare-Event Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Coverage plus probability accuracy for low-frequency consequential outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Rare-Event Fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-probability diagnostic for designated rare-event classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the target law and \(Q=\sum_{i=1}^Nw_i\delta_{\xi_i}\) a finite scenario law. For a nonempty measurable event family \(\mathcal A\) satisfying \(P(A)>0\) for every \(A\in\mathcal A\), define the worst relative probability error by \[R_{\mathcal A}(P,Q)=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\frac{|Q(A)-P(A)|}{P(A)}.\] Given \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the scenario model has \(\varepsilon\)-rare-event fidelity on \(\mathcal A\) precisely when \(R_{\mathcal A}(P,Q)\le\varepsilon\). Events with \(P(A)=0\) are excluded because the relative error is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rare-event fidelity bounds relative, rather than absolute, probability error over a prescribed family of positive-probability rare events.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a measurable event family.
\(0<P(A)\) for every \(A\in\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\mathcal A}(P,Q)\le\varepsilon\).
review_flags: locator supports rare-event probability estimation; exact fidelity terminology requires review

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relative-error condition fits Rare-Event Fidelity, but the cited importance-sampling section does not clearly support this particular fidelity definition over an arbitrary event family.

children.title: Extreme-Scenario Coverage
children.top_down_role: Representation of consequential extreme outcomes within finite scenarios.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Scenario Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric coverage diagnostic restricted to a designated extreme subset of uncertainty space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Xi,d)\) be a metric uncertainty space, let \(E\subseteq\Xi\) be the designated extreme region, and let \(S=\{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\}\) be the scenario support. Its extreme-region covering radius is \[r_E(S)=\sup_{\xi\in E}\min_{1\le i\le N}d(\xi,\xi_i).\] For a prescribed resolution \(\rho\ge0\), the scenario set has \(\rho\)-extreme-scenario coverage of \(E\) when \(r_E(S)\le\rho\). This condition concerns support placement only; it does not certify that scenario weights reproduce probabilities within \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in the designated extreme region must lie within the chosen radius of at least one scenario.
assumptions_latex: \((\Xi,d)\) is a metric space.
\(E\) is nonempty and \(S\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_E(S)\le\rho\).

notation.meaning: Designated extreme subset of the uncertainty space.
Covering radius of the scenario support over the extreme region.

source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

review_flags: source is provisional for the covering-radius formulation

source_witnesses.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covering-radius condition is precise and appropriate for Extreme-Scenario Coverage. The cited sequential-maximin-design section is only indirect support and does not establish the extreme-region scenario diagnostic.

children.title: Tail-Mass Allocation
children.top_down_role: Probability mass assigned to extreme or rare scenario regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Mass Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-allocation diagnostic for a partition of the target distribution's tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_1,\ldots,T_K\) be pairwise disjoint measurable tail strata, let \(P\) be the target law, and let \(Q=\sum_{i=1}^N w_i\delta_{\xi_i}\) be the scenario law. Given tolerances \(\varepsilon_k\ge 0\), the scenario weights have admissible tail-mass allocation when \[\left|\sum_{i:\,\xi_i\in T_k}w_i-P(T_k)\right|\le\varepsilon_k\quad\text{for every }k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}.\] Consequently, for \(T=\bigcup_{k=1}^K T_k\), the total tail-mass error is at most \(\sum_{k=1}^K\varepsilon_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario weights must reproduce the target probability mass in every prescribed tail stratum, within stratum-specific tolerances; their total error over the union is bounded by the sum of those tolerances.
assumptions_latex: \(T_1,\ldots,T_K\) are pairwise disjoint and measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left|Q(T)-P(T)\right|\le\sum_{k=1}^K\varepsilon_k\).

notation.meaning: Probability weight assigned to scenario i.
Permitted mass error in tail stratum k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: partitionwise probability-mass matching is a standard discrete-approximation diagnostic

children.title: Scenario Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Structural mismatch between scenario models plus the relevant uncertainty process.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by systematic mismatch between target and scenario expectations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the operational uncertainty law, \(Q\) the scenario law, \(X\) the feasible set, and \(f:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) an integrable loss. For tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the scenario model is \(\varepsilon\)-misspecified for the objective class when \[\sup_{x\in X}\left|\mathbb E_P[f(x,\xi)]-\mathbb E_Q[f(x,\xi)]\right|>\varepsilon.\] If \(x_Q\in\arg\min_{x\in X}\mathbb E_Q[f(x,\xi)]\), misspecification is decision-relevant whenever \(\mathbb E_P[f(x_Q,\xi)]-\inf_{x\in X}\mathbb E_P[f(x,\xi)]\) exceeds the accepted regret tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Misspecification occurs when scenario expectations differ materially from operational expectations and may induce excessive true decision regret.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x,\cdot)\) is integrable under \(P\) and \(Q\) for every \(x\in X\).
The displayed infimum and scenario minimizer are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in X}|\mathbb E_P f(x,\xi)-\mathbb E_Q f(x,\xi)|>\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: A decision optimized under the scenario law.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform expectation mismatch directly formalizes distributional misspecification for an objective class

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expectation-discrepancy condition is a plausible failure boundary and the decision-regret qualification is appropriate, but no authoritative source supports the selected formalization or terminology.

children.title: Scenario Overfitting
children.top_down_role: Excessive adaptation of a scenario model to limited calibration data.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Overfitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection-induced failure of an empirical scenario optimizer to generalize.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\) be sampled scenarios, let \(F(x)=\mathbb E_P[f(x,\xi)]\), and let \(F_N(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x,\xi_i)\). Choose \(x_N\in X\) satisfying \(F_N(x_N)\le\inf_{x\in X}F_N(x)+\eta\). Given tolerances \(\eta,\varepsilon\ge0\), scenario overfitting is diagnosed when \[F_N(x_N)-\inf_{x\in X}F_N(x)\le\eta\quad\text{but}\quad F(x_N)-\inf_{x\in X}F(x)>\varepsilon.\] Thus near-optimality on the sampled scenarios coexists with unacceptable population regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario solution overfits when it is nearly optimal in sample but has excessive expected regret under the true distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x,\cdot)\) is measurable and integrable under \(P\) for every \(x\in X\).
The empirical and population infima are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_N(x_N)-\inf_{x\in X}F_N(x)\le\eta\) and \(F(x_N)-\inf_{x\in X}F(x)>\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Decision selected by approximate empirical optimization.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: empirical near-optimality combined with excessive population regret is an optimization generalization failure

children.title: Out-of-Sample Scenario Failure
children.top_down_role: Degradation of decision quality beyond the calibration sample.

knowledge_statements.title: Out-of-Sample Scenario Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational failure test using an independent validation distribution or sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_N\) be selected using training scenarios, and let \(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_M\) be an independent validation sample from the operational law \(P\). For a measurable violation function \(g\), define \[\widehat p_M(x_N)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^M\mathbf 1\{g(x_N,\zeta_j)>0\}.\] Given a permitted violation probability \(\alpha\) and statistical margin \(r_M\ge0\), an out-of-sample scenario failure is declared when \(\widehat p_M(x_N)-r_M>\alpha\). If \(r_M\) yields a valid one-sided lower confidence bound, this inequality certifies at its associated confidence level that the operational violation probability exceeds \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independently validated scenario decision fails when a valid lower confidence bound on its operational violation probability exceeds the permitted level.
assumptions_latex: The validation observations are independent of the training scenarios and are sampled from \(P\).
\(g(x_N,\zeta)\) is measurable.
\(r_M\) yields a valid one-sided lower confidence bound for the stated sampling regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat p_M(x_N)-r_M>\alpha\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: independent holdout violation testing is a standard out-of-sample diagnostic
confidence-radius construction and authoritative locator required

children.title: Complexity-Control Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Indicators relating scenario richness to supported data evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity-Control Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform-deviation certificate separating empirical fit from decision-class complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F=\{\xi\mapsto f(x,\xi):x\in X\}\) take values in \([0,B]\), and let \(F\) and \(F_N\) denote population and sample means. For independent Rademacher variables \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_N\), define \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_N(\mathcal F)=\mathbb E_\sigma[\sup_{h\in\mathcal F}N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\sigma_i h(\xi_i)]\). A complexity-control certificate at confidence \(1-\delta\) is \[\sup_{x\in X}|F_N(x)-F(x)|\le2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_N(\mathcal F)+3B\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2N}}.\] A large right-hand side signals inadequate complexity control or sample size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empirical Rademacher complexity and a confidence term provide a candidate high-probability bound on uniform generalization error across the decision class.
assumptions_latex: \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\) are independent with common law \(P\).
Every \(h\in\mathcal F\) is measurable and takes values in \([0,B]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in X}|F_N(x)-F(x)|\le2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_N(\mathcal F)+3B\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2N)}\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).

notation.meaning: Loss-function class induced by feasible decisions.

review_flags: exact constant convention varies among empirical Rademacher bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sample Average Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a finite-sample empirical approximation to a stochastic optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\) be a possibly high-dimensional random variable, and suppose samples \(W^1,\ldots,W^N\) are generated from a known probability distribution or obtained from historical data. Replacing the original stochastic optimization problem by \[\max_x \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N F(x,W^n)\] and solving this sampled problem as an approximation of the original problem is called sample average approximation (SAA). For fixed samples, the sampled problem is a deterministic optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample average approximation replaces the original stochastic optimization problem with an optimization problem whose objective is the average of the objective values over generated or historical samples. Once those samples are fixed, the sampled problem is deterministic.
assumptions_latex: W\text{ is a possibly high-dimensional random variable}
N\in\mathbb{N},\quad N\ge 1
W^1,\ldots,W^N\text{ are generated from a known probability distribution or obtained from historical data}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-sure uniform convergence of SAA objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform consistency of sample-average objective functions on a compact decision set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be nonempty and compact. Suppose that for every \(x\in\Theta\), \(Y(\cdot,\xi)\) is continuous at \(x\) almost surely and there exists \(\delta_x>0\) such that \(\{Y(y,\xi):y\in B(x,\delta_x)\}\) is uniformly integrable. Then \(f_n\to f\) uniformly on \(\Theta\) almost surely as \(n\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local almost-sure continuity and local uniform integrability throughout a nonempty compact decision set imply almost-sure uniform convergence of the SAA objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Sample Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-shot SAA design using a single fixed training sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible set \(X\), loss \(f\), sampling law \(P\), sample size \(N\), and optimization tolerance \(\eta\ge0\). Draw one sample \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\) from \(P\), construct \[F_N(x)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x,\xi_i),\] and compute a decision \(x_N\in X\) satisfying \(F_N(x_N)\le\inf_{x\in X}F_N(x)+\eta\). Stop after this solve and output \(x_N\), together with \(F_N(x_N)\) and the realized sample. No independent replication or data-dependent sample enlargement is performed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Draw one fixed sample, solve its sample-average problem once, and return an approximately optimal empirical decision.
assumptions_latex: The scenarios are sampled from the prescribed law \(P\).
The empirical objective is finite on at least one feasible decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_N(x_N)\le\inf_{x\in X}F_N(x)+\eta\).

notation.meaning: Sample-average objective formed from the single sample.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the canonical one-shot SAA construction

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Replication Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SAA design using multiple mutually independent training samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a replication count \(R\), sample size \(N\), feasible set \(X\), loss \(f\), law \(P\), and optimization tolerance \(\eta\ge0\). For each \(r\in\{1,\ldots,R\}\), independently draw \(\xi_{r1},\ldots,\xi_{rN}\), form \(F_N^{(r)}(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x,\xi_{ri})\), and compute \(x_N^{(r)}\in X\) satisfying \(F_N^{(r)}(x_N^{(r)})\le\inf_{x\in X}F_N^{(r)}(x)+\eta\). Output all replicated solutions and objective values. If the candidates are compared or one is selected, evaluate them on a common validation sample independent of all training replications rather than comparing their distinct training objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve independently sampled SAA problems and, if their candidates are compared, evaluate them on one common independent validation sample.
assumptions_latex: \(R,N\) are positive integers.
All training replications are mutually independent and distributed according to \(P\).
Any validation sample used for comparison is independent of every training replication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_N^{(r)}(x_N^{(r)})\le\inf_{x\in X}F_N^{(r)}(x)+\eta\) for every \(r\in\{1,\ldots,R\}\).

notation.meaning: Optimization tolerance used in every replication.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential SAA Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested-sample SAA algorithm with repeated optimization and diagnostic stopping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input increasing sample sizes \(N_1<N_2<\cdots\), tolerances \(\eta_k\), and a stopping predicate \(S_k\). Draw an infinite independent stream \((\xi_i)_{i\ge1}\). At iteration \(k\), form the nested objective \(F_{N_k}(x)=N_k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_k}f(x,\xi_i)\), compute \(x_k\in X\) with \(F_{N_k}(x_k)\le\inf_{x\in X}F_{N_k}(x)+\eta_k\), and evaluate \(S_k\) using declared diagnostics. If \(S_k\) holds, output \(x_k\); otherwise enlarge the sample to \(N_{k+1}\) and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly enlarge a nested sample, solve the updated SAA problem, and stop when a declared diagnostic criterion holds.
assumptions_latex: The sample stream is independent with common law \(P\).
Each empirical problem can be solved to tolerance \(\eta_k\).
The stopping predicate uses only information available through iteration \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\tau\) is output at \(\tau=\inf\{k:S_k\text{ holds}\}\), when \(\tau<\infty\).

notation.meaning: Cumulative sample size at iteration k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Sampling Method for SAA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential SAA procedure using separate optimization and gap-estimation samples and threshold-based termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(k=1\) and \(v_1\) as prescribed. At iteration \(k\), generate \(\mu_k\) optimization samples and compute \(\widehat x^k=x^{\mu_k}\). These samples may extend the previous optimization sample, but they are independent of the \(v_k\) samples used for gap estimation. Generate \(v_k\) IID samples and form \(G_k=G_{v_k}(\widehat x^k)\) and \(s_k^2=s_{v_k}^2(\widehat x^k)\). If \(s_k>b\) or \(G_k>l'b+\varepsilon'\), increment \(k\), select a new \(v_k\), resample when \(k\) is a multiple of \(k_f\), and repeat. Otherwise return \(x^v=\widehat x^k\). If \(\mu_k=2v_k\), the stated total sample count, including resampling, is \(3\sum_{i=1}^k v_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve successive SAA problems using optimization samples and assess each candidate with an independent IID gap-estimation sample. Enlarge or refresh the samples while either the variability or estimated-gap threshold fails; otherwise return the current candidate.

\widehat x^k=x^{\mu_k}\text{ is computed from }\mu_k\text{ optimization samples}
\text{the }v_k\text{ gap-estimation samples are IID and independent of the optimization samples}

children.title: SAA Sample-Size Design
children.top_down_role: Selection of sample sizes relative to accuracy, confidence, plus computational cost.

knowledge_statements.title: SAA Sample-Size Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-decision sample size guaranteeing uniform SAA objective accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite with \(|X|=M\), let \(0\le f(x,\xi)\le B\) almost surely for every \(x\in X\), and let \(F_N(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Nf(x,\xi_i)\) for independent samples from \(P\). For accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) and confidence \(1-\delta\), Hoeffding's inequality and a union bound give \[N\ge\frac{B^2}{2\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{2M}{\delta}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P\left\{\sup_{x\in X}|F_N(x)-F(x)|\le\varepsilon\right\}\ge1-\delta.\] Any exact empirical minimizer then has population regret at most \(2\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many decisions and bounded losses, logarithmic dependence on decision count suffices for uniform SAA accuracy and bounded regret.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite with \(|X|=M\).
The samples are independent with common law \(P\).
\(0\le f(x,\xi)\le B\) almost surely for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\ge B^2\log(2M/\delta)/(2\varepsilon^2)\) ensures uniform error at most \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct finite-class Hoeffding union bound
authoritative concentration or SAA locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-class Hoeffding union-bound formula and resulting two-epsilon regret statement are mathematically consistent, and complexity_bound is appropriate for this sample-size-design leaf. An inspectable authoritative concentration or SAA locator is still required.

children.title: Adaptive Sample Allocation
children.top_down_role: Data allocation across replications, stages, or uncertainty regions.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(X\) is nonempty, and each candidate sampling stratum or scenario class admits conditionally unbiased observations with finite variance.
At stage \(k\), allocations are measurable with respect to the information \(\mathcal F_k\) available before drawing the next batch.
Every allocation component required for consistency receives infinitely many samples almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting stratified SAA estimator is unbiased conditionally on the chosen allocation, and its variance is \(\sum_{h=1}^H p_h^2\sigma_h^2(x)/n_{k,h}\).

notation.meaning: Probability and conditional standard deviation of stratum \(h\)
Cumulative sample count assigned to stratum \(h\) by stage \(k\)

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports adaptive allocation for sequential SAA.
A source is needed for the precise measurability and consistency conditions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive stratified allocation with conditionally unbiased sampling and persistent exploration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\neq\varnothing\), let strata \(h=1,\ldots,H\) have probabilities \(p_h>0\), and let \(F(x,\xi)\) have conditional variance \(\sigma_h^2(x)<\infty\) in stratum \(h\). Initialize \(n_{0,h}\geq1\). At stage \(k\), use \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable variance estimates \(\widehat\sigma_{k,h}\) to choose a batch allocation \(m_{k,h}\), for example by approximately minimizing \(\sum_h p_h^2\widehat\sigma_{k,h}^2/(n_{k,h}+m_{k,h})\) subject to \(m_{k,h}\in\mathbb N_0\) and \(\sum_hm_{k,h}=b_k\). Draw samples independently within each stratum, update \(n_{k+1,h}=n_{k,h}+m_{k,h}\), and solve the resulting stratified SAA problem. Stop under a separately specified sequential criterion; otherwise require \(n_{k,h}\to\infty\) almost surely for every \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate each new scenario batch using current stratum-variance estimates, retain conditional unbiasedness, and ensure every necessary stratum is sampled indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Sample Allocation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the leaf, but adaptive allocation based on previous observations does not by itself make the cumulative stratified estimator conditionally unbiased given the realized allocation. A source and stronger sampling/estimator conditions are required for that claim and for consistency under persistent exploration.

children.title: Sequential Stopping Criteria
children.top_down_role: Evidence thresholds used to terminate sequential sampling.

assumptions_latex: At stage \(k\), a candidate solution \(x_k\), a lower-bound estimate \(L_k\), and an independent validation estimate \(U_k\) are available.
A computable confidence radius \(r_k(\alpha_k)\) satisfies the stated stagewise coverage guarantee.
The error budgets obey \(\sum_{k\geq1}\alpha_k\leq\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stopping when \(U_k-L_k+r_k(\alpha_k)\leq\varepsilon\) yields an \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate with error probability at most \(\alpha\), subject to the asserted coverage guarantees.

notation.meaning: Stage-\(k\) lower and upper optimal-value estimators
Optimality tolerance and total error level

review_flags: The supplied optimal-stopping locator is not specific to sequential SAA certification.
A source is needed for a valid sequential or error-spending confidence construction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error-spending stopping rule based on independent validation and an SAA lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stages \(k=1,2,\ldots\), let \(L_k\) estimate the true optimal value \(v^*\), and let \(U_k\) independently estimate the true objective value at the current candidate \(x_k\). Choose \(\alpha_k>0\) with \(\sum_{k\geq1}\alpha_k\leq\alpha\), and construct \(r_k(\alpha_k)\geq0\) so that \(\mathbb P\{f(x_k)-v^*>U_k-L_k+r_k(\alpha_k)\}\leq\alpha_k\). The sequential rule stops at \(\tau=\inf\{k:U_k-L_k+r_k(\alpha_k)\leq\varepsilon\}\) and returns \(x_\tau\). By the union bound, the probability of ever stopping with \(f(x_\tau)-v^*>\varepsilon\) is at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop when a confidence-adjusted validation gap is below tolerance, distributing the total error probability across stages to preserve sequential validity.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Stopping Criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and union-bound argument fit the stopping-criterion leaf, provided the stated stagewise guarantees hold for the adaptively generated candidates. No cited source establishes a valid SAA confidence construction with those guarantees.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coverage and almost-sure termination of sequential SAA stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage and finite-termination guarantees for sequential sampling in two-stage stochastic linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a two-stage stochastic linear program with relatively complete recourse, an almost surely finite second-stage value, and a nonempty compact feasible region \(X\). For fixed \(\varepsilon>\varepsilon'>0\), \(p>0\), and \(0<\alpha<1\), if the sequential sampling method stops at iteration \(v\), then \(\liminf_{l\downarrow l'}\mathbb P\bigl(\Delta_v(x^v)\le l s_v(x^v)+\varepsilon\bigr)\ge1-\alpha\). For fixed \(\varepsilon'>0\) and \(l>l'>0\), the stopping iteration is finite almost surely: \(\mathbb P(v<\infty)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated two-stage stochastic linear programs, a stopped sequential SAA run has the specified lower coverage guarantee for its gap bound, and under positive tolerance and strictly separated constants its stopping iteration is finite almost surely.

\text{the second-stage value is finite almost surely}
X\text{ is compact and nonempty}
\varepsilon>\varepsilon'>0,\quad p>0,\quad 0<\alpha<1\text{ for the coverage assertion}
\varepsilon'>0,\quad l>l'>0\text{ for the almost-sure termination assertion}

knowledge_statements.title: Latin Hypercube SAA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized Latin hypercube construction for a transform-based stochastic input model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty feasible set, let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^d)\), and let \(\xi=T(U)\). For each coordinate \(j\), independently choose a permutation \(\pi_j\) of \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and independent jitters \(V_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), and set \(U_{ij}=(\pi_j(i)-1+V_{ij})/N\). Then every interval \([(r-1)/N,r/N)\) is used exactly once in coordinate \(j\), up to null boundary events, while each \(U_i\) is marginally uniform on \([0,1]^d\). With \(\xi_i=T(U_i)\), Latin-hypercube SAA minimizes \(\widehat f_N^{\mathrm{LHS}}(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N F(x,\xi_i)\) over \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Construct scenarios from a randomized Latin hypercube so that every coordinate stratum is represented once, then minimize the resulting average loss.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(X\) is nonempty.
The random input can be represented as \(\xi=T(U)\) with \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]^d\).
The SAA loss \(F(x,T(u))\) is integrable for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each scenario has the target marginal distribution, and the resulting objective is the average loss over a Latin hypercube design.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear control variates with known control means and decision-dependent coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\), let \(C(\xi)\in\mathbb R^q\) have known mean \(\mu_C\), and define \(\widehat f_N^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(F(x,\xi_i)-\beta(x)^{\mathsf T}(C(\xi_i)-\mu_C)\bigr)\). For every fixed coefficient \(\beta(x)\), \(\mathbb E[\widehat f_N^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)]=f(x)\). If \(\Sigma_C=\operatorname{Cov}(C(\xi))\) is nonsingular, the variance-minimizing coefficient is \(\beta^*(x)=\Sigma_C^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(C(\xi),F(x,\xi))\). Control-variate SAA minimizes \(\widehat f_N^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\) over \(x\in X\), with coefficients fixed or estimated under a design preserving the required consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract a zero-mean linear control from each sampled loss; the covariance-based coefficient gives the smallest pointwise estimator variance.

knowledge_statements.title: Importance-Sampled SAA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unnormalized importance sampling for an expectation under a target probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty feasible set, let \(P\ll Q\), let \(w=dP/dQ\), and draw \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\) independently from \(Q\). For \(x\in X\), define \(f(x)=\mathbb E_P[F(x,\xi)]\) and \(\widehat f_{N,Q}(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N w(\xi_i)F(x,\xi_i)\). Whenever \(wF(x,\cdot)\in L^1(Q)\), the change-of-measure identity gives \(\mathbb E_Q[w(\xi)F(x,\xi)]=f(x)\), so \(\widehat f_{N,Q}(x)\) is pointwise unbiased. Importance-sampled SAA solves \(\min_{x\in X}\widehat f_{N,Q}(x)\). Consistency of its optimal values or solutions additionally requires a uniform law or epi-convergence for the weighted loss class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample scenarios from a proposal law, multiply each loss by the target-to-proposal density ratio, and optimize the weighted average over the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(X\) is nonempty.
The target law \(P\) is absolutely continuous with respect to the sampling law \(Q\).
The weighted loss \(w(\xi)F(x,\xi)\) is integrable under \(Q\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The importance-sampled objective is pointwise unbiased for the target expectation and can replace the ordinary SAA objective under suitable uniform-convergence conditions.
review_flags: The exact hypotheses and notation in the provisional importance-sampling section require checking.
