knowledge_statements.title: Subsampling Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Without-replacement subsampling approximation for a statistic with a known convergence rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given data \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\), statistic \(T_N\), subsample size \(m<N\), rate sequence \(\tau_n\), and \(B\) replications, draw subsets \(I_b\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}\) uniformly without replacement with \(|I_b|=m\). Compute
\[W_b=\tau_m\bigl(T_m(Z_{I_b})-T_N(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N)\bigr),\qquad b=1,\ldots,B.\]
Use empirical quantiles of \(\{W_b\}\) to approximate the law of \(\tau_N(T_N-\theta)\) and invert them for a confidence interval. The asymptotic convention is \(m\to\infty\) and \(m/N\to0\); output also records \(m\), \(B\), and \(\tau_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Draw smaller subsets without replacement, recenter and rescale their statistics, and use the resulting empirical distribution for validation.
assumptions_latex: The normalized statistic \(\tau_N(T_N-\theta)\) has a nondegenerate limiting distribution.
The subsample size satisfies \(m\to\infty\) and \(m/N\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The empirical distribution of the subsample roots is used to estimate quantiles of \(\tau_N(T_N-\theta)\).
review_flags: The supplied sources do not document subsampling consistency or its rate conventions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction fits a subsampling-validation algorithm, but convergence of the normalized statistic and m/N→0 alone do not fully state the conditions needed for quantile consistency. A source is required to determine the missing regularity assumptions.

children.title: Cross-Validation Designs
children.top_down_role: Fold construction, repeated validation designs, plus their use in solution assessment.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Validation Designs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: K-fold out-of-sample comparison of candidate SAA decision rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Partition \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) into nonempty folds \(V_1,\ldots,V_K\). For each candidate rule \(A_j\) and fold \(k\), train \(x_{j,-k}=A_j(\{Z_i:i\notin V_k\})\) and compute
\[E_{jk}=|V_k|^{-1}\sum_{i\in V_k}f(x_{j,-k},Z_i),\qquad \operatorname{CV}_j=\sum_{k=1}^K\frac{|V_k|}{N}E_{jk}.\]
Select any \(j^*\in\arg\min_j\operatorname{CV}_j\), retrain \(A_{j^*}\) on all observations, and output the retrained decision together with \(\operatorname{CV}_{j^*}\). Within each fold, validation observations must not influence the corresponding trained decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Train each candidate without one fold, score it on that fold, aggregate held-out losses, select the best rule, and retrain it on all data.
assumptions_latex: The folds form a partition of the observed indices.
Each fold-specific decision uses only observations outside its validation fold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the full-data decision from a rule minimizing weighted cross-validated loss.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports this K-fold validation design for SAA rules.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The K-fold procedure fits the cross-validation algorithm leaf, but no source is supplied and the candidate-rule index set and conditions ensuring the displayed argmin exists are not explicit.

children.title: Resampling Dependence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Validity limits caused by dependent replicates, reused observations, or unstable selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Resampling Dependence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete optimism caused by evaluating a data-adaptive decision on its training sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\) be uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,M\}\), let decisions be subsets \(A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,M\}\) with \(|A|\le N\), and define \(f(A,z)=\mathbf 1\{z\notin A\}\). Given training observations \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\), choose \(\widehat A=\{Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\}\). Its reused-sample loss is identically
\[N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N f(\widehat A,Z_i)=0,\]
whereas its true loss is
\[F(\widehat A)=1-\frac{|\widehat A|}{M}\ge1-\frac{N}{M}.\]
Thus when \(M\gg N\), training-sample reuse reports perfect performance although independent validation loss is near one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision can memorize every training outcome and score zero on reused data while having true loss almost one, demonstrating validation leakage.
assumptions_latex: \(M>N\) and \(Z\) is uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,M\}\).
The evaluator reuses the observations that determined \(\widehat A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The in-sample validation error is zero while \(F(\widehat A)\ge1-N/M\).
review_flags: The counterexample is explicit and checkable, but no supplied locator supports its use as a resampling-dependence boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit memorization example is mathematically checkable and its counterexample kind fits the dependence-boundary leaf, but the record supplies neither a citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale as required for candidate evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Testing of Optimality Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-sample Wald assessment of a smooth first-order condition for a fixed SAA candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a candidate \(\widehat x\), draw an independent validation sample \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\) and compute \(g_i=\nabla_x F(\widehat x,\xi_i)\), \(\bar g_m=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m g_i\), and \(\widehat\Sigma_m=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(g_i-\bar g_m)(g_i-\bar g_m)^{\mathsf T}\). Test \(H_0:\mathbb E[g_i]=0\) against \(H_1:\mathbb E[g_i]\ne0\) using \(T_m=m\bar g_m^{\mathsf T}\widehat\Sigma_m^{-1}\bar g_m\). Reject at asymptotic level \(\alpha\) when \(T_m>\chi^2_{d,1-\alpha}\); otherwise report nonrejection, not a proof of optimality. If \(\widehat\Sigma_m\) is singular, use a declared rank-adjusted generalized-inverse test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use independent validation gradients and a Wald statistic to test zero expected gradient. Rejection contradicts the tested first-order condition; nonrejection does not establish optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d\) is fixed relative to the validation sample.
\(F(\cdot,\xi)\) is differentiable near \(\widehat x\), with finite second gradient moment.
The validation gradients satisfy a multivariate central limit theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under \(H_0\) and nonsingular covariance, \(T_m\Rightarrow\chi_d^2\), yielding an asymptotic level-\(\alpha\) test.

notation.meaning: Upper quantile of the chi-square distribution.

review_flags: A source specific to independent-sample statistical tests of SAA optimality conditions is required.
Boundary-constrained candidates require a projected or KKT-residual version.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Wald calculation is plausible for an unconstrained interior candidate with nonsingular gradient covariance, but the stated assumptions do not establish that zero expected gradient is the relevant optimality condition. A source specific to independent-sample SAA optimality testing and treatment of singular covariance is required.

children.title: Training-Sample Reuse
children.top_down_role: Assessment settings that reuse observations involved in fitting or candidate selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Training-Sample Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimistic assessment caused by evaluating an SAA solution on scenarios used to construct it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)\), let \(\widehat x=A(D)\) be selected by minimizing or otherwise using \(\widehat f_D(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n F(x,\xi_i)\), and let the reported assessment be \(\widehat f_D(\widehat x)\). Training-sample reuse occurs because the same random data determine both \(\widehat x\) and its assessed value. Consequently, conditional unbiasedness generally fails: \(\mathbb E[\widehat f_D(\widehat x)\mid\widehat x]=f(\widehat x)\) need not hold, where \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\). An independent sample \(D'\) restores \(\mathbb E[\widehat f_{D'}(\widehat x)\mid\widehat x]=f(\widehat x)\) when integrability holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusing optimization scenarios for assessment makes the estimate data-dependent and generally optimistic. A conditionally independent holdout sample gives an unbiased value estimate for the selected candidate.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x,\xi)\) is integrable for every assessed candidate.
The selection map \(A\) may depend arbitrarily on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identity \(\mathbb E[\widehat f_D(\widehat x)\mid\widehat x]=f(\widehat x)\) is not generally valid under training-sample reuse.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports validation leakage for SAA.
A source quantifying the direction or magnitude of reuse bias is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-unbiasedness warning is mathematically plausible, but the plain statement claims generally optimistic bias although the displayed result establishes only that unbiasedness can fail for an arbitrary selection rule. A source is needed to support the leakage characterization and any directional bias claim.

children.title: Candidate-Selection Leakage
children.top_down_role: Leakage introduced when validation information influences candidate selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Candidate-Selection Leakage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leakage from choosing among candidates using the sample later reported as an unbiased assessment set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_K\) be candidates independent of an assessment sample \(V\), and let \(\widehat f_V(x)\) estimate \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\xi)]\). Candidate-selection leakage occurs when \(V\) is used to choose \(\widehat k\in\arg\min_{1\le k\le K}\widehat f_V(x_k)\) and the same value \(\widehat f_V(x_{\widehat k})\) is reported as if \(x_{\widehat k}\) had been fixed before observing \(V\). Even when every \(\widehat f_V(x_k)\) is unbiased, \(\mathbb E[\min_k\widehat f_V(x_k)]\le\min_k f(x_k)\); thus selection invalidates fixed-candidate assessment semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting the best candidate on an assessment sample and reporting that same score leaks selection information, producing an optimistically selected minimum even when each candidate score is unbiased.
assumptions_latex: \(K<\infty\) and all displayed expectations exist.
Each candidate is fixed independently of \(V\) before selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Using \(V\) for both selection and reporting creates candidate-selection leakage.

notation.meaning: Assessment sample reused for candidate selection.
Index selected using the assessment sample.

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly treats candidate-selection leakage in SAA validation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selection-minimum inequality is correct under the stated finite-expectation assumptions and the definition fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports its use as an SAA validation-leakage concept.

children.title: Tuning-Induced Leakage
children.top_down_role: Bias arising when validation outcomes guide tuning or experimental design.

knowledge_statements.title: Tuning-Induced Leakage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leakage caused by adapting algorithmic or modeling hyperparameters to assessment outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{A_\lambda:\lambda\in\Lambda\}\) be candidate-generation procedures trained on data \(D\), and let \(V\) be designated for final assessment. Tuning-induced leakage occurs when the chosen parameter \(\widehat\lambda=T(D,V)\) depends nontrivially on \(V\), while \(\widehat f_V(A_{\widehat\lambda}(D))\) is reported using fixed-procedure uncertainty guarantees. Conditional on \(D\), the assessed solution is then a function of \(V\), so the observations in \(V\) are not independent of the final selection event. Valid fixed-candidate confidence statements therefore require fresh assessment data or inference explicitly adjusted for the tuning rule and search over \(\Lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If validation outcomes tune model or algorithm settings, the final candidate depends on the assessment sample. Ordinary fixed-candidate confidence guarantees then require fresh data or selection adjustment.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) and \(V\) are initially independent samples.
The reported guarantee was derived for a candidate fixed independently of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(T(D,V)\) genuinely varies with \(V\), ordinary fixed-candidate assessment on \(V\) is not justified.

notation.meaning: Candidate-generation procedure indexed by a tuning parameter.
Sample reused for tuning and final assessment.

review_flags: No supplied source locator directly addresses tuning-induced validation leakage.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly identifies dependence of the final candidate on the assessment sample, but the asserted invalidity of fixed-candidate confidence guarantees requires an authoritative source or a precisely specified inferential result.

children.title: Nested Validation Separation
children.top_down_role: Structural separation of selection, tuning, plus final assessment samples.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Validation Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-separation condition supporting unbiased outer assessment after inner candidate selection and tuning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition mutually independent data into training data \(D_{\mathrm{tr}}\), inner validation data \(D_{\mathrm{in}}\), and outer assessment data \(D_{\mathrm{out}}\). Let the final candidate satisfy \(\widehat x=A(D_{\mathrm{tr}},D_{\mathrm{in}})\), allowing arbitrary inner selection and tuning, but no dependence on \(D_{\mathrm{out}}\). For \(\widehat f_{\mathrm{out}}(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m F(x,\zeta_i)\), nested validation separation is the measurability condition \(\widehat x\perp D_{\mathrm{out}}\). Under integrability, \(\mathbb E[\widehat f_{\mathrm{out}}(\widehat x)\mid\widehat x]=f(\widehat x)\). Any subsequent adaptation to outer outcomes destroys this condition and requires another untouched assessment layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Training and inner validation may select and tune the candidate, but the outer assessment sample must remain independent and untouched until final evaluation.
assumptions_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{tr}},D_{\mathrm{in}},D_{\mathrm{out}}\) are mutually independent.
\(F(\widehat x,\xi)\) is conditionally integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The outer estimate is conditionally unbiased for \(f(\widehat x)\) when \(\widehat x\perp D_{\mathrm{out}}\).

notation.meaning: Inner sample used for selection or tuning.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports nested validation separation for SAA.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outer-sample conditional-unbiasedness claim is plausible under independence and integrability, but independence is incorrectly called a measurability condition. No source is supplied for the nested-validation formulation in the SAA setting.

children.title: Two-Stage Recourse Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Value-function and dual-certificate decompositions for two-stage recourse models.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Recourse Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual geometric representation of linear two-stage recourse with scenario-independent recourse matrix and cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) and \(q\in\mathbb R^r\), define \(Q(x,\xi)=\inf\{q^{\mathsf T}y:Wy=h(\xi)-T(\xi)x,\ y\ge0\}\), with value \(+\infty\) when infeasible. The feasible right-hand sides form the fixed polyhedral cone \(\mathcal C=W\mathbb R_+^r\). Whenever the primal value is finite, linear-programming duality gives \(Q(x,\xi)=\sup\{\pi^{\mathsf T}(h(\xi)-T(\xi)x):W^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q\}\). Thus scenarios alter only the right-hand side and its affine dependence on \(x\); the primal cone and dual polyhedron are common to all scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed recourse, every scenario shares the same recourse cone and dual feasible polyhedron; only the right-hand side changes with the scenario and first-stage decision.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) and \(q\) do not depend on \(\xi\).
For the stated dual equality, the recourse linear program has a finite value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The geometry is governed by \(\mathcal C=W\mathbb R_+^r\) and \(\mathcal D=\{\pi:W^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q\}\), both independent of \(\xi\).

notation.meaning: Cone of feasible recourse right-hand sides.

children.title: Complete Recourse
children.top_down_role: Global second-stage feasibility across admissible right-hand-side realizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical complete-recourse condition for a fixed linear recourse matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed recourse matrix \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) has complete recourse if every right-hand side in \(\mathbb R^m\) is attainable by a nonnegative recourse action: \[W\mathbb R_+^r=\mathbb R^m.\] Equivalently, for every \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), the system \(Wy=b\), \(y\ge0\), is feasible. This condition depends only on \(W\), not on the first-stage feasible set or the distribution of \(\xi\), and guarantees feasibility of the second-stage equality system for every possible affine right-hand side \(h(\xi)-T(\xi)x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete recourse means every possible second-stage right-hand side can be generated by a nonnegative recourse decision, independently of first-stage restrictions or scenario support.
assumptions_latex: \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) is fixed across scenarios.
Second-stage variables satisfy \(y\in\mathbb R_+^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), there exists \(y\ge0\) such that \(Wy=b\).

notation.meaning: Cone of attainable recourse right-hand sides.

children.title: Relatively Complete Recourse
children.top_down_role: Second-stage feasibility restricted to first-stage feasible decisions plus modeled realizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Relatively Complete Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recourse feasibility restricted to feasible first-stage decisions and relevant scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the first-stage feasible set. A two-stage model has relatively complete recourse if, for every \(x\in X\), the system \(Wy=h(\xi)-T(\xi)x\), \(y\ge0\), is feasible for almost every \(\xi\). Equivalently, \[h(\xi)-T(\xi)x\in W\mathbb R_+^r\quad\text{for every }x\in X\text{ and almost every }\xi.\] Unlike complete recourse, this property need not cover right-hand sides that cannot arise from feasible first-stage decisions and scenarios in the distributional support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relatively complete recourse requires second-stage feasibility only for right-hand sides generated by feasible first-stage decisions and almost every relevant scenario.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the declared first-stage feasible set.
\(W\), \(h(\xi)\), and \(T(\xi)\) define the second-stage equality system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(x\in X\), recourse is feasible with probability one.

notation.meaning: Cone of attainable recourse right-hand sides.

children.title: Recourse-Regime Implications
children.top_down_role: Consequences of each recourse regime for feasibility cuts, domains, plus decomposition behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Regime Implications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical hierarchy and feasibility consequences of complete and relatively complete recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(W\), complete recourse implies relatively complete recourse for every choice of \(X\), \(h\), \(T\), and scenario distribution, because \(W\mathbb R_+^r=\mathbb R^m\) contains every generated right-hand side. The converse is false: relative completeness constrains only \(\{h(\xi)-T(\xi)x:x\in X\}\) almost surely. Under relatively complete recourse, the extended recourse value \(Q(x,\xi)\) avoids \(+\infty\) caused by infeasibility for every \(x\in X\) almost surely, although it may still equal \(-\infty\) unless the recourse objective is bounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete recourse always implies relative completeness, but not conversely. Relative completeness removes infeasibility on the feasible first-stage domain, while objective boundedness remains a separate requirement.
assumptions_latex: The recourse constraints are \(Wy=h(\xi)-T(\xi)x\), \(y\ge0\).
Infeasible recourse is assigned value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete recourse \(\Longrightarrow\) relatively complete recourse \(\Longrightarrow\) almost-sure recourse feasibility on \(X\), with no implied lower boundedness.

children.title: Recourse Completeness Failure
children.top_down_role: Boundary cases where feasible first-stage decisions can produce infeasible recourse problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Completeness Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional example separating complete recourse, relative completeness, and infeasible recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take \(W=[1]\), \(y\ge0\), and recourse constraint \(y=\xi-x\). Since \(W\mathbb R_+=\mathbb R_+\ne\mathbb R\), complete recourse fails. If \(X=\{0\}\) and \(\mathbb P(\xi=1)=1\), relatively complete recourse nevertheless holds because the only generated right-hand side equals \(1\). If instead \(\mathbb P(\xi=-1)>0\), then for \(x=0\) the constraint requires \(y=-1\) on an event of positive probability, so relative completeness fails and the extended recourse value is \(+\infty\) on that event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative scalar recourse variable cannot cover negative right-hand sides. Distributional support can therefore distinguish relative completeness from complete recourse or make recourse infeasible.
assumptions_latex: Infeasible second-stage problems receive value \(+\infty\).
The first-stage feasible set is \(X=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The example has relative but not complete recourse when \(\xi=1\) almost surely, and lacks relative completeness when \(\mathbb P(\xi=-1)>0\).
review_flags: The concrete counterexample is constructed from the standard definition rather than attributed verbatim to the source.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete-Recourse Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral effective-domain geometry when some generated right-hand sides admit no recourse action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(W\), define the scenario-wise feasible first-stage domain by \(\mathcal X_\xi=\{x:h(\xi)-T(\xi)x\in W\mathbb R_+^r\}\). Since \(W\mathbb R_+^r\) is a closed polyhedral cone, \(\mathcal X_\xi\) is a polyhedron. By the dual-cone characterization, \[\mathcal X_\xi=\{x:u^{\mathsf T}(h(\xi)-T(\xi)x)\ge0\ \text{for every }u\text{ with }W^{\mathsf T}u\ge0\}.\] Under incomplete recourse, this set can be a proper subset of the declared first-stage domain; outside it, \(Q(x,\xi)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incomplete recourse restricts each scenario to a polyhedral subset of first-stage decisions, characterized by dual-cone inequalities; outside that subset the recourse value is infinite.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) is a finite-dimensional fixed recourse matrix.
Infeasible recourse is assigned extended value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effective domain of \(Q(\cdot,\xi)\) is the polyhedron \(\mathcal X_\xi\), which may exclude feasible first-stage decisions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Violation-Compensating Recourse Function Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple, fixed linear, and nonlinear recourse constructions that compensate realized positive constraint violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each constraint, define \(g_i^+(x,\xi)=\max\{g_i(x,\xi),0\}\). A simple recourse function is \(Q(x,\xi)=\min_y\{\sum_{i=1}^m q_i y_i:y_i\ge g_i^+(x,\xi),\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). A more general fixed linear recourse function is \(Q(x,\xi)=\min_{y\in Y}\{q^{\mathsf T}y:Wy\ge g^+(x,\xi)\}\), where \(Y\subset\mathbb R^{\bar n}\) is polyhedral and \(W\) and \(q\) are fixed. The simple formulation is a special case under matching dimensions, costs, feasible set, and \(W=I\). Nonlinear recourse may instead be represented by \(Q(x,\xi)=\min_{y\in Y}\{q(y):H_i(y)\ge g_i^+(x,\xi),\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), for given functions \(q\) and \(H_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive part of each realized constraint violation can be covered by a recourse action. This produces simple separable recourse, more general fixed linear recourse, or nonlinear recourse formulations.
assumptions_latex: g_i^+(x,\xi)=\max\{g_i(x,\xi),0\},\quad i=1,\ldots,m
Y\subset\mathbb R^{\bar n}\text{ is polyhedral and }W,q\text{ are fixed in the linear-recourse formulation}
q:\mathbb R^{\bar n}\to\mathbb R\text{ and }H_i:\mathbb R^{\bar n}\to\mathbb R\text{ are given in the nonlinear formulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q(x,\xi)\text{ can be represented by the stated simple, fixed linear, or nonlinear violation-compensating recourse problem.}

source_evidence.locator: Basic Concepts / 1.4.2. Deterministic Equivalents / Definition 1.4.2-extra-1

knowledge_statements.title: Violation-Compensating Recourse Function Representations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-scenario linear recourse function and its polyhedral representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, effective domain, and piecewise-linear representation of the recourse function for a finite-scenario two-stage stochastic linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\mathbf x=\mathbf b\) and \(\mathbf x\geq0\), define \(Q_i(\mathbf x)\) as the optimum value of \(\min\{\mathbf q_i^T\mathbf y_i:W_i\mathbf y_i=\boldsymbol\xi_i-T_i\mathbf x,\ \mathbf y_i\geq0\}\), using value \(+\infty\) when the subproblem is infeasible, and let \(Q(\mathbf x)=\sum_{i=1}^N p_iQ_i(\mathbf x)\). The two-stage problem is \(\min\{\mathbf c^T\mathbf x+Q(\mathbf x):A\mathbf x=\mathbf b,\ \mathbf x\geq0\}\). Its finite domain is \(K=\bigcap_{i=1}^N K_i\). Each \(K_i\) admits a subdivision into convex polyhedra on which \(Q_i\) is linear, and a common refinement gives such a subdivision for \(Q\). For a dual-feasible basis \(B\), the region \(B^{-1}(\boldsymbol\xi_i-T_i\mathbf x)\geq0\) has value \(Q_i(\mathbf x)=\mathbf q_{iB}^TB^{-1}(\boldsymbol\xi_i-T_i\mathbf x)\). On \(\{\mathbf x:A\mathbf x=\mathbf b,\ \mathbf x\geq0\}\setminus K\), \(Q(\mathbf x)=+\infty\), and this exceptional set need not be a convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recourse function is the probability-weighted sum of the scenario second-stage optimal values, and the two-stage model minimizes first-stage cost plus this function. Its finite domain is the intersection of the scenario recourse-feasible sets. Feasible bases yield polyhedral regions on which the scenario values, and hence the aggregate value on a common refinement, are linear. Outside the common domain the recourse value is positive infinity, and that exceptional set need not be a convex polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(A\mathbf x=\mathbf b\) and \(\mathbf x\geq0\).
For \(\mathbf x\in K\), every scenario recourse problem has a finite optimum.
An infeasible scenario recourse problem is assigned value \(+\infty\).
\(Q(\mathbf x)=\sum_{i=1}^N p_iQ_i(\mathbf x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}Q=K=\bigcap_{i=1}^N K_i\); on \(K\), \(Q\) is piecewise linear over a polyhedral subdivision, whereas \(Q(\mathbf x)=+\infty\) on the first-stage feasible set outside \(K\).

children.title: Polyhedral Recourse
children.top_down_role: Piecewise-linear recourse geometry relevant to classical decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real convex polyhedral structure of a linear fixed-recourse value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(x,\xi)=\inf\{q^{\mathsf T}y:Wy=h(\xi)-T(\xi)x,\ y\ge0\}\), using \(+\infty\) for infeasibility, and suppose no feasible instance is unbounded below. For fixed \(\xi\), \(Q(\cdot,\xi)\) is an extended-real convex polyhedral function. On its effective domain it has the dual representation \[Q(x,\xi)=\sup_{\pi\in\mathcal D}\pi^{\mathsf T}(h(\xi)-T(\xi)x),\qquad \mathcal D=\{\pi:W^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q\}.\] Hence its epigraph is polyhedral, and wherever the value is finite it is piecewise affine; dual optimal solutions supply affine supporting cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear fixed recourse produces an extended-real convex polyhedral value function. On its feasible domain it is piecewise affine, and dual solutions generate supporting cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) and \(q\) are fixed, and \(h(\xi)-T(\xi)x\) is affine in \(x\).
Every feasible recourse problem under consideration is bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each fixed \(\xi\), \(Q(\cdot,\xi)\) is convex polyhedral and admits affine dual supporting cuts.

notation.meaning: Dual multiplier defining an affine cut.

children.title: Piecewise-Quadratic Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse functions with region-dependent quadratic structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Quadratic Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polyhedral representation of a convex quadratic recourse value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A recourse function \(Q:X\to\mathbb R\) is piecewise quadratic on a polyhedral set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) if there exist polyhedra \(P_1,\ldots,P_K\) covering \(X\), symmetric matrices \(H_k\succeq0\), vectors \(g_k\), and scalars \(a_k\) such that \[Q(x)=\tfrac12x^\top H_kx+g_k^\top x+a_k\quad\text{for every }x\in P_k.\] The formulas must agree on overlaps. Hence \(Q\) is continuous and convex when the resulting pasted function is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Piecewise-quadratic recourse equals a quadratic expression on each cell of a finite polyhedral partition, with consistent values on cell overlaps.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral.
\(K<\infty\) and \(H_k\succeq0\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) has a finite polyhedral partition on which it is quadratic.

notation.meaning: quadratic, linear, and constant coefficients on cell k

review_flags: locator supports recourse context; exact piecewise-quadratic formulation requires confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general recourse section does not establish the stated finite piecewise-quadratic representation. Positive-semidefinite cell Hessians and agreement on overlaps do not by themselves ensure global convexity, while the scope note specifically claims convex recourse.

children.title: Nonlinear Recourse
children.top_down_role: Convex or nonconvex nonlinear recourse outside polyhedral representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real second-stage value function with a nonaffine objective or feasible graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\in\mathcal S\) be a scenario, let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(Y_s\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_s}\). Given maps \(q_s:X\times Y_s\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(g_s:X\times Y_s\to\mathbb R^{r_s}\), and \(h_s:X\times Y_s\to\mathbb R^{t_s}\), define \[Q_s(x)=\inf\{q_s(x,y):y\in Y_s,\ g_s(x,y)\leq0,\ h_s(x,y)=0\},\qquad x\in X,\] where the inequality is componentwise and the infimum of an empty feasible set is \(+\infty\). This is nonlinear recourse when the objective or feasible graph depends nonaffinely on \((x,y)\). It is convex nonlinear recourse when \(q_s\) is jointly convex and the feasible graph \(\{(x,y)\in X\times Y_s:g_s(x,y)\leq0,\ h_s(x,y)=0\}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear recourse is the extended optimal value of a second-stage problem whose objective or feasible graph depends nonaffinely on the first- and second-stage decisions. The convex variant additionally has a jointly convex objective and convex feasible graph.
assumptions_latex: \(s\in\mathcal S\), \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and \(Y_s\subseteq\mathbb R^{m_s}\).
\(g_s\) and \(h_s\) have respectively \(r_s\) and \(t_s\) real-valued components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_s:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty,-\infty\}\) is the scenario-\(s\) recourse value function.

notation.meaning: numbers of inequality and equality constraints in scenario s

children.title: Recourse-Class Transition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Changes in cut representation, oracle requirements, plus convergence scope across recourse classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Class Transition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural boundary separating polyhedral, piecewise-quadratic, and general nonlinear value functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q(x)=\inf_y\{q(x,y):g(x,y)\leq0\}\), linear programming recourse with affine parameter dependence yields a polyhedral convex value function under finite attainment. Convex quadratic programming recourse can yield a piecewise-quadratic value function when finitely many polyhedral active-set regions cover the parameter domain. Once the objective, feasible graph, or parameter dependence is genuinely nonlinear, neither finite polyhedrality nor a finite piecewise-quadratic representation follows without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LP structure supports polyhedral recourse; regular parametric QP structure supports piecewise-quadratic recourse; general nonlinear structure crosses both representation boundaries.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is finite and attained on the parameter domain under discussion.
Active-set claims are restricted to finitely many polyhedral critical regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{LP recourse}\Rightarrow\text{polyhedral}\), while \(\text{regular parametric QP recourse}\Rightarrow\text{piecewise quadratic}\); neither implication extends automatically to general nonlinear recourse.
review_flags: exact transition theorem and regularity hypotheses need an authoritative source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transition-boundary role is appropriate, but the LP and parametric-QP implications require an authoritative source specifying feasibility, duality, parameter dependence, and critical-region assumptions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: L-shaped decomposition algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternates feasibility-cut generation, recourse evaluation, optimality-cut generation, and master reoptimization for a two-stage recourse problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set $K=L=0$ and $\widehat\theta=-\infty$, and solve the first-stage LP for $\widehat x$; stop if it is infeasible. Otherwise, repeatedly call the feasibility-cut procedure at $\widehat x$. If it produces a cut, re-solve the master. If it produces no cut, evaluate $\mathcal Q(\widehat x)$ and stop when $\widehat\theta\geq\mathcal Q(\widehat x)$; otherwise set $L\leftarrow L+1$, construct $-\beta_L^{\mathsf T}x+\theta\geq\alpha_L$, and re-solve the master. Stop also if any re-solved master is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The L-shaped algorithm begins with the first-stage LP. At each master solution it first searches for a recourse-feasibility cut. If none is found, it evaluates the recourse function and either stops when the current theta estimate reaches that value or adds an optimality cut. It re-solves the master after each added cut and also stops if that master is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal Q(\widehat x)\text{ is evaluated only after the feasibility-cut search returns no cut}
\operatorname{feascut}\text{ and }\operatorname{master}\text{ implement the referenced cut-generation and master-solution routines}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure stops if the initial or updated master is infeasible, or after no feasibility cut is found and }\widehat\theta\geq\mathcal Q(\widehat x);\text{ otherwise it adds a feasibility or optimality cut and continues.}

source_evidence.locator: Recourse Problems / 3.2.2. Optimality / Algorithm 3.2.2-extra-4

knowledge_statements.title: L-shaped decomposition algorithm

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Single-Cut L-Shaped Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregated-cut decomposition for a finite-scenario two-stage linear stochastic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the feasibility- and optimality-cut collections as empty. At iteration \(v\), solve the master problem \(\min c^Tx+\theta\) subject to the first-stage constraints, accumulated feasibility cuts \(D_\ell x\ge d_\ell\), and accumulated optimality cuts \(E_\ell x+\theta\ge e_\ell\). If no optimality cut is present, set \(\theta^v=-\infty\) and exclude it when computing \(x^v\). If \(x^v\notin K_2\), add at least one feasibility cut and repeat. Otherwise, for each \(k=1,\ldots,K\), solve \(\min\{q_k^Ty:Wy=h_k-T_kx^v,\ y\ge0\}\), obtain an optimal multiplier \(\pi_k^v\), and define \(E=\sum_{k=1}^Kp_k(\pi_k^v)^TT_k\), \(e=\sum_{k=1}^Kp_k(\pi_k^v)^Th_k\), and \(w^v=e-Ex^v\). If \(\theta^v\ge w^v\), stop with \(x^v\) optimal; otherwise add \(Ex+\theta\ge e\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The single-cut L-shaped method alternates between a first-stage master problem and scenario recourse problems. It adds feasibility cuts when recourse is infeasible and otherwise aggregates scenario dual information into one expected-recourse optimality cut. It stops when the master recourse estimate is at least the computed recourse value.
assumptions_latex: k=1,\ldots,K\text{ indexes finitely many realizations with probabilities }p_k
x^v\in K_2\implies \{y\ge0:Wy=h_k-T_kx^v\}\ne\varnothing\quad(k=1,\ldots,K)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta^v\ge e-Ex^v\implies x^v\text{ is optimal};\quad \theta^v<e-Ex^v\implies Ex+\theta\ge e\text{ is added}.

source_evidence.locator: Two-Stage Recourse Problems / 5.1. The L-Shaped Method / Algorithm 5.1-extra-1

knowledge_statements.title: Master Approximation Architecture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multicut L-shaped master for finite-scenario convex recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given scenarios \(s=1,\ldots,S\), probabilities \(p_s>0\), and valid affine lower models \(\ell_{sj}(x)\leq Q_s(x)\), initialize finite cut sets \(J_s^0\). At iteration \(k\), solve \[\min_{x\in X,\,\theta\in\mathbb R^S}c^\top x+\sum_{s=1}^S p_s\theta_s\quad\text{subject to }\theta_s\geq\ell_{sj}(x),\ j\in J_s^k.\] Query every recourse oracle at the resulting \(x^k\), append violated valid cuts, and stop when no required cut is violated beyond tolerance. Output \(x^k\) and the master value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The master minimizes first-stage cost plus scenario epigraph variables constrained by accumulated valid recourse cuts, adding violated oracle cuts iteratively.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the first-stage feasible set.
Every \(\ell_{sj}\) is a globally valid lower bound for \(Q_s\) on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\leq\min_{x\in X}\{c^\top x+\sum_s p_sQ_s(x)\}\), where \(L_k\) is the master optimum.

notation.meaning: master epigraph approximation of scenario recourse
scenario-s cut indices available at iteration k

review_flags: exact L-shaped master coverage requires confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic approximations locator does not confirm this multicut L-shaped algorithm. The statement also permits empty initial cut sets, which can leave epigraph variables unbounded below, and it does not state relatively complete recourse or incorporate returned feasibility cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Recourse Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex scenario oracle returning values and supporting cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scenario \(s\) and query \(\bar x\in X\), solve the second-stage problem defining \(Q_s(\bar x)\). If its optimum is finite and attained, return \(v_s=Q_s(\bar x)\) and \(g_s\in\partial Q_s(\bar x)\), defining \[\ell_s(x)=v_s+g_s^\top(x-\bar x)\leq Q_s(x).\] If the second stage is infeasible, return a valid feasibility inequality separating \(\bar x\) from the domain of \(Q_s\). The oracle output is the cut together with its scenario and query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario oracle solves recourse at a trial point and returns either a supporting optimality cut or a valid feasibility cut.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_s\) is proper, closed, and convex for an optimality query.
The oracle solves the scenario subproblem exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_s(x)\leq Q_s(x)\) for all \(x\in X\), or the returned feasibility inequality excludes \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: scenario recourse subgradient at the query point
affine supporting function returned by the oracle

review_flags: oracle and feasibility-cut details require confirmation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Properness, closedness, and convexity do not guarantee a subgradient at every finite query point. A feasibility inequality excluding an infeasible query also needs suitable closed-convex domain and separation assumptions. The supplied locator does not confirm these oracle details.

children.title: Master Lower-Bound System
children.top_down_role: Bounds certified by the current master approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Master Lower-Bound System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound certificate from globally valid master cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat Q_s^k(x)=\max_{j\in J_s^k}\ell_{sj}(x)\), where every cut satisfies \(\ell_{sj}(x)\leq Q_s(x)\) for all \(x\in X\). Define \[L_k=\inf_{x\in X}\left\{c^\top x+\sum_{s=1}^S p_s\widehat Q_s^k(x)\right\}.\] Then \(L_k\leq z^*\), where \(z^*=\inf_{x\in X}\{c^\top x+\sum_s p_sQ_s(x)\}\). Adding valid cuts makes the sequence nondecreasing: \(L_{k+1}\geq L_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimized master value is a certified lower bound because each accumulated scenario model underestimates its true recourse function.
assumptions_latex: \(p_s\geq0\) for every scenario.
\(\ell_{sj}(x)\leq Q_s(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
The master infimum is computed without optimistic numerical error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\leq z^*\) and, for nested cut sets, \(L_{k+1}\geq L_k\).

notation.meaning: current lower approximation of scenario recourse
optimal value of the original two-stage problem

children.title: Incumbent Upper-Bound System
children.top_down_role: Bounds obtained from evaluated feasible incumbent decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Upper-Bound System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-bound certificate obtained by exact evaluation of feasible first-stage incumbents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and let scenarios \(s=1,\ldots,S\) have probabilities \(p_s\geq0\) with \(\sum_{s=1}^S p_s=1\). Define \[z^*=\inf_{x\in X}\left\{c^\top x+\sum_{s=1}^S p_sQ_s(x)\right\}.\] For each evaluated incumbent \(x^i\in X\) with \(Q_s(x^i)\in\mathbb R\) known exactly for every scenario, define \[V_i=c^\top x^i+\sum_{s=1}^S p_sQ_s(x^i),\qquad U_k=\min_{0\leq i\leq k}V_i.\] Then \(z^*\leq U_k\), and adding another evaluated incumbent gives \(U_{k+1}\leq U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact objective evaluation at each feasible incumbent gives an upper bound. Storing the smallest evaluated value yields a certified, nonincreasing incumbent upper-bound sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(x^i\in X\) is first-stage feasible for every stored incumbent.
\(Q_s(x^i)\in\mathbb R\) is evaluated exactly for every stored incumbent and scenario.
\(p_s\geq0\) and \(\sum_{s=1}^S p_s=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^*\leq U_k\) and \(U_{k+1}\leq U_k\).

notation.meaning: exact objective value of evaluated incumbent i
best incumbent upper bound through iteration k
optimal value of the original two-stage minimization problem

review_flags: locator supports bound systems generally; stochastic incumbent specialization requires confirmation

children.title: Bound-Gap Certification
children.top_down_role: Joint interpretation of master bounds, incumbent bounds, plus reported optimality gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Gap Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute and relative optimality certificates from valid lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(L\leq z^*\leq U\) and \(U<+\infty\). The absolute gap is \(G_{\mathrm{abs}}=U-L\). For a fixed scale \(\delta>0\), define \[G_{\mathrm{rel}}=\frac{U-L}{\max\{\delta,|U|\}}.\] If \(G_{\mathrm{abs}}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\), the incumbent is absolutely \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\)-optimal. If \(G_{\mathrm{rel}}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\), it satisfies the declared scale-relative tolerance. Both conclusions require certified bounds computed under consistent objective conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid lower and upper bounds certify incumbent optimality when their absolute or explicitly scaled relative gap meets the declared tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(L\leq z^*\leq U<+\infty\).
\(\delta>0\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\geq0\), and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U-z^*\leq U-L\); hence the chosen gap test certifies the corresponding incumbent tolerance.

notation.meaning: certified relative gap under scale delta

children.title: Bound Inconsistency Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Detection of invalid ordering, stale incumbents, or unreliable bound comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound Inconsistency Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary consistency tests for reported master and incumbent bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, certified bounds must satisfy \(L_k\leq z^*\leq U_k\). Thus \(L_k>U_k+\tau\) for a declared numerical tolerance \(\tau\geq0\) is an inconsistency certificate. Likewise, a decrease in \(L_k\) under nested valid cut sets or an increase in the best-incumbent value \(U_k\) indicates a bookkeeping, cut-validity, feasibility, objective-scaling, scenario-weight, or numerical-certification failure; it does not certify convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossed bounds or violated expected monotonicity expose invalid cuts, infeasible incumbents, inconsistent scaling, bookkeeping errors, or uncertified numerical solves.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
Master cut sets and incumbent sets are nested across compared iterations.
\(\tau\geq0\) is the declared comparison tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k>U_k+\tau\), \(L_{k+1}<L_k-\tau\), or \(U_{k+1}>U_k+\tau\) triggers diagnostic failure.
review_flags: diagnostic taxonomy lacks a supplied authoritative locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The crossed-bound and monotonicity tests follow from certified nested bound systems, but no source is supplied for the stated diagnostic taxonomy or its attribution of possible causes.

children.title: Master Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate master solutions, alternate optima, plus unstable dual information.

knowledge_statements.title: Master Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of active master representations at an optimal master solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a polyhedral master problem \(\min\{d^\top z:Az\geq b\}\). A feasible solution \(z^*\) is master-degenerate if the active-row matrix \(A_{I(z^*)}\), where \(I(z^*)=\{i:A_i z^*=b_i\}\), contains more active constraints than are needed to describe the local minimal face; equivalently, the active normals admit redundant linear dependence. This permits multiple basic or multiplier representations of the same master solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master solution is degenerate when redundant, linearly dependent active constraints allow multiple bases or multiplier descriptions of the same point.
assumptions_latex: The master is represented as a finite-dimensional polyhedral optimization problem.
\(z^*\) is feasible and optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active constraint representation at \(z^*\) is nonunique.

notation.meaning: indices of constraints active at the master solution

review_flags: exact degeneracy convention and authoritative locator are missing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source fixes the intended degeneracy convention. For a general optimal point on a positive-dimensional face, linear dependence of active normals, redundant face descriptions, multiple bases, and multiple multiplier representations are not automatically equivalent as stated.

children.title: Recourse Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Degenerate scenario subproblems affecting certificate selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of dual certificates or subgradients at a recourse query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For linear recourse \(Q_s(x)=\min_y\{q_s^\top y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ y\geq0\}\), let \[D_s(x)=\arg\max_{\pi}\{\pi^\top(h_s-T_sx):W_s^\top\pi\leq q_s\}.\] The recourse problem is dual-degenerate at \(x\) when \(D_s(x)\) contains distinct optimal multipliers that yield distinct vectors \(-T_s^\top\pi\). Then the same recourse value admits multiple valid supporting cuts, and the oracle's cut is not uniquely determined by the query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse is dual-degenerate when one query has multiple optimal multipliers producing different valid subgradients and hence different supporting cuts.
assumptions_latex: The scenario linear recourse problem has a finite attained optimum.
Strong duality holds at the query point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\pi_1,\pi_2\in D_s(x)\) with \(-T_s^\top\pi_1\neq-T_s^\top\pi_2\).

notation.meaning: set of optimal scenario dual multipliers at x
recourse subgradient generated by a dual optimum

review_flags: dual-degeneracy definition requires an exact decomposition reference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula correctly describes multiple optimal dual multipliers producing distinct recourse subgradients, but calling precisely this condition recourse or dual degeneracy requires an exact decomposition reference; standard LP degeneracy and dual-solution multiplicity are not synonymous.

children.title: Weak Master Approximations
children.top_down_role: Loose outer approximations that provide limited progress toward the recourse function.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Master Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid lower models whose error remains large near master trial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat Q_s^k\leq Q_s\) be the current master model. It is \(\eta\)-weak at a trial point \(x^k\) when \[Q_s(x^k)-\widehat Q_s^k(x^k)>\eta\] for a prescribed \(\eta\geq0\). More generally, weakness on a region \(R\subseteq X\) is measured by \(\sup_{x\in R}(Q_s(x)-\widehat Q_s^k(x))\). Validity alone guarantees a lower bound but provides no useful local accuracy; large model error can repeatedly direct the master toward poorly represented regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master approximation is weak when it remains a valid underestimate but has excessive recourse-model error at trial points or across a relevant region.
assumptions_latex: \(\widehat Q_s^k(x)\leq Q_s(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
\(\eta\geq0\) is a declared model-accuracy threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_s(x^k)-\widehat Q_s^k(x^k)>\eta\) certifies local approximation weakness, not bound invalidity.

notation.meaning: current master lower model of scenario recourse

review_flags: the eta-weak terminology is a local formalization requiring review

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The model-error formula is coherent and fits the failure-boundary leaf, but the coined eta-weak terminology and the claimed stalling mechanism are not supported by the generic approximations locator.

children.title: Degeneracy-Induced Stalling
children.top_down_role: Stagnation attributable to repeated weak certificates or unstable supporting information.

assumptions_latex: The master is solved exactly and recourse separation uses exact dual optimization.
At the current master solution \((\bar x,\bar\theta)\), the unresolved gap satisfies \(\bar\theta<Q(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pure dual degeneracy cannot stall exact L-shaped separation at an unresolved incumbent; stalling requires failure of exact separation, cut insertion, or master progress rules.

notation.meaning: Current master solution and recourse epigraph estimate
Dual-optimal face at the current first-stage point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact separation makes every dual-optimal cut violated whenever the master underestimates recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear-recourse boundary separating genuine degeneracy from implementation-induced stalling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(\bar x)=\max_{\pi\in D}\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-T\bar x)\) and suppose \(D^*(\bar x)\) contains multiple dual optima. If \(\bar\theta<Q(\bar x)\), then every \(\pi\in D^*(\bar x)\) generates \(\theta\geq\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\), which is violated at \((\bar x,\bar\theta)\). Hence an exact implementation that inserts a violated cut must change the master relaxation or certify progress. Repetition without progress can occur only if the procedure accepts duplicate or nonviolated inexact cuts, omits separation, tolerates the violation as zero, or repeatedly resolves the master without enforcing the new cut; dual degeneracy alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With exact separation, every dual optimum cuts off an underestimated incumbent. Persistent stalling therefore requires numerical, insertion, or master-progress failure, not degeneracy alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Induced Stalling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-separation boundary is mathematically plausible and the failure_boundary kind fits the leaf, but the specialized claim that degeneracy alone cannot cause stalling has no inspectable source.

assumptions_latex: For each scenario \(s\), recourse is a feasible bounded linear program at the evaluated first-stage point.
Scenario probabilities satisfy \(p_s>0\) and \(\sum_s p_s=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual-feasible points generate valid scenario or aggregated lower-bounding optimality cuts, and dual-optimal points make those cuts tight at the generating first-stage point.

notation.meaning: Scenario or aggregate recourse epigraph variables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear two-stage recourse, covering disaggregated and probability-aggregated optimality cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q_s(x)=\min\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ y\geq0\}\), define \(D_s=\{\pi:W_s^{\mathsf T}\pi\leq q_s\}\). Weak duality implies that every \(\pi_s\in D_s\) certifies the valid scenario cut \(\theta_s\geq\pi_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\). With \(Q(x)=\sum_s p_sQ_s(x)\), any selection \(\pi_s\in D_s\) also certifies \(\theta\geq\sum_s p_s\pi_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\). If each \(\pi_s\) is dual-optimal at \(\bar x\), the corresponding right-hand side equals the represented recourse value at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual-feasible recourse solutions certify scenario-wise or aggregated lower bounds; dual-optimal solutions produce cuts tight at the generating first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality-Cut Families
Feasibility-Cut Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas-ray feasibility certificates for linear two-stage recourse when the alternative-dual cone is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scenario \(s\), define \(R_s=\{r:W_s^{\mathsf T}r\leq0\}\) and assume that \(R_s\) is pointed. The system \(W_sy=h_s-T_sx\), \(y\geq0\), is feasible exactly when \(r^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\leq0\) for every \(r\in R_s\). Because \(R_s\) is a pointed polyhedral cone, it suffices to impose these inequalities for generators of its extreme rays. Thus, if \(\bar x\in X\) has infeasible scenario recourse, a ray \(r\in R_s\) with \(r^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_s\bar x)>0\) certifies infeasibility and yields the feasibility cut \(r^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a pointed alternative-dual cone, its extreme-ray inequalities characterize scenario recourse feasibility; a violated ray inequality certifies infeasibility and supplies a feasibility cut.
assumptions_latex: Scenario recourse has the form \(W_sy=h_s-T_sx\) with \(y\geq0\).
The first-stage candidate belongs to the master domain \(X\).
The polyhedral cone \(R_s=\{r:W_s^{\mathsf T}r\leq0\}\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extreme rays of the pointed alternative-dual cone generate inequalities that are necessary and sufficient for scenario recourse feasibility.

notation.meaning: Scenario technology, right-hand side, and coupling matrices

children.title: Pareto-Optimal Cuts
children.top_down_role: Nondominated supporting cuts selected within the relevant master region.

assumptions_latex: The master domain \(X\) is nonempty.
Each compared affine function is a valid lower bound on \(Q\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid cut is Pareto-optimal precisely when no other valid cut dominates it on \(X\).

notation.meaning: Affine lower bounds defining two cuts

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: dominance over the master domain is the standard Pareto criterion for Benders cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance definition relative to the declared master domain, not the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For affine valid lower bounds \(\ell_i(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_i\) satisfying \(\ell_i(x)\leq Q(x)\) for all \(x\in X\), the cut \(\theta\geq\ell_1(x)\) dominates \(\theta\geq\ell_2(x)\) on \(X\) if \(\ell_1(x)\geq\ell_2(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and strict inequality holds for at least one \(x\in X\). A valid cut \(\theta\geq\ell(x)\) is Pareto-optimal for \(X\) when no distinct valid affine cut dominates it under this relation. Pareto optimality therefore depends on the chosen master domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid recourse cut is Pareto-optimal when no other valid affine cut is everywhere at least as strong and somewhere strictly stronger on the master domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Pareto-Optimal Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and domain-relative dominance criterion fit the leaf and are internally precise, but no inspectable source supports the stated Pareto-optimal-cut convention.

children.title: Core-Point Strengthening
children.top_down_role: Cut selection or refinement guided by interior reference points.

assumptions_latex: The master domain has a core point \(x^\circ\in\operatorname{relint}(\operatorname{conv}X)\).
The dual-optimal face \(D^*(\bar x)\) at the generating point is nonempty.
Linear recourse duality holds on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximizing cut value at a core point over the dual-optimal face selects a cut that is tight at \(\bar x\) and Pareto-optimal on \(X\).

notation.meaning: Generating first-stage point and core point
Dual-optimal face at the generating point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard core-point auxiliary optimization for selecting a nondominated Benders cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single recourse block; the same auxiliary selection applies scenario-wise in a multicut model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\bar x\), form \(D^*(\bar x)=\{\pi\in D:\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-T\bar x)=Q(\bar x)\}\). Choose a core point \(x^\circ\in\operatorname{relint}(\operatorname{conv}X)\), solve \(\pi^\circ\in\arg\max_{\pi\in D^*(\bar x)}\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx^\circ)\), and output \(\theta\geq(\pi^\circ)^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\). Stop after an optimizer of the auxiliary problem is obtained. The face constraint preserves tightness at \(\bar x\), while optimization at the relative-interior core point selects a Pareto-optimal cut over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize over dual solutions already optimal at the incumbent, selecting the one whose cut is strongest at a relative-interior core point.
knowledge_statements.title: Core-Point Strengthening

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits core-point strengthening, but the Pareto-optimality guarantee is a specialized theorem-level claim requiring an authoritative source and its exact hypotheses.

children.title: Dominance-Based Cut Strengthening
children.top_down_role: Cut improvements assessed through dominance over the master domain.

assumptions_latex: A finite candidate family \(\mathcal L\) consists of affine lower bounds valid for \(Q\) on \(X\).
Dominance comparisons over \(X\) can be solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns exactly the nondominated members of the candidate family and preserves validity of every retained cut.

notation.meaning: Finite family of candidate affine lower bounds

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pairwise dominance filtering is a direct consequence of the stated dominance order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dominance filtering within a supplied finite family of valid affine cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nd}}=\mathcal L\). For each ordered pair \((\ell_i,\ell_j)\) of distinct retained bounds, solve \(m_{ij}=\min_{x\in X}(\ell_i(x)-\ell_j(x))\). If \(m_{ij}\geq0\) and \(\max_{x\in X}(\ell_i(x)-\ell_j(x))>0\), delete \(\ell_j\), since \(\ell_i\) dominates it. Continue until no deletion occurs, then output the cuts \(\theta\geq\ell(x)\) for \(\ell\in\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nd}}\). Because deletion never alters a retained affine function, validity is preserved, and the output contains no pairwise dominated candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly remove any valid candidate cut that is everywhere weaker than another candidate and strictly weaker somewhere on the master domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance-Based Cut Strengthening

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly describes exact dominance filtering within a finite valid family, and its kind fits the leaf, but the proposed computational strengthening variant has no source.

children.title: Strengthening Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which stronger-looking cuts lose validity or useful dominance.

assumptions_latex: The intended recourse epigraph is \(E=\{(x,\theta):x\in X,\ \theta\geq Q(x)\}\).
A proposed strengthened cut has affine right-hand side \(\widetilde\ell\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strengthening is valid exactly when \(\widetilde\ell(x)\leq Q(x)\) throughout \(X\); local tightness or sampled validity is insufficient.

notation.meaning: Original and strengthened affine lower bounds

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: global lower-bound validity follows directly from containment of the recourse epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global validity boundary for any modification of an L-shaped optimality cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strengthened inequality \(\theta\geq\widetilde\ell(x)\) is valid for \(E\) if and only if \(\widetilde\ell(x)\leq Q(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). In particular, let \(\widetilde\ell=\ell+\delta\), where \(\ell\leq Q\) on \(X\), \(\delta(\bar x)=0\), and \(\delta(x')>Q(x')-\ell(x')\) for some \(x'\in X\). Then the modified cut remains tight wherever the original cut was tight at \(\bar x\), yet excludes \((x',Q(x'))\in E\) and is invalid. Thus incumbent tightness, coefficient enlargement, or validation on finitely many sampled points does not establish global validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strengthened cut must remain below recourse everywhere on the master domain. Tightness at the incumbent or success on sampled points does not suffice.
knowledge_statements.title: Strengthening Validity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits and the global epigraph-validity criterion is precise, but the record supplies no inspectable source for this strengthening boundary.

children.title: Inexact Cuts
children.top_down_role: Certificates produced from approximate subproblem information.

assumptions_latex: The recourse primal and dual are linear and satisfy strong duality at \(\bar x\).
A computed multiplier \(\widehat\pi\) is intended to generate an optimality cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual-feasible but suboptimal multipliers yield valid inexact cuts; multipliers with uncertified feasibility need not yield valid cuts.

notation.meaning: Cut right-hand side generated by the computed multiplier

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak duality separates harmless dual suboptimality from unsafe dual infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for approximate linear-recourse optimality cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\widehat\ell(x)=\widehat\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\). If \(\widehat\pi\in D=\{\pi:W^{\mathsf T}\pi\leq q\}\), weak duality gives \(\widehat\ell(x)\leq Q(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), even when \(Q(\bar x)-\widehat\ell(\bar x)>0\); the resulting inexact cut is valid but not tight. If instead \(W^{\mathsf T}\widehat\pi\nleq q\), the same inequality has no dual certificate and may exceed \(Q\). Therefore an approximate optimality tolerance affects strength, whereas an uncorrected feasibility residual affects validity; the latter cannot be treated as harmless inexactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suboptimal dual-feasible solutions give valid but weak cuts. Approximate multipliers that violate dual feasibility may instead produce invalid cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between dual-feasible suboptimal multipliers and infeasible multipliers is mathematically sound and fits a failure boundary, but no source supports the inexact-cut classification.

children.title: Invalid Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cuts that exclude admissible epigraph points or lack global support.

assumptions_latex: The target recourse epigraph is \(E=\{(x,\theta):x\in X,\ \theta\geq Q(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cut is invalid exactly when it excludes at least one point of the true recourse epigraph.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: invalidity is failure of containment of the true recourse epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic invalidity criterion for an L-shaped optimality cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proposed optimality cut \(\theta\geq\ell(x)\), with affine \(\ell\), is invalid for the recourse epigraph \(E\) when it is not satisfied by every point of \(E\). Equivalently, invalidity holds precisely when there exists \(x'\in X\) such that \(\ell(x')>Q(x')\), because then the true epigraph point \((x',Q(x'))\) is removed. A cut may be valid at the generating point or at every previously visited master point and still be invalid under this definition; validity is a universal condition over \(X\), not a finite test-set property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimality cut is invalid when its affine lower bound exceeds true recourse at any feasible first-stage point, thereby excluding a true epigraph point.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits and the epigraph-containment criterion is exact, but the record has no cited source.

children.title: Numerically Unstable Cuts
children.top_down_role: Cuts degraded by scaling, cancellation, tolerance, or conditioning problems.

assumptions_latex: The exact valid cut is \(\theta\geq a^{\mathsf T}x+b\) on a bounded domain \(X\).
Implementation stores coefficients \((\widehat a,\widehat b)\) and uses reliability tolerance \(\tau>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implemented cut is numerically unstable at tolerance \(\tau\) when coefficient error can alter its value by more than \(\tau\) somewhere on \(X\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the condition directly bounds propagated affine-coefficient error over the master domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational coefficient-error condition relative to a bounded master domain and declared tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the propagated cut-value error by \(\Delta_X=\sup_{x\in X}|(\widehat a-a)^{\mathsf T}x+(\widehat b-b)|\). The implemented cut is numerically unstable at tolerance \(\tau\) when \(\Delta_X>\tau\), because rounding or solver error can change master separation or validity decisions by more than the accepted tolerance. A computable bound is \(\Delta_X\leq\|\widehat a-a\|_*\sup_{x\in X}\|x\|+|\widehat b-b|\) for any norm and its dual. Large coefficient magnitudes or dynamic range are warning indicators, but instability is determined by propagated error relative to \(X\) and \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut is numerically unstable when coefficient errors can change its value beyond the declared reliability tolerance somewhere on the bounded master domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerically Unstable Cuts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits an operational instability threshold, but this is not a canonical definition and the implication for separation or validity decisions depends on margins and implementation details. A numerical Benders source is required.

children.title: Cut-Reliability Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Structural checks for certificate validity, accuracy, plus numerical reliability.

assumptions_latex: Each cut is accompanied by its generating scenario, point, multiplier, and solver tolerances.
Recourse can be independently reevaluated at diagnostic points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cut passes diagnostics only when certificate residuals, generating-point consistency, and independent validity checks all meet their declared tolerances.

notation.meaning: Computed dual multiplier and generated affine cut

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: residual, consistency, and independent reevaluation tests directly target the listed reliability failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic algorithm for linear-recourse optimality cuts with explicit tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each cut \(\widehat\ell(x)=\widehat\pi^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\), compute \(r_d=\|(W^{\mathsf T}\widehat\pi-q)_+\|_\infty\) and independently evaluate \(Q(\bar x)\), giving \(r_g=|Q(\bar x)-\widehat\ell(\bar x)|\). On a prescribed validation set \(V\subseteq X\), compute \(r_v=\max_{x\in V}(\widehat\ell(x)-Q(x))_+\). Reject or recompute the cut if \(r_d>\tau_d\) or \(r_v>\tau_v\); flag it as weak or inexact if \(r_g>\tau_g\). Stop after every stored cut is classified, and output the residual vector and classification. Passing finite-set validation is diagnostic evidence, not a proof of global validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check dual feasibility, generating-point consistency, and independent recourse violations. Classify or recompute cuts using declared tolerances, while treating sampled validation as nonconclusive.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Reliability Diagnostics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the diagnostics leaf and the residual tests are coherent, but the particular protocol, tolerances, and pass/classification semantics lack an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multicut L-Shaped Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-separated optimality-cut variant for a finite-scenario two-stage linear stochastic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the feasibility-cut collection and each scenario's optimality-cut collection as empty. At iteration \(v\), solve a master problem with objective \(c^Tx+\sum_{k=1}^K\theta_k\), the first-stage constraints, accumulated feasibility cuts, and separate cuts \(E_{\ell(k)}x+\theta_k\ge e_{\ell(k)}\) for each scenario \(k\). If scenario \(k\) has no optimality cut, set \(\theta_k^v=-\infty\) and exclude it when computing \(x^v\). Apply the single-cut method's recourse-feasibility step, adding feasibility cuts when necessary. Otherwise solve each scenario subproblem and obtain an optimal multiplier \(\pi_k^v\). Whenever \(\theta_k^v<p_k(\pi_k^v)^T(h_k-T_kx^v)\), add the scenario-specific cut with \(E=p_k(\pi_k^v)^TT_k\) and \(e=p_k(\pi_k^v)^Th_k\). If no scenario inequality is violated, stop with \(x^v\) optimal; otherwise repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multicut L-shaped method maintains a separate recourse estimate and optimality-cut collection for each scenario. It adds a cut only for scenarios whose estimates understate their dual recourse values and stops when no scenario inequality is violated.
assumptions_latex: k=1,\ldots,K\text{ indexes finitely many realizations with probabilities }p_k
x^v\in K_2\implies \{y\ge0:Wy=h_k-T_kx^v\}\ne\varnothing\quad(k=1,\ldots,K)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall k,\ \theta_k^v\ge p_k(\pi_k^v)^T(h_k-T_kx^v)\right]\implies x^v\text{ is optimal};\quad\text{each violated scenario inequality generates a separate cut}.
