assumptions_latex: There are finitely many scenarios with \(p_s>0\) and \(\sum_s p_s=1\).
Each scenario recourse function \(Q_s\) admits dual optimality cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The single-cut regime uses one aggregate epigraph variable and adds one probability-weighted cut per separation round.

notation.meaning: Scenario dual multipliers selected in round k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-aggregated L-shaped representation for finite-scenario linear recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(x)=\sum_s p_sQ_s(x)\). The single-cut master represents expected recourse with one variable \(\theta\) and inequalities \(\theta\geq\sum_s p_s(\pi_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\), where \(\pi_s^k\in D_s\) is selected for every scenario in separation round \(k\). At a trial point \(x^k\), choosing each \(\pi_s^k\) dual-optimal makes the aggregate cut right-hand side equal \(Q(x^k)\). Thus one iteration contributes one probability-weighted supporting inequality rather than separate variables and cuts for individual scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One epigraph variable represents expected recourse, and each iteration aggregates all scenario dual supports into a single probability-weighted optimality cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Cut Regime
Scenario-Disaggregated Multicut Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario, two-stage linear recourse with one master epigraph variable per scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite scenario set with probabilities \(p_s>0\), and let \(Q_s(x)=\max_{\pi\in D_s}\pi^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\), where \(D_s=\{\pi:W_s^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q_s\}\). After generating dual solutions \(\pi_s^j\in D_s\), the scenario-disaggregated master uses variables \(x\) and \((\theta_s)_{s\in S}\): \[\min\left\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\sum_{s\in S}p_s\theta_s:x\in X,\ \theta_s\ge (\pi_s^j)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\ \text{for every generated }(s,j)\right\}.\] Thus every scenario contributes its own recourse approximation and, ordinarily, one new optimality cut per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multicut master maintains a separate recourse variable and separate supporting cuts for every scenario, while weighting their sum by scenario probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite and \(p_s>0\) for all \(s\in S\).
Each recourse value admits the displayed dual representation.
Generated dual solutions are feasible in their scenario dual polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s\theta_s\) is a separable polyhedral lower approximation of \(\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(x)\).

notation.meaning: dual feasible polyhedron for scenario s
master approximation variable for scenario s

children.title: Partial Cut Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Fixed grouping of scenario certificates between single-cut and fully disaggregated regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Cut Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed partition interpolates between single-cut and fully disaggregated L-shaped masters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P=\{G_1,\ldots,G_m\}\) partition a finite scenario set \(S\), and define \(p_G=\sum_{s\in G}p_s\). For dual solutions \(\pi_s^j\in D_s\), introduce one variable \(\theta_G\) per block and impose \[p_G\theta_G\ge\sum_{s\in G}p_s(\pi_s^j)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx),\qquad G\in\mathcal P.\] The master objective is \(c^{\mathsf T}x+\sum_{G\in\mathcal P}p_G\theta_G\). Singleton blocks give the multicut regime; the single block \(S\) gives the single-cut regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial aggregation assigns one recourse variable and one combined cut to each block of a scenario partition, interpolating between single-cut and multicut formulations.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a partition of finite \(S\).
\(p_s>0\) and \(\pi_s^j\in D_s\) for every scenario used in a cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities are valid lower-supporting cuts for the probability-weighted recourse of each block.

children.title: Adaptive Cut Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Iteration-dependent revision of scenario groups or aggregation granularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Cut Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition refinement adapts cut granularity while retaining all previously generated valid inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite scenario set \(S\), an initial partition \(\mathcal P_0\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At iteration \(k\), solve the master containing all retained block cuts, evaluate every \(Q_s(x^k)\), and obtain dual optimizers \(\pi_s^k\). Compute block discrepancies \(d_G^k=\max_{s,t\in G}|Q_s(x^k)-Q_t(x^k)|\). Split every \(G\in\mathcal P_k\) with \(d_G^k>\tau_k\), forming a refinement \(\mathcal P_{k+1}\), and add valid cuts for its blocks. Stop when the incumbent upper-minus-lower bound is at most \(\varepsilon\); output the incumbent. Never delete a valid old cut solely because its originating block was split.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method evaluates scenario recourse, splits blocks whose scenario values differ too much, adds cuts for the refined partition, and stops at the prescribed optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: Every scenario subproblem returns its value and a dual optimizer.
\(\tau_k\ge0\), and every updated partition refines its predecessor.
The master supplies a valid lower bound and incumbents supply valid upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output has certified absolute optimality gap at most \(\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a specific adaptive algorithm, including a particular discrepancy rule, refinement policy, and gap claim. No source supports that precise method or its required convergence conditions.

children.title: Scenario Clustering Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria for grouping scenarios into shared cut blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Clustering Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A complete-link threshold criterion for forming aggregation blocks at a specified incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\), a scale parameter \(\lambda\ge0\), and scenario dual optimizers \(\pi_s\in\arg\max_{\pi\in D_s}\pi^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\). Define \[d_x(s,t)=|Q_s(x)-Q_t(x)|+\lambda\left\|T_s^{\mathsf T}\pi_s-T_t^{\mathsf T}\pi_t\right\|_2.\] For a threshold \(\tau\ge0\), a partition \(\mathcal P\) satisfies the complete-link clustering criterion when \[\max_{s,t\in G}d_x(s,t)\le\tau\qquad\text{for every }G\in\mathcal P.\] The criterion controls within-block disagreement in both recourse values and local cut slopes; it does not itself guarantee minimal block count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenarios may share a block only when their recourse values and cut slopes are pairwise close at the current first-stage point.
assumptions_latex: Each scenario has a finite recourse value and an attained dual optimizer at \(x\).
A common norm and compatible slope dimension are used across scenarios.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every admissible block has complete-link diameter at most \(\tau\) under \(d_x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The value-and-slope complete-link metric is a particular clustering design rather than a canonical necessary condition. An authoritative source is required for this exact criterion.

children.title: Aggregation-Regime Switching
children.top_down_role: Transitions among coarse, partial, plus disaggregated cut representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation-Regime Switching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A gap-preserving switch among scenario partitions using valid retained cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input candidate partitions \(\mathfrak P\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and switching scores \(R_k(\mathcal P)\). At iteration \(k\), choose \(\mathcal P_k\in\arg\min_{\mathcal P\in\mathfrak P}R_k(\mathcal P)\), solve the corresponding master, evaluate all scenario subproblems at \(x^k\), and add the valid block cuts induced by \(\mathcal P_k\). Retain every earlier inequality that remains expressible in the current master, or replace it by an explicitly equivalent inequality under the new variables. Stop only when a valid upper bound \(U_k\) and lower bound \(L_k\) satisfy \(U_k-L_k\le\varepsilon\); output the incumbent attaining \(U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method switches partitions according to a score, preserves or exactly translates valid cuts, and terminates only with a valid optimality-gap certificate.
assumptions_latex: Every candidate partition covers the same finite scenario set.
Each generated block inequality is valid for the original recourse function.
\(L_k\) and \(U_k\) remain globally valid bounds after switching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upon termination, the returned incumbent has absolute optimality gap at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: valid global lower and upper bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record specifies an algorithm with an unspecified score family and nontrivial cut-translation requirements. No source establishes this precise switching scheme or its invariant-bound conditions.

children.title: Cut-Count Growth
children.top_down_role: Accumulation of active or stored cuts across decomposition iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Count Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic cut-count bound for fixed-partition L-shaped iterations without cut deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a fixed partition of \(S\) into \(m=|\mathcal P|\) nonempty blocks. Suppose each iteration adds at most one optimality cut per block and at most \(r_k\) feasibility cuts. If no cut is deleted, then after \(K\) iterations the number \(N_K\) of generated cuts satisfies \[N_K\le N_0+Km+\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_k.\] If recourse is relatively complete, so no feasibility cuts are required, then \(N_K\le N_0+K|\mathcal P|\). Hence single-cut growth is at most one cut per iteration, whereas full scenario disaggregation grows by at most \(|S|\) cuts per iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a fixed partition and no deletion, optimality cuts grow by at most the number of blocks per iteration, plus any feasibility cuts.
assumptions_latex: The partition is fixed for all \(K\) iterations.
At most one optimality cut is added per block per iteration.
Cuts are not deleted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_K\le N_0+K|\mathcal P|+\sum_{k=1}^{K}r_k\).

notation.meaning: number of cuts after K iterations
feasibility cuts added at iteration k

children.title: Master-Size Scaling
children.top_down_role: Growth of master variables, constraints, plus associated solve burden.

knowledge_statements.title: Master-Size Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear master-size accounting in block count, retained cuts, and first-stage dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the first-stage formulation have \(n\) variables and \(a\) structural constraints. For a partition \(\mathcal P\) with \(m=|\mathcal P|\) blocks, introduce one epigraph variable per block and retain \(N\) decomposition cuts. The resulting linear master has \(n+m\) variables and \(a+N\) explicit constraints, apart from bound rows and any reformulation auxiliaries. Under the fixed-partition rule adding one cut per block per iteration and retaining all cuts, after \(K\) iterations it has at most \(n+m\) variables and \(a+N_0+Km\) constraints when recourse is relatively complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-aggregated master adds one variable per block; with one retained cut per block per iteration, its constraint count grows linearly in iterations and blocks.
assumptions_latex: The master is represented explicitly as a linear program.
One epigraph variable is used for each aggregation block.
Recourse is relatively complete for the iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The master size is at most \((n+m)\) variables and \((a+N_0+Km)\) constraints after \(K\) iterations.

children.title: Approximation Strength
children.top_down_role: Tightness of the master representation over relevant decision regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition refinement strengthens the projected recourse epigraph relaxation for aligned scenario cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P'\) refine \(\mathcal P\), and suppose the two partitioned masters minimize the same first-stage objective over the same set \(X\) and use identical scenario dual vectors \(\pi_s^j\) for every aligned cut index \(j\). For each \(G'\in\mathcal P'\), the refined master imposes \[p_{G'}\theta_{G'}\ge\sum_{s\in G'}p_s(\pi_s^j)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx).\] Under the identification \[p_G\theta_G=\sum_{G'\in\mathcal P':\,G'\subseteq G}p_{G'}\theta_{G'}\qquad(G\in\mathcal P),\] every refined-master feasible point projects to a coarse-master feasible point. Consequently, the refined master has lower-bound value no smaller than the coarse master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For identical aligned scenario cut data, every feasible point of a refined-partition master projects to a feasible point of the coarse-partition master, so refinement cannot weaken the master lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P'\) refines \(\mathcal P\).
The compared masters use identical scenario dual vectors for every aligned cut index.
Both masters minimize the same first-stage objective over the same set \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(\mathcal P')\ge L(\mathcal P)\), where \(L(\mathcal P)\) is the master lower-bound value.

notation.meaning: optimal value of the partitioned master

children.title: Aggregation Tradeoff Frontier
children.top_down_role: Interaction among representation size, cut volume, plus approximation quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Tradeoff Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto frontier balancing master size against lower-bound strength across scenario partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a common collection of scenario cut data. For every admissible partition \(\mathcal P\), let \(C(\mathcal P)\) be a master-complexity measure, such as variable-plus-constraint count, and let \(L(\mathcal P)\) be its master lower-bound value. A partition \(\mathcal P\) is on the aggregation tradeoff frontier if no admissible partition \(\mathcal Q\) satisfies \[C(\mathcal Q)\le C(\mathcal P),\qquad L(\mathcal Q)\ge L(\mathcal P),\] with at least one strict inequality. Thus the frontier consists exactly of partitions whose complexity cannot be reduced without losing bound strength and whose bound cannot be strengthened without increasing complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition lies on the tradeoff frontier when no other partition is both no larger and no weaker, with one strict improvement.
assumptions_latex: All partitions use the same scenario set and aligned cut data.
The complexity and lower-bound measures are evaluated under a common master convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is frontier-efficient exactly when it is nondominated for minimizing \(C\) and maximizing \(L\).

notation.meaning: master lower-bound value for partition P

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:Pareto nondominance definition specialized to partitioned L-shaped masters

children.title: Finite Convergence of the L-Shaped Method

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Convergence of the L-Shaped Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination for finite-support uncertainty, with separate stated outcomes for existence of an optimizer and infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\xi\) has finite support, the L-shaped algorithm converges in finitely many iterations to an optimal solution of \(\min\{c^Tx+\mathcal Q(x):x\in K_1\cap K_2\}\) whenever an optimal solution exists; if the problem is infeasible, the algorithm proves infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With finitely many realizations, the L-shaped method finitely finds an optimizer when one exists and finitely proves infeasibility when the model is infeasible. The extract does not state an outcome for a feasible problem having no optimizer.
assumptions_latex: |\operatorname{supp}(\xi)|<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \arg\min_{x\in K_1\cap K_2}\bigl(c^Tx+\mathcal Q(x)\bigr)\ne\varnothing\implies\text{finite termination at an optimizer};\qquad K_1\cap K_2=\varnothing\implies\text{finite proof of infeasibility}.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Finite-Cut Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of exact L-shaped decomposition for finite-scenario linear recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a finite-scenario two-stage linear stochastic program with a nonempty first-stage polyhedron \(X\), finite optimal value, and exact solution of every master and scenario recourse subproblem. Suppose that, for each scenario \(s\), all admissible optimality cuts are selected from a finite set of relevant dual extreme points and all admissible feasibility cuts are selected from a finite set of relevant extreme-ray generators. Assume the initial master is a well-defined valid relaxation. At every nonterminal iteration, add at least one previously absent violated feasibility cut when some scenario recourse system is infeasible, or at least one previously absent violated optimality cut when the master underestimates finite recourse. Terminate when no such violated cut exists. Then the L-shaped method performs only finitely many cut-generating iterations and terminates at an optimal first-stage solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact L-shaped decomposition terminates optimally after finitely many cut-generating iterations when only finitely many extreme-point and extreme-ray cuts are admissible and every nonterminal iteration adds a new violated cut.
assumptions_latex: The scenario set is finite, and all first- and second-stage models are linear polyhedral programs.
The initial master is a well-defined valid relaxation; masters and scenario subproblems are solved exactly; and the optimal value is finite.
The admissible extreme-point optimality cuts and extreme-ray feasibility cuts form finite sets.
Every nonterminal iteration adds at least one previously absent violated admissible cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm generates finitely many distinct cuts and terminates with an optimal first-stage solution.

notation.meaning: a scenario in the finite scenario set

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dual extreme point certifies a globally valid affine lower support for linear recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scenario \(s\), define the extended recourse value \[Q_s(x)=\inf\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ y\ge0\},\] with \(Q_s(x)=+\infty\) when the recourse system is infeasible, and assume \(Q_s(x)>-\infty\) for every first-stage point under consideration. Let \(D_s=\{\pi:W_s^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q_s\}\). If \(Q_s(\bar x)\) is finite, strong duality holds at \(\bar x\), and \(\bar\pi_s\in D_s\) is an optimal extreme point, then \[Q_s(x)\ge\bar\pi_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\quad\text{for every considered }x,\qquad Q_s(\bar x)=\bar\pi_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_s\bar x).\] If \(\theta_s\) is the master epigraph variable representing scenario recourse, then \(\theta_s\ge\bar\pi_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\) is a globally valid optimality cut that is tight at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal dual extreme point produces a globally valid affine lower bound on the extended scenario recourse value, tight at the point where the finite subproblem was solved; the corresponding epigraph inequality is an optimality cut.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_s(x)>-\infty\) for every first-stage point under consideration, with infeasible recourse assigned value \(+\infty\).
The scenario recourse problem and its dual satisfy strong duality at \(\bar x\), where \(Q_s(\bar x)\) is finite.
\(\bar\pi_s\) is a dual-feasible optimal extreme point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_s\ge\bar\pi_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\) is a valid optimality cut, tight at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: optimal dual extreme point at the incumbent

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Ray Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dual recession ray separates first-stage points whose scenario recourse system is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scenario \(s\), consider the recourse feasibility system \(W_sy=h_s-T_sx\), \(y\ge0\), and the cone \(R_s=\{r:W_s^{\mathsf T}r\le0\}\). If an extreme ray \(r_s\in R_s\) satisfies \(r_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_s\bar x)>0\), then Farkas' alternative certifies that no \(y\ge0\) solves \(W_sy=h_s-T_s\bar x\). Moreover, every first-stage point admitting feasible recourse must satisfy \[r_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\le0.\] Hence this inequality is a valid feasibility cut and strictly separates the infeasible point \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession ray with positive residual proves scenario recourse infeasibility and yields a valid inequality excluding the offending first-stage point.
assumptions_latex: The recourse constraints are \(W_sy=h_s-T_sx\) with \(y\ge0\).
\(r_s\) is an extreme ray satisfying \(W_s^{\mathsf T}r_s\le0\).
\(r_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_s\bar x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recourse is infeasible at \(\bar x\), and \(r_s^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\le0\) is valid for every recourse-feasible \(x\).

notation.meaning: dual recession cone for scenario s

children.title: Nonpolyhedral Recourse Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of finite-cut arguments outside polyhedral recourse geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpolyhedral Recourse Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the classical finite-cut argument when recourse is convex but nonpolyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[-1,1]\) and let the recourse value be \(Q(x)=x^2\). A cutting-plane L-shaped model formed from finitely many exact supporting cuts has the form \(m_K(x)=\max_{i\in K}\{2x_i x-x_i^2\}\), where \(K\) is finite. Each cut equals \(Q\) only at its generating point \(x_i\), so \(m_K(x)<Q(x)\) for every \(x\notin\{x_i:i\in K\}\). Thus no finite collection of these affine cuts represents \(Q\) on \(X\). Consequently, the classical finite-convergence proof based on exhausting finitely many polyhedral recourse faces does not extend to general nonpolyhedral recourse without an additional termination tolerance or structural assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth quadratic recourse function cannot be represented by finitely many tangent cuts, so the classical finite-face convergence argument fails.
assumptions_latex: Cuts are exact supporting hyperplanes generated at finitely many trial points.
Termination requires exact representation rather than a positive tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_K\not\equiv Q\) for every finite \(K\); polyhedral finite-cut convergence is not guaranteed.

children.title: Unbounded Subproblem Boundary
children.top_down_role: Convergence implications of unbounded master or scenario subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Subproblem Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of optimality-cut generation when a trial-point recourse problem is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a trial point \(x\), consider \(Q(x)=\inf\{q^{\mathsf T}y:Wy=h-Tx,\ y\geq0\}\). If this system has a feasible point \(y_0\) and there exists \(d\geq0\) satisfying \(Wd=0\) and \(q^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(y_0+td\) is feasible for every \(t\geq0\) and its objective tends to \(-\infty\). Hence \(Q(x)=-\infty\), the dual subproblem has no finite optimal multiplier, and no finite supporting optimality cut for \(Q\) can be extracted. The ordinary L-shaped master update is therefore undefined unless the model excludes this case or supplies a separate diagnostic treatment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-cost feasible recession direction makes recourse unbounded, leaving no finite dual multiplier from which to form an optimality cut.
assumptions_latex: The recourse subproblem is a finite-dimensional linear program.
The trial-point constraint system is feasible.
A negative-cost feasible recession direction exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(x)=-\infty\), so the standard optimality-cut update is unavailable.

children.title: Inexact-Solve Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits created by approximate subproblem solutions or uncertain certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Solve Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between certified approximate cuts and uncontrolled errors in master or scenario solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x+Q(x)\), and suppose iteration \(k\) uses a scenario oracle with error bound \(\varepsilon_k\geq0\). Finite exact convergence of the classical L-shaped method is not implied if master problems or scenario duals are solved only approximately. In particular, a purported cut \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x+b_k\) is safe only when it is certified to satisfy \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x+b_k\leq Q(x)\) for every feasible \(x\). Persistent errors with \(\inf_k\varepsilon_k>0\) generally support only tolerance-level termination, while uncertified cuts may overestimate \(Q\), invalidate the master lower bound, and eliminate an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent solve errors prevent an exact finite-convergence guarantee; uncertified cuts can also destroy the master’s lower-bound validity.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is convex on the first-stage feasible set.
Scenario or master computations may have bounded nonzero error.
The classical stopping test compares master and incumbent bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact finite termination requires stronger error control than \(\inf_k\varepsilon_k>0\) and requires globally valid cuts.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited classical L-shaped section does not specifically support the claims about persistent oracle errors, certified inexact cuts, or exact termination under error sequences. A source treating inexact Benders or L-shaped methods is required to determine the necessary error conditions and conclusion.

children.title: Finite-Convergence Breakdown Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where classical finite termination no longer follows.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Convergence Breakdown Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined boundary of the standard finite-convergence theorem for linear two-stage recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The classical exact L-shaped finite-convergence argument applies when the first-stage master and scenario recourse problems are polyhedral, every required subproblem has a finite optimum or a valid feasibility certificate, solves and cuts are exact, and the algorithm does not regenerate previously processed information indefinitely. Removing any of these pillars breaks that argument: nonpolyhedral recourse can require infinitely many supporting planes; an unbounded-below subproblem yields no optimality cut; and persistent or uncertified computational error prevents exact bound closure. These failures negate the theorem's guarantee, although a particular instance may still terminate finitely for other reasons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonpolyhedral recourse, unbounded subproblems, or persistent inexactness each invalidates a pillar of the standard finite-convergence argument.
assumptions_latex: The reference guarantee is the exact finite-scenario linear L-shaped method.
Termination means exact certification of optimality.
No alternative finite-termination mechanism is presumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of a stated pillar removes the classical finite-convergence guarantee but does not prove nontermination of every instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Regularized Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratically stabilized cutting-plane decomposition for convex two-stage objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonempty closed convex set \(X\), a global cutting model \(m_k\leq F\), a center \(z_k\in X\), and \(\rho_k>0\), compute \[x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{m_k(x)+\frac{\rho_k}{2}\lVert x-z_k\rVert^2\right\}.\] Solve the scenario subproblems at \(x_{k+1}\), append certified feasibility or supporting optimality cuts to obtain \(m_{k+1}\), and compare actual and predicted decreases. If a prescribed serious-step test holds, set \(z_{k+1}=x_{k+1}\); otherwise set \(z_{k+1}=z_k\). Maintain an incumbent upper bound \(U_k\) and, separately from the stabilized objective, a valid global lower bound \(L_k=\inf_{x\in X}m_k(x)\) whenever this infimum is finite and computable. If infeasibility is certified, return that certificate; if \(U_k-L_k\) is at most the requested tolerance, return the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal term stabilizes cutting-plane trial points around a serious-step center, while certification uses bounds from the original cutting model rather than the proximal master value.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex on the nonempty closed convex set \(X\).
Every appended cut is globally valid.
Each stabilized master has a solution, and any lower bound used for termination is computed from the unregularized global model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever the stated infeasibility or bound-gap test is reached, the method returns the corresponding certificate or tolerance-certified incumbent.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal{Q}(a^v)\to-\infty\ \text{as }v\to\infty\quad\text{or}\quad \{a^v\}\text{ converges to a solution of the original problem.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularized Decomposition Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximally stabilized decomposition for a two-stage recourse problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize r=v=0, s_k=0 for k=1,\ldots,K, and choose a feasible point a^1. At each iteration, increment v and solve the regularized cut master problem
\[\min_{x,\theta}\;c^Tx+\sum_{k=1}^K\theta_k+\tfrac12\lVert x-a^v\rVert^2\]
subject to Ax=b, x\geq0, the accumulated feasibility cuts D_\ell x\geq d_\ell, and the accumulated scenario optimality cuts E_{\ell(k)}x+\theta_k\geq e_{\ell(k)}. If
\[c^Tx^v+e^T\theta^v=c^Ta^v+\mathcal Q(a^v),\]
stop with a^v optimal. A generated feasibility cut gives a^{v+1}=a^v. Otherwise, solve the scenario subproblems and add every optimality cut required by test (5.1.19). If no scenario requires such a cut, set a^{v+1}=x^v. If cuts are added, set a^{v+1}=x^v when
\[c^Tx^v+\mathcal Q(x^v)\leq c^Ta^v+\mathcal Q(a^v),\]
and otherwise set a^{v+1}=a^v. A generalized regularizer may have the form \alpha\lVert x-a^v\rVert^2 with \alpha>0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible center, the method repeatedly solves a quadratically regularized master problem containing accumulated feasibility and scenario optimality cuts. Feasibility cuts retain the center. If no scenario requires an optimality cut, the trial point becomes the new center; after cuts are added, the trial point is accepted only when it does not worsen the original objective. The stated Step 1 equality is the stopping test. A positive tunable quadratic coefficient is also described.
assumptions_latex: a^1\text{ is feasible}
k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}
\alpha>0\text{ for the generalized regularizer}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^Tx^v+e^T\theta^v=c^Ta^v+\mathcal Q(a^v)\Longrightarrow a^v\text{ is optimal}

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region L-Shaped Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: L-shaped cutting-plane method with an explicit neighborhood around the current serious-step center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z_k\in X\), radius \(\Delta_k>0\), norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\), and cutting model \(m_k\leq F\), solve \[x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{m_k(x):x\in X,\ \lVert x-z_k\rVert\leq\Delta_k\}.\] Evaluate scenario subproblems at \(x_{k+1}\), add certified cuts, and compare the actual decrease \(F(z_k)-F(x_{k+1})\) with the predicted decrease \(F(z_k)-m_k(x_{k+1})\). Accept \(x_{k+1}\) as the new center when their ratio exceeds a prescribed threshold; otherwise retain \(z_k\). Enlarge the radius after reliable steps, shrink it after poor steps, and stop when the global bound gap meets the requested tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The master trial point is restricted to a radius around the center, with acceptance and radius changes based on model accuracy.

The cutting model is a global lower model.
Trust-region masters and scenario evaluations are solved to the required accuracy.

children.title: Level Stabilization
children.top_down_role: Stabilization through controlled objective levels or level-set restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Level Stabilization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based stabilization using a target level between current lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(F^\star=\inf_{x\in X}F(x)\), and let \(m_k\leq F\) be a global convex lower model. Given a center \(z_k\in X\), certified bounds \(L_k\leq F^\star\leq U_k\), and \(\beta_k\in(0,1)\), set \(\ell_k=L_k+\beta_k(U_k-L_k)\). If the set \(\{x\in X:m_k(x)\leq\ell_k\}\) is nonempty, compute \[x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{\frac12\lVert x-z_k\rVert^2:m_k(x)\leq\ell_k\right\},\] evaluate the scenario subproblems, append valid cuts, and update the incumbent and center according to the prescribed serious-step rule. If the level set is empty and \(\underline L_k=\min_{x\in X}m_k(x)\) is computable, replace \(L_k\) by \(\max\{L_k,\underline L_k\}\). Return the incumbent when \(U_k-L_k\) is within tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an intermediate objective level and project the center onto the corresponding model level set; an empty level set permits a lower-bound update when the model minimum is computed.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and finite-dimensional.
\(m_k\) is a globally valid closed convex lower model.
Finite certified bounds satisfy \(L_k\leq F^\star\leq U_k\), and the model minimum used in an empty-level update is attained and computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonempty level set yields its nearest point to \(z_k\); an empty level set together with a computed model minimum yields a valid strengthened lower bound.

children.title: Bundle Stabilization
children.top_down_role: Stabilization using retained subgradient information plus localized master models.

knowledge_statements.title: Bundle Stabilization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal cutting-plane stabilization retaining selected subgradients and function values as a bundle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), let \(I_k\) be a finite index set and retain the bundle \(B_k=\{(x_i,F(x_i),g_i):i\in I_k,\ g_i\in\partial F(x_i)\}\). Form \[m_k(x)=\max_{i\in I_k}\{F(x_i)+g_i^{\mathsf T}(x-x_i)\}.\] Given a center \(z_k\in X\) and \(\rho_k>0\), minimize \[m_k(x)+\frac{\rho_k}{2}\lVert x-z_k\rVert^2\] over \(X\). Evaluate \(F\) and a valid subgradient at the minimizer, add this information to the bundle, and optionally aggregate or delete cuts while preserving the global lower-model property. Move the center after sufficient actual decrease; otherwise take a null step. Stop only when a certified optimality measure or a valid global upper-minus-lower bound gap is within tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite bundle of past subgradients builds a global lower model, while a proximal term and serious-step test stabilize its minimization.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex on the closed convex set \(X\).
Exact or certified inexact subgradients generate globally valid lower cuts.
Bundle management preserves model validity, and termination uses a certified optimality measure or valid global bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each nonterminal iteration produces either a serious center update or a null step that enriches or safely aggregates the lower model.

notation.meaning: finite index set for stored oracle information

children.title: Level-Bundle Hybrid Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Bundle Hybrid Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid stabilization combining a bundle lower model, a target level, and proximal center control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the bundle model \(m_k\leq F\), choose \(\ell_k=L_k+\beta_k(U_k-L_k)\) with \(\beta_k\in(0,1)\), and compute \[x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{\frac12\lVert x-z_k\rVert^2:m_k(x)\leq\ell_k\right\}.\] If the level set is empty, update \(L_k\) from \(\min_{x\in X}m_k(x)\). Otherwise query the scenario oracle at \(x_{k+1}\), add the resulting valid cuts to the bundle, update \(U_k\), and apply a serious-step test to the center. Bundle aggregation may be used provided it preserves the lower-model property. Return an incumbent when the bound gap meets tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hybrid projects onto a bundle-model level set, combining level control with accumulated cuts and serious-step center updates.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex on closed convex \(X\).
The bounds bracket the optimal value.
Every retained or aggregated bundle cut is globally valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hybrid either improves the lower bound, enriches the bundle, or accepts a center update while maintaining valid bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Stabilization-Center Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Serious-step and null-step rule governing the reference point of a stabilized master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_k\) be the center, let \(x_{k+1}\) minimize the stabilized master, and define predicted decrease \(p_k=F(z_k)-m_k(x_{k+1})\). After evaluating \(F(x_{k+1})\), define actual decrease \(a_k=F(z_k)-F(x_{k+1})\). For a fixed \(\eta\in(0,1)\), take a serious step and set \(z_{k+1}=x_{k+1}\) when \(p_k>0\) and \(a_k\geq\eta p_k\); otherwise take a null step and set \(z_{k+1}=z_k\). In either case, append the new valid oracle cuts. Stop when the certified model or bound gap is within tolerance, returning the best incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move the center only when actual improvement is a sufficient fraction of predicted improvement; otherwise retain it and refine the model.
assumptions_latex: \(m_k\leq F\) on the feasible set.
The trial-point objective value is evaluated consistently with the serious-step test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{k+1}=x_{k+1}\) on a serious step and \(z_{k+1}=z_k\) on a null step.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Quadratic L-Shaped Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: L-shaped master augmented by convex quadratic stabilization pieces or scenariowise quadratic models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a polyhedral L-shaped lower model \(m_k\leq F\), center \(z_k\), and finitely many positive-semidefinite matrices \(H_{kj}\), form the piecewise-quadratic model \[\widehat m_k(x)=\max_j\left\{m_{kj}(x)+\frac12(x-z_k)^{\mathsf T}H_{kj}(x-z_k)\right\},\] where every component \(m_{kj}(x)+\frac12(x-z_k)^{\mathsf T}H_{kj}(x-z_k)\) is a certified lower model. Minimize \(\widehat m_k\) over the first-stage feasible set, solve the scenario subproblems at the trial point, and append or update valid components. Apply a serious-step rule to the center and stop when certified upper and lower bounds differ by at most the requested tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The master minimizes a maximum of convex quadratic lower pieces, then updates those pieces using new scenario information.
assumptions_latex: The first-stage feasible set is closed and each master attains its minimum.
Every \(H_{kj}\) is positive semidefinite.
Each quadratic component is certified not to exceed the true objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat m_k\leq F\) remains a convex piecewise-quadratic master model and supplies a valid lower bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Positive-semidefinite curvature added to an affine or polyhedral lower model is not automatically a lower model of the objective. Although validity is imposed as an assumption, the cited general regularized-decomposition section does not identify the structural conditions or exact piecewise-quadratic L-shaped variant that supplies such certified components.

children.title: Parameter Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Behavioral dependence on regularization, radius, level, or acceptance parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stalling mechanisms caused by extreme or inadequately updated stabilization parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a proximal trial point minimizes \(m_k(x)+(\rho_k/2)\lVert x-z_k\rVert^2\), and every subgradient of \(m_k\) near \(z_k\) has norm at most \(G\). Its optimality condition gives \(\lVert x_{k+1}-z_k\rVert\leq G/\rho_k\). Thus excessively large \(\rho_k\) can force negligible steps; if \(\sum_k1/\rho_k<\infty\), the total possible center travel may be finite. Analogously, trust-region radii satisfying \(\sum_k\Delta_k<\infty\) may prevent the iterates from reaching a distant optimizer. Convergence therefore requires parameter-update safeguards responsive to model agreement; positivity of the parameters alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overly strong proximal penalties or summably small trust regions can restrict total movement and cause stabilization to stall away from an optimizer.
assumptions_latex: Local model subgradients are bounded by \(G<\infty\).
Centers can move only to accepted trial points.
No independent mechanism overrides the stated stabilization restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Summably restrictive stabilization can preclude sufficient center movement, so unrestricted parameter choices do not guarantee convergence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general stabilization sections do not specifically support the summability-based failure claims or the asserted convergence safeguards. The subgradient bound is also stated only 'near' the center without ensuring that every computed trial point lies in that region, so applicability of the step bound is uncertain.

children.title: Stalling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Persistent lack of meaningful bound or incumbent progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Stalling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic definition for stabilized L-shaped or bundle iterations, not a convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A run is in a stalling regime if it generates infinitely many iterations without satisfying its stopping test and there exist \(K\in\mathbb N\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that every \(k\ge K\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\ge\varepsilon\), while \(\Delta_k\to0\) and \(\lVert y_k-x_k\rVert\to0\). Thus the stabilized master ceases to propose materially different points before its centers reach the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stalling occurs when trial displacements and predicted improvements vanish while the incumbent centers remain a positive distance from every optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, and convex on a nonempty closed convex set \(X\).
The solution set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x)\) is nonempty.
At iteration \(k\), a stabilized cutting-plane master produces a trial point \(y_k\), center \(x_k\), model \(m_k\le F\), and predicted decrease \(\Delta_k=F(x_k)-m_k(y_k)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists K\in\mathbb N\ \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall k\ge K:\ \operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\ge\varepsilon,\qquad \Delta_k\to0,\qquad \lVert y_k-x_k\rVert\to0.\]

notation.meaning: Nonempty set of minimizers of the true objective over the feasible set.
Predicted objective decrease supplied by the stabilized master.

children.title: Serious-Step Failure
children.top_down_role: Repeated rejection of candidate points under serious-step acceptance logic.

knowledge_statements.title: Serious-Step Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eventual rejection criterion for the standard actual-versus-predicted decrease test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Serious-step failure occurs when the algorithm continues to obtain strictly positive model-predicted decreases but, from some iteration onward, every trial fails the acceptance test. Under the stated center-update rule, there exists \(K\in\mathbb N\) such that every \(k\ge K\) satisfies \(\Delta_k>0\), \(\rho_k<\eta\), and \(x_{k+1}=x_k\). This predicate diagnoses failure of center advancement; it does not imply that the fixed center is nonoptimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Serious-step failure means that every sufficiently late trial is rejected despite positive predicted improvement, so the stability center never advances.
assumptions_latex: For each iteration with \(\Delta_k>0\), define the actual decrease \(A_k=F(x_k)-F(y_k)\) and agreement ratio \(\rho_k=A_k/\Delta_k\).
A serious step is accepted exactly when \(\rho_k\ge\eta\), where \(\eta\in(0,1)\).
The center update is \(x_{k+1}=y_k\) after a serious step and \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) after a rejected, null step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists K\in\mathbb N\ \forall k\ge K:\quad \Delta_k>0,\quad \rho_k<\eta,\quad x_{k+1}=x_k.\]

notation.meaning: Actual reduction divided by model-predicted reduction.
Threshold for accepting a serious step.

children.title: Null-Step Proliferation
children.top_down_role: Excessive sequences of model-refinement steps without accepted center movement.

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Step Proliferation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-asymptotic-density formulation; weaker finite-window diagnostics are implementation dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Null-step proliferation is the failure regime in which null iterations have upper asymptotic density one: \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}N(k)/k=1\). If serious steps occur at indices \(s_j\) and \(r_j=s_{j+1}-s_j-1\) is the intervening null-block length, then \((r_j)\) is unbounded whenever infinitely many serious steps occur. The condition records excessive model-refinement iterations and does not alone establish nonconvergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Null-step proliferation occurs when the fraction of null iterations has limsup one; if serious steps continue indefinitely, the intervening null-step blocks must have unbounded length.
assumptions_latex: Each iteration is classified as serious or null by a fixed acceptance test.
For \(k\ge1\), let \(N(k)\) count null steps among iterations \(0,\ldots,k-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{N(k)}{k}=1.\]

notation.meaning: Number of null iterations before iteration k.
Number of null iterations between consecutive serious-step indices.

children.title: Scenario Bunching
children.top_down_role: Grouping of scenario subproblems into larger computational blocks.

assumptions_latex: The finite scenario set \(S\) has probabilities \(p_s>0\) with \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\).
For fixed first-stage \(x\), scenario recourse values \(Q_s(x)\) share no second-stage variables or constraints across scenarios.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Q(x)=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}Q_B(x),\qquad Q_B(x)=\sum_{s\in B}p_sQ_s(x).\]

notation.meaning: A partition of the scenario set into nonempty disjoint bunches.
Probability-weighted recourse contribution of bunch B.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact partitioning of a finite, additively separable two-stage recourse function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Scenario bunching selects a partition \(\mathcal P=\{B_1,\ldots,B_K\}\) of \(S\) and treats every bunch as one computational unit. For each \(B\in\mathcal P\), its exact contribution is \(Q_B(x)=\sum_{s\in B}p_sQ_s(x)\). Because the original recourse is scenario-additive, \(Q(x)=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}Q_B(x)\); bunching changes task granularity and possibly the form of generated aggregate cuts, but not the represented recourse value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario bunching partitions scenarios into computational groups and sums each group's weighted recourse values without changing the exact total recourse function.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Bunching

children.title: Full Scenario Decomposability
children.top_down_role: Independent scenario-level recourse evaluation under complete separability.

knowledge_statements.title: Full Scenario Decomposability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite two-stage model with coupling only through the fixed first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Full scenario decomposability holds when fixing \(x\) separates the deterministic equivalent into \(|S|\) independent recourse problems. Each \(Q_s(x)\) can then be evaluated without accessing variables or constraints belonging to any \(t\ne s\), and their probability-weighted sum exactly recovers \(Q(x)\). The scenario partition therefore exposes \(|S|\) scenario-level computational tasks, subject to available resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After fixing the first-stage decision, every scenario recourse problem can be evaluated independently, and their probability-weighted values exactly reconstruct total recourse.
assumptions_latex: The finite-scenario recourse function is \(Q(x)=\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(x)\), where \(S\) is finite, \(p_s>0\), and \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\).
Conditional on \(x\), each scenario subproblem has its own second-stage variables and constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Q(x)=\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(x),\qquad Q_s(x)\text{ is computable independently for every }s\in S.\]

notation.meaning: Optimal second-stage value in scenario s for fixed x.

children.title: Bunch-Size Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Computational effects of coarse versus fine scenario groupings.

assumptions_latex: A partition \(\mathcal P=\{B_1,\ldots,B_K\}\) of \(S\) is used, and \(b=\max_{B\in\mathcal P}|B|\).
Scenario contributions are additive and no cross-scenario constraints occur.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\le |S|,	\qquad b\ge \left\lceil\frac{|S|}{K}\right\rceil,	\qquad Q(x)=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}Q_B(x).\]

notation.meaning: Number of scenario bunches and hence maximum simultaneous bunch tasks.
Largest number of scenarios assigned to one bunch.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural granularity tradeoff, excluding hardware, communication, and solver-specific runtime models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(|S|\) scenarios partitioned into \(K\) bunches, the largest bunch size satisfies \(b\ge\lceil |S|/K\rceil\). Increasing \(K\) can expose more independent tasks and reduce the unavoidable largest bunch, while decreasing \(K\) aggregates more scenario work per task and reduces the number of separate results or cuts. Under additive recourse, every partition remains exact because \(Q(x)=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}Q_B(x)\); only computational granularity changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: More bunches expose more parallel tasks and permit smaller largest groups; fewer bunches aggregate more work, while additive recourse remains exact for every partition.
knowledge_statements.title: Bunch-Size Tradeoffs

children.title: Decomposability Loss Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Couplings or shared structures that prevent full scenario separation.

assumptions_latex: For fixed \(x\), second-stage variables are partitioned as \(y=(y_B)_{B\in\mathcal P}\).
The recourse feasible set is described by linear constraints that may involve variables from multiple bunches.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Y(x)=\prod_{B\in\mathcal P}Y_B(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{no irreducible constraint or variable couples distinct bunches}.\]

notation.meaning: Feasible second-stage set at fixed first-stage decision.
Feasible set local to scenario bunch B.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian-product boundary for exact independent solution of scenario bunches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact independent bunch solution is available precisely when, after fixing \(x\) and removing redundant constraints, the second-stage feasible set factors as \(Y(x)=\prod_{B\in\mathcal P}Y_B(x)\) and the objective is additive across the same blocks. An irreducible constraint containing variables from two distinct bunches, or a second-stage variable shared by them, destroys that product representation. Such coupled bunches must be merged or coordinated by an additional decomposition layer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent bunch solution ends when an irreducible constraint or shared second-stage variable couples different bunches, preventing a Cartesian-product feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Decomposability Loss Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general recourse section does not establish the partition-specific necessary-and-sufficient boundary. Moreover, Cartesian factorization of the feasible set alone does not yield independent optimization unless the objective is additive across the same blocks, and the phrase 'irreducible constraint' needs a precise representation-invariant definition.

children.title: Simple-Recourse Methods
children.top_down_role: Specialized decomposition for separable simple-recourse structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Simple-Recourse Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario linear simple recourse with separable positive and negative deviations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\), compute \(r_s=h_s-T_sx\), set \(y_s^+=(r_s)_+\) and \(y_s^-=(-r_s)_+\), and evaluate \(Q_s(x)=(q_s^+)^{\mathsf T}y_s^++(q_s^-)^{\mathsf T}y_s^-\). Choose a vector \(v_s\) componentwise with \((v_s)_i=(q_s^+)_i\) when \((r_s)_i>0\), \((v_s)_i=-(q_s^-)_i\) when \((r_s)_i<0\), and \((v_s)_i\in[-(q_s^-)_i,(q_s^+)_i]\) when \((r_s)_i=0\). Then \(-T_s^{\mathsf T}v_s\in\partial Q_s(x)\). For a finite scenario set, aggregate values and selected subgradients using the probabilities \(p_s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple recourse evaluates positive and negative residual deviations directly; a valid subgradient uses the active penalty, with any value in the penalty interval at a zero residual.
assumptions_latex: For each \(s\in S\), recourse satisfies \(y_s^+-y_s^-=h_s-T_sx\), with \(y_s^+,y_s^-\ge0\).
Penalty vectors satisfy \(q_s^+,q_s^-\ge0\).
The finite scenario set \(S\) has probabilities \(p_s>0\) satisfying \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Q_s(x)=(q_s^+)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)_+ +(q_s^-)^{\mathsf T}(T_sx-h_s)_+.\]

notation.meaning: A selected subgradient of the residual penalty function.

children.title: Network-Recourse Methods
children.top_down_role: Specialized decomposition exploiting flow or network structure in recourse.

assumptions_latex: For each scenario \(s\), the recourse matrix \(A_s\) is a node-arc incidence matrix of a directed network.
Arc-flow bounds and costs are linear, and the balance vector \(h_s-T_sx\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Q_s(x)=\min\{c_s^{\mathsf T}y:A_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ \ell_s\le y\le u_s\}.\]

notation.meaning: Node-arc incidence matrix for scenario s.
Optimal node potentials or balance-constraint multipliers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear capacitated network recourse solved separately for each finite scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\), form the scenario node-balance vector \(d_s=h_s-T_sx\) and solve the capacitated minimum-cost flow problem defining \(Q_s(x)\) by a network-flow algorithm. Obtain optimal balance multipliers \(\pi_s\), form the recourse subgradient \(-T_s^{\mathsf T}\pi_s\), and add the corresponding affine optimality cut to the first-stage master. Repeat scenario solves and master updates until the incumbent value minus the master lower bound is within the selected tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network recourse solves each scenario as a minimum-cost flow problem and uses optimal node potentials to generate first-stage recourse cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Network-Recourse Methods

children.title: Hybrid Simple-Network Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse structures containing both separable penalties plus network-constrained components.

assumptions_latex: After row and column permutations, each scenario recourse matrix is block diagonal.
Every diagonal block is either a simple-recourse block \([I,-I]\) or a directed-network incidence block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Q_s(x)=Q_s^{\mathrm{simp}}(x)+Q_s^{\mathrm{net}}(x).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-separable hybrid, excluding constraints coupling simple and network recourse variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If scenario recourse variables and constraints partition into uncoupled simple and network blocks, then the feasible set is their Cartesian product and the linear objective is additive. Consequently, \(Q_s(x)=Q_s^{\mathrm{simp}}(x)+Q_s^{\mathrm{net}}(x)\). The simple component is evaluated by positive and negative residual parts, while the network component is solved as a minimum-cost flow. The sum of their subgradients is a subgradient of \(Q_s\) and therefore defines a valid scenario cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncoupled simple-recourse and network-flow blocks can be solved by their specialized methods, with their values and subgradients added exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Simple-Network Recourse

children.title: Special-Recourse Recognition
children.top_down_role: Identification of recourse structure eligible for specialized processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Special-Recourse Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient structural recognition test for simple, network, or block-hybrid linear recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sufficient recognition condition is that, after decomposing the bipartite row-column incidence graph of \(W_s\), admissible row and column permutations and positive diagonal scalings transform the matrix into a block diagonal matrix whose grouped simple-recourse part has the form \([I,-I]\) and whose remaining diagonal blocks are directed node-arc incidence matrices. The simple part admits direct deviation evaluation, and each incidence block admits a network-flow solution. If both types occur without cross-block constraints, the scenario has hybrid special recourse; otherwise this sufficient test is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Special recourse is recognized when admissible permutations and positive scalings expose uncoupled simple-deviation and directed-network incidence blocks.
assumptions_latex: The scenario recourse problem is the linear program \(\min\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y:W_sy=h_s-T_sx,\ y\ge0\}\).
Recognition uses only row and column permutations, deletion of redundant rows, and positive diagonal row and column scalings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R P_rW_sP_c C=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(W^{\mathrm{simp}},W^{\mathrm{net}}_1,\ldots,W^{\mathrm{net}}_J\right),\qquad W^{\mathrm{simp}}=[I,-I],\] where each \(W^{\mathrm{net}}_j\) is a directed node-arc incidence matrix.

notation.meaning: Positive diagonal row and column scaling matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Linearization Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kelley-type inner linearization of convex recourse in a two-stage master problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Query an initial point \(x_0\in X\). At iteration \(k\), form \(m_k\) from the cuts generated at \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\), solve \(L_k=\min_{x\in X}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+m_k(x)\}\), and let \(x_{k+1}\) be a minimizer. Let \(\bar x_k\in\{x_0,ldots,x_k\}\) have the smallest evaluated true objective. If \(F(\bar x_k)-L_k\le\varepsilon\), output \(\bar x_k\); otherwise query \(Q(x_{k+1})\) and \(g_{k+1}\in\partial Q(x_{k+1})\), append the resulting affine minorant, and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner linearization repeatedly minimizes accumulated affine recourse underestimators, queries an exact recourse cut at the new master point, and stops when the evaluated incumbent and master lower bound are sufficiently close.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x+Q(x)\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(X\), with finite optimal value.
An oracle returns \(Q(x_k)\) and \(g_k\in\partial Q(x_k)\) at every queried point.
Every generated master problem has a finite attained minimum, and the prescribed tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(\bar x_k)-L_k\le\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F(\bar x_k)-\inf_{x\in X}F(x)\le\varepsilon.\]

notation.meaning: Maximum of accumulated affine minorants of recourse.

children.title: Basis-Factorization Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Decomposition exploiting simplex bases, factorization reuse, plus related linear-algebra structure.

assumptions_latex: The deterministic equivalent is a finite-scenario two-stage linear program with relatively complete recourse.
Each scenario recourse problem admits an optimal basic solution at every master iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each optimal scenario dual vector \(\pi_s^k\) generates the valid cut \(\theta_s\ge (\pi_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\).

notation.meaning: Scenario recourse matrix and right-hand-side data
Maintained primal basis and its factorization

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: revised-simplex dual multipliers give valid recourse cuts under linear-programming duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Revised-simplex implementation of scenario subproblems in finite two-stage linear recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a master point \(x^k\), solve independently for every scenario \(s\) the linear program \[Q_s(x^k)=\min_{y_s\ge0}\{q_s^{\mathsf T}y_s:W_sy_s=h_s-T_sx^k\}.\] Maintain a nonsingular basis \(B_s\) and factors \(B_s=L_sU_s\); use triangular solves and simplex pivots until primal and dual feasibility hold. Recover \(\pi_s^k=B_s^{-\mathsf T}q_{B_s}\), add \(\theta_s\ge(\pi_s^k)^{\mathsf T}(h_s-T_sx)\) to the master, and repeat until the master lower bound and evaluated recourse upper bound differ by at most the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve each scenario by revised simplex, reuse its basis factors, extract a dual recourse cut, and repeat master optimization until the certified bound gap meets tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Factorization Decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The revised-simplex cut construction is plausible and the algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the architecture-specific basis-factorization and stopping claims lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Interior-Point Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Decomposition architectures built around barrier solves or interior-point linear algebra.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual interior-point decomposition through scenario-block elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each primal-dual iteration, write the Newton equations as \[K_s\Delta z_s+A_s\Delta x=r_s\quad(s=1,\ldots,S),\qquad K_0\Delta x+\sum_{s=1}^S A_s^{\mathsf T}\Delta z_s=r_0.\] Factor the scenario blocks \(K_s\) independently, form \[H=K_0-\sum_{s=1}^S A_s^{\mathsf T}K_s^{-1}A_s,\qquad b=r_0-\sum_{s=1}^S A_s^{\mathsf T}K_s^{-1}r_s,\] solve \(H\Delta x=b\), and recover \(\Delta z_s=K_s^{-1}(r_s-A_s\Delta x)\). Apply a common feasible step length and stop when the primal, dual, and complementarity residuals satisfy their prescribed tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate independently factorable scenario Newton blocks, solve a nonsingular master Schur-complement system, recover the scenario directions, and terminate using interior-point residual tests.
assumptions_latex: The deterministic-equivalent Newton system has the displayed block-arrow structure.
Every scenario block \(K_s\) is nonsingular.
The Schur complement \(H=K_0-\sum_{s=1}^S A_s^{\mathsf T}K_s^{-1}A_s\) is nonsingular.
Iterates remain in the interior of the primal-dual cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Block elimination produces a nonsingular master Schur-complement system whose solution uniquely determines all scenario Newton directions.

children.title: Factorization Reuse Regimes
children.top_down_role: Reuse of scenario or master matrix factorizations across related solves.

assumptions_latex: Successive scenario linear systems have an identical coefficient matrix, or an unchanged simplex basis matrix.
Stored factors are nonsingular and retained with sufficient numerical accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unchanged coefficient or basis matrix requires new triangular solves but no new numerical factorization.

notation.meaning: Scenario linear-system matrix at outer iteration k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: identical nonsingular matrices share an LU factorization across right-hand sides
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact symbolic and numerical reuse for repeated scenario linear solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact numerical factorization reuse for scenario \(s\) is admissible between iterations \(k\) and \(k+1\) precisely when \(M_s^{k+1}=M_s^k\) and the stored factorization \(P_sM_s^kQ_s=L_sU_s\) remains accepted by the solver's stability test. Then \(M_s^{k+1}z=r_s^{k+1}\) is solved using only permutations and triangular substitutions. If only the sparsity pattern is unchanged, symbolic analysis may be reused but numerical refactorization is required; if the pattern changes, both symbolic analysis and numerical factorization must be recomputed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reuse numerical factors only when the matrix is unchanged and stable; reuse symbolic analysis alone when merely the sparsity pattern remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Reuse Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition and symbolic-versus-numerical reuse distinction are mathematically plausible and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the solver-stability and recomputation claims.

children.title: Solver-Architecture Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparative implications of basis-oriented versus barrier-oriented decomposition.

assumptions_latex: Scenario subproblems are independent conditional on the current master information.
Communication and synchronization costs are represented explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scenario decomposition replaces serial scenario work by parallel span plus coordination, while retaining the same aggregate arithmetic work.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: work-span accounting for conditionally independent scenario solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work, span, memory, and synchronization tradeoffs of solver decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For one outer iteration, a monolithic serial architecture expends scenario work \(\sum_s C_s\), whereas an ideal scenario-decomposed architecture has the same total arithmetic work but parallel time bounded below by \(\max\{\max_s C_s,(\sum_sC_s)/P\}\) and increased by \(C_0+C_{\mathrm{comm}}\). Replicating scenario data permits concurrent solves but increases aggregate memory; centralizing factorizations reduces replication but introduces contention. Thus decomposition improves elapsed time only when saved scenario span exceeds master, communication, synchronization, and load-imbalance costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposition preserves total scenario work but can reduce elapsed time through parallelism, at the price of coordination, imbalance, contention, and replicated memory.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Architecture Tradeoffs

children.title: Scenario-Wise Nonanticipativity Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Scenario splitting through dualization, penalization, and consensus treatment of nonanticipativity.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Lectures on Stochastic Programming: Modeling and Theory

assumptions_latex: Each scenario feasible set \(X_s\) is nonempty, and every scenario Lagrangian infimum is finite.
The deterministic equivalent imposes nonanticipativity through \(x_s=z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonanticipativity dual is \(\sup_{\lambda:\sum_s\lambda_s=0}\sum_s\inf_{x_s\in X_s}(p_sf_s(x_s)+\lambda_s^{\mathsf T}x_s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario Lagrangian relaxation of consensus nonanticipativity equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(v=\inf\{\sum_{s=1}^S p_sf_s(x_s):x_s\in X_s,\ x_s=z\ \forall s\}\). Dualizing only \(x_s=z\) gives \[L(x,z,\lambda)=\sum_s\bigl(p_sf_s(x_s)+\lambda_s^{\mathsf T}x_s\bigr)-\left(\sum_s\lambda_s\right)^{\mathsf T}z.\] Minimization over unrestricted \(z\) is finite exactly when \(\sum_s\lambda_s=0\). Hence the dual function decomposes as \(g(\lambda)=\sum_s\inf_{x_s\in X_s}(p_sf_s(x_s)+\lambda_s^{\mathsf T}x_s)\), and the Lagrangian scenario dual is \(\sup\{g(\lambda):\sum_s\lambda_s=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relax consensus equations with zero-sum multipliers. The resulting dual objective is a sum of independent scenario infima and can therefore be evaluated scenario-wise.
knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Scenario Decomposition
Nonanticipativity Dual-Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificates from decomposed nonanticipativity relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v\) be the optimal value of the primal minimization problem with constraints \(x_s=z\), and let multipliers satisfy \(\sum_{s=1}^S\lambda_s=0\). If certified values \(\ell_s\) satisfy \[\ell_s\le\inf_{x_s\in X_s}\bigl(p_sf_s(x_s)+\lambda_s^{\mathsf T}x_s\bigr)\quad(s=1,\ldots,S),\] then \[L=\sum_{s=1}^S\ell_s\le v.\] Thus \((\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_S,\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_S)\) is a verifiable global lower-bound certificate. Exact scenario minima give \(L=g(\lambda)\); independently certified inexact scenario lower bounds also remain valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-sum multipliers together with certified lower bounds for every scenario Lagrangian subproblem form a verifiable lower-bound certificate for the original minimization problem.
assumptions_latex: The primal is a minimization problem with consensus constraints \(x_s=z\).
The multipliers satisfy \(\sum_{s=1}^S\lambda_s=0\).
Each reported value \(\ell_s\) is a valid lower bound for its scenario Lagrangian subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sum \(L=\sum_{s=1}^S\ell_s\) satisfies \(L\le v\) and is a global primal lower-bound certificate.

notation.meaning: Zero-sum nonanticipativity multiplier for scenario s

children.title: Dual Bundle Methods
children.top_down_role: Bundle-based maximization of nonsmooth nonanticipativity dual functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Bundle Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal bundle maximization of the concave nonanticipativity dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\bar\lambda^0\in\Lambda\) and query \((g(\lambda^0),d^0)\). From bundle \(I_k\), form the concave upper model \[m_k(\lambda)=\min_{i\in I_k}\left\{g(\lambda^i)+(d^i)^{\mathsf T}(\lambda-\lambda^i)\right\}.\] Choose \[\lambda^{k+1}\in\arg\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\left\{m_k(\lambda)-\frac{\rho_k}{2}\|\lambda-\bar\lambda^k\|^2\right\},\] query the oracle, and append its plane. Accept a serious step by setting \(\bar\lambda^{k+1}=\lambda^{k+1}\) when actual dual ascent is a prescribed fraction of predicted ascent; otherwise retain the center. Stop when the model-predicted ascent is within tolerance and return the best evaluated dual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build a polyhedral upper model from dual supergradients, maximize its proximal regularization, and use serious or null steps until predicted improvement is negligible.
assumptions_latex: The feasible multiplier space \(\Lambda\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The concave dual oracle returns a finite value and supergradient at every queried multiplier.
The proximal weight satisfies \(\rho_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proximal cutting-plane subproblem produces stabilized feasible trial multipliers and maintains a valid polyhedral upper model of the concave dual function.

notation.meaning: Concave dual function and feasible multiplier set
Proximal center and positive proximal weight
Polyhedral upper model of the concave dual function

assumptions_latex: The feasible multiplier set \(\Lambda\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
At each iterate, the scenario oracle supplies a supergradient of the concave dual function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projected supergradient ascent preserves multiplier feasibility and searches for a maximum of the nonsmooth concave dual.

notation.meaning: Dual multiplier and feasible multiplier set
Dual supergradient assembled from scenario residuals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected supergradient ascent for a nonsmooth concave scenario dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\lambda^0\in\Lambda\). At iteration \(k\), solve the scenario Lagrangian subproblems, evaluate \(g(\lambda^k)\), and assemble a supergradient \(d^k\) from their nonanticipativity residuals. Update \[\lambda^{k+1}=\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda^k+\alpha_kd^k),\qquad \alpha_k>0.\] For the zero-sum multiplier space, \(\Pi_\Lambda\) subtracts the scenario mean multiplier component. Record the largest evaluated dual value. Stop when a certified primal-dual gap meets tolerance, or under a search-only convention when the step and projected residual satisfy prescribed tolerances; output the best multiplier and dual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ascend along scenario-derived dual supergradients, project onto the zero-sum multiplier space, and retain the best certified dual value encountered.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Dual Search

children.title: Dual Stabilization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Localization or regularization choices for nonsmooth dual progress.

assumptions_latex: A concave dual function is represented by a bundle upper model \(m_k\).
The feasible multiplier set \(\Lambda\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proximal, trust-region, and level stabilization restrict trial multipliers relative to a center or target while preserving feasibility in \(\Lambda\).

notation.meaning: Bundle model and feasible multiplier set
Proximal weight, trust radius, and target level

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three standard stabilization forms for nonsmooth dual master problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a stability center \(\bar\lambda^k\in\Lambda\), standard stabilized dual trials are represented by: proximal stabilization, \[\arg\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\left\{m_k(\lambda)-\frac{\rho_k}{2}\|\lambda-\bar\lambda^k\|^2\right\};\] trust-region stabilization, \(\arg\max\{m_k(\lambda):\lambda\in\Lambda,\ \|\lambda-\bar\lambda^k\|\le\Delta_k\}\); and level stabilization, choosing a point in \(\{\lambda\in\Lambda:m_k(\lambda)\ge\ell_k\}\) closest to \(\bar\lambda^k\). Here \(\rho_k>0\), \(\Delta_k>0\), and the level set must be nonempty. Parameter updates respond to serious and null steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal penalties, trust regions, and target levels are alternative ways to keep nonsmooth dual trial multipliers near a stable center.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Stabilization Regimes

children.title: Dual Oracle Inexactness
children.top_down_role: Effects of approximate scenario solves on dual values plus subgradient information.

assumptions_latex: The scenario oracle returns a feasible Lagrangian point whose value is within \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\) of the exact scenario infimum.
The multiplier space is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual from an \(\varepsilon_k\)-optimal scenario solution is an \(\varepsilon_k\)-supergradient, but its approximate objective value is not automatically a certified dual lower bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error scenario oracles for nonsmooth nonanticipativity dual search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose approximate scenario minimizers at \(\lambda^k\) have aggregate Lagrangian value \(\widetilde g_k\) satisfying \(g(\lambda^k)\le\widetilde g_k\le g(\lambda^k)+\varepsilon_k\). Their aggregate nonanticipativity residual \(\widetilde d^k\) satisfies the inexact supergradient inequality \[g(\mu)\le g(\lambda^k)+(\widetilde d^k)^{\mathsf T}(\mu-\lambda^k)+\varepsilon_k\quad\text{for all }\mu\in\Lambda.\] Because \(\widetilde g_k\) is an upper approximation to the infimum defining \(g(\lambda^k)\), it is not itself a certified primal lower bound. Certification requires independent scenario lower bounds, while convergence rules must control or drive \(\varepsilon_k\) to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate scenario minimizers yield error-tolerant dual supergradients, but their objective values are not certified lower bounds unless separate scenario lower bounds are available.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Oracle Inexactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive-error supergradient inequality and warning about approximate infimum values are plausible and appropriately typed, but this nontrivial inexact-oracle result requires an inspectable source.

children.title: Positive Duality Gaps
children.top_down_role: Regimes where nonanticipativity dual bounds do not recover the primal optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Duality Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonconvex consensus example with a strict Lagrangian duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,x_2\in\{0,1,2\}\), impose \(x_1=x_2\), and define \[(f_1(0),f_1(1),f_1(2))=(0,100,0),\qquad (f_2(0),f_2(1),f_2(2))=(100,0,100).\] The primal optimal value is \(v=100\). Relaxing \(x_1=x_2\) with \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) gives \[g(\lambda)=\min\{0,100+\lambda,2\lambda\}+\min\{100,-\lambda,100-2\lambda\}.\] Its dual optimal value is \(\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R}g(\lambda)=0\), so the Lagrangian duality gap is \(v-\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R}g(\lambda)=100\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two discrete scenarios have consensus optimum 100, whereas their nonanticipativity Lagrangian dual has optimal value 0, giving a positive duality gap of 100.
assumptions_latex: The scenario decisions satisfy \(x_1,x_2\in\{0,1,2\}\).
Nonanticipativity requires \(x_1=x_2\).
The scenario costs are the displayed functions \(f_1\) and \(f_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal value is \(100\), the nonanticipativity Lagrangian dual value is \(0\), and the positive duality gap is \(100\).

notation.meaning: Multiplier for the equality x1 equals x2
