children.title: Scenario-Tree Explosion
children.top_down_role: Growth in tree nodes, branches, plus stagewise subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Tree Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact node and leaf counts for a full stagewise branching tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a scenario tree have root stage \(0\), horizon \(T\), and uniform branching factor \(b_t\geq1\) from stage \(t-1\) to stage \(t\). Then the number of stage-\(t\) nodes is \(N_t=\prod_{s=1}^t b_s\), the number of leaves is \(L=\prod_{s=1}^T b_s\), and the total number of nodes is \[N=1+\sum_{t=1}^T\prod_{s=1}^t b_s.\] For constant branching \(b>1\), \(N=(b^{T+1}-1)/(b-1)\) and \(L=b^T\); hence explicit tree construction and any per-node computation require exponential resources in the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With constant branching greater than one, scenario-tree leaves and total nodes grow exponentially with the number of stages.
assumptions_latex: The tree is full through horizon \(T\).
Every stage-\(t-1\) node has exactly \(b_t\) children.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=1+\sum_{t=1}^T\prod_{s=1}^t b_s\), which is \(\Theta(b^T)\) when \(b_t=b>1\).

notation.meaning: number of nodes at stage t

children.title: Cut Proliferation
children.top_down_role: Rapid accumulation of node-specific value-function cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Proliferation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Growth of stored cuts under nodewise and combinatorial cut-generation policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal N\) be the set of nonterminal tree nodes and let \(K_n(k)\) denote the cuts retained at node \(n\) after \(k\) iterations. If at most \(r_n\) cuts are added per iteration and none are deleted, then \[K_n(k)\leq K_n(0)+kr_n,\qquad K_{\mathrm{tot}}(k)\leq K_{\mathrm{tot}}(0)+k\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}r_n.\] Thus even one new cut per visited node gives \(\Theta(k|\mathcal N|)\) stored cuts when all nodes are visited. Moreover, explicitly enumerating one aggregate cut for every selection of a child cut can create up to \(\prod_{m\in\mathcal C(n)}K_m(k)\) candidate combinations at node \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without deletion or aggregation, nodewise cuts grow linearly in iterations and tree size; enumerating combinations of child cuts can grow multiplicatively.
assumptions_latex: Cuts are retained permanently.
At most \(r_n\) new cuts are stored at node \(n\) per iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_{\mathrm{tot}}(k)\leq K_{\mathrm{tot}}(0)+k\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}r_n\).

notation.meaning: cuts retained at node n after k iterations
maximum cuts added at node n per iteration

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Cut Storage Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-storage cost for explicit affine cuts distributed over tree nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At node \(n\), suppose each affine cut \(\alpha_{nj}+\beta_{nj}^{\mathsf T}x\) acts on a state of dimension \(d_n\), and \(K_n\) cuts are stored densely. Storing all cut coefficients and intercepts requires exactly \(\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}K_n(d_n+1)\) scalar slots, hence memory \[M=\Theta\!\left(\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}K_n(d_n+1)\right).\] If \(K_n=K\) and \(d_n=d\), then \(M=\Theta(|\mathcal N|K(d+1))\). With one retained cut per node per iteration, this becomes \(\Theta(|\mathcal N|k(d+1))\) after \(k\) iterations, excluding solver bases, tree data, and sparse-index overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense storage scales with the sum, over nodes, of retained cuts times state dimension plus one intercept.
assumptions_latex: Cut slopes are stored densely.
Each node-\(n\) cut contains \(d_n\) slope coefficients and one intercept.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=\Theta(\sum_{n\in\mathcal N}K_n(d_n+1))\) scalar storage locations.

children.title: Master-Burden Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where tree size or cut volume overwhelms master-level computation.

assumptions_latex: A finite scenario tree is used for a multistage linear stochastic program.
Each nonterminal node master contains a polyhedral approximation of its downstream value function.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If node \(n\) has \(d_n\) state variables and \(K_n\) retained cuts, its explicit master description requires \(\Theta(d_nK_n)\) cut-coefficient storage and contains \(K_n\) additional inequalities. Across the tree, cut storage is \(\Theta\!\left(\sum_n d_nK_n\right)\). Thus nested decomposition crosses the master-burden boundary when forming, storing, or repeatedly solving these growing node masters dominates the work and memory of generating new child-subproblem information; the boundary depends on solver behavior and sparsity, not only on scenario count.

notation.meaning: Decision-state dimension at scenario-tree node n.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit-cut storage boundary for finite-tree nested Benders decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite scenario tree, let node \(n\) have a master state of dimension \(d_n\) and retain \(K_n\) affine Benders cuts. Explicit storage of its cut matrix requires \(\Theta(d_nK_n)\) coefficients, while the master has \(K_n\) cut inequalities in addition to its structural constraints. Hence total cut storage satisfies
\[S=\Theta\!\left(\sum_n d_nK_n\right).\]
The master-burden boundary is reached when the memory or repeated-solution cost of these enlarged masters exceeds the corresponding cost of generating additional child-subproblem cuts. No solver-independent time threshold follows from \(d_n\) and \(K_n\) alone, because sparsity, warm starts, and cut deletion affect solution time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit node-master storage grows with state dimension times retained cuts; master burden becomes limiting when storing or resolving those masters costs more than generating downstream cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampled Policy Exploration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward exploration step of finite-horizon SDDP with pre-decision states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration \(k\), initialize \(x_0^k=x_0\). For \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), choose
\[u_t^k\in\arg\min_{u\in U_t(x_t^k)}\left\{c_t(x_t^k,u)+\mathbb E\!\left[\underline V_{t+1}^k\bigl(f_t(x_t^k,u,\xi_{t+1})\bigr)\mid\mathcal F_t\right]\right\}.\]
After choosing \(u_t^k\), sample \(\xi_{t+1}^k\) from its conditional law given \(\mathcal F_t\) and set \(x_{t+1}^k=f_t(x_t^k,u_t^k,\xi_{t+1}^k)\). The resulting feasible sampled trajectory supplies visited states to the backward refinement step. Repeated iterations explore states reachable under the evolving approximate policy and sampling law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each stage, choose a feasible decision using the current value approximation, then sample the next disturbance, update the state, and retain the visited states for backward refinement.
assumptions_latex: A finite-horizon stochastic control problem is formulated with pre-decision states \(x_t\).
The feasible set \(U_t(x_t)\), stage cost, transition map, and conditional disturbance law are measurable, and the displayed conditional expectations are finite.
The decision \(u_t\) is chosen using \(\mathcal F_t\) before \(\xi_{t+1}\) is observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recursion produces a feasible nonanticipative sampled trajectory and visits only states reachable under the evolving approximate policy and the prescribed sampling law.

notation.meaning: Current approximation of the stage-t cost-to-go function.
Pre-decision state visited at stage t in iteration k.
Decision selected at stage t in iteration k.
Next disturbance sampled after the stage-t decision.

knowledge_statements.title: Backward Value-Function Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward cut update for convex finite-horizon SDDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Process stages in the order \(t=T,T-1,\ldots,1\). At the forward state \(x_{t-1}^k\), solve the convex stage subproblems using the newest available lower approximation \(\underline V_{t+1}^{k+1}\). Let \(Q_t^k\) denote the resulting approximate Bellman value. From optimal dual solutions and an exact or otherwise validity-preserving treatment of the conditional expectation, form an affine function
\[\ell_t^k(x)=\alpha_t^k+(\beta_t^k)^{\mathsf T}x\le Q_t^k(x)\le V_t(x).\]
When the approximate subproblem is solved exactly and strong duality holds, the support is tight for the approximate value at the trial state:
\[\ell_t^k(x_{t-1}^k)=Q_t^k(x_{t-1}^k).\]
Update
\[\underline V_t^{k+1}(x)=\max\{\underline V_t^k(x),\ell_t^k(x)\}.\]
Every such update preserves the lower-bound property and is pointwise nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The backward pass solves approximate stage problems at visited states, derives affine supports of those approximate Bellman values, and adds the valid cuts to the lower value models.
assumptions_latex: Each approximate stage problem is convex and satisfies strong duality at the sampled predecessor state.
Existing future-value approximations are pointwise lower bounds on the corresponding exact values.
Conditional expectations are evaluated exactly or by a construction that guarantees each generated cut is a valid lower bound; unbiasedness alone is not sufficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each generated cut is a lower bound on the exact stage value, is tight at the trial state for the solved approximate Bellman value under exact solution, and yields a pointwise nondecreasing valid lower approximation when added.

notation.meaning: Current lower approximation of the stage-t cost-to-go function.
Approximate Bellman value formed using the current future-value approximation.
Affine cut generated for stage t at iteration k.
Forward-pass predecessor state used for refinement.

assumptions_latex: The exact stage cost-to-go function is convex on a convex state domain.
Every generated affine cut is a global lower bound on that function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum of retained cuts is a convex polyhedral lower approximation. Adding a valid cut raises or preserves the approximation everywhere, while deleting cuts preserves validity but may weaken the bound.

notation.meaning: Index set of retained stage-t cuts after iteration k.
Polyhedral lower approximation of the cost-to-go function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral lower models used by convex SDDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For stage \(t\), let each retained affine function be \(\ell_{tj}(x)=\alpha_{tj}+\beta_{tj}^{\mathsf T}x\) and satisfy \(\ell_{tj}(x)\le V_t(x)\) for every state \(x\) in the convex domain \(X_t\). The cut-family representation is
\[\underline V_t^k(x)=\max_{j\in J_t^k}\{\alpha_{tj}+\beta_{tj}^{\mathsf T}x\}.\]
Then \(\underline V_t^k\) is convex and polyhedral, and \(\underline V_t^k(x)\le V_t(x)\) on \(X_t\). If \(J_t^k\subseteq J_t^{k+1}\), then \(\underline V_t^k(x)\le\underline V_t^{k+1}(x)\le V_t(x)\) for every \(x\in X_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost-to-go approximation is the maximum of valid affine lower cuts; adding cuts strengthens the polyhedral lower bound pointwise.
knowledge_statements.title: Cost-to-Go Cut Families

children.title: Out-of-Sample Policy Simulation
children.top_down_role: Simulation-based evaluation of a fixed SDDP policy on fresh trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Out-of-Sample Policy Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent Monte Carlo evaluation of a fixed SDDP policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Freeze a feasible nonanticipative policy \(\pi\) before evaluation. Generate \(N\ge2\) independent test trajectories from the target information process, apply \(\pi\) without re-estimation, and record the total costs \(Z_1^\pi,\ldots,Z_N^\pi\). Return
\[\widehat J_N(\pi)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i^\pi,\qquad s_N^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(Z_i^\pi-\widehat J_N(\pi)\bigr)^2.\]
Writing \(J(\pi)=\mathbb E[Z_1^\pi]\), if \(\mathbb E[|Z_1^\pi|]<\infty\), then \(\mathbb E[\widehat J_N(\pi)]=J(\pi)\) and \(\widehat J_N(\pi)\to J(\pi)\) almost surely. If \(\operatorname{Var}(Z_1^\pi)<\infty\), the estimated standard error is \(s_N/\sqrt{N}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Freeze the policy, simulate at least two independent test trajectories, and use their mean cost and sample variance to estimate out-of-sample performance and its standard error.
assumptions_latex: A feasible nonanticipative policy \(\pi\) is fixed independently of the evaluation sample.
The evaluation costs \(Z_1^\pi,\ldots,Z_N^\pi\) are independent and identically distributed under the target information process.
The sample size satisfies \(N\ge2\), and the policy cost is integrable; finite variance is additionally required for the standard-error statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sample mean is an unbiased and strongly consistent estimator of \(J(\pi)\). Under finite variance, \(s_N/\sqrt{N}\) estimates its standard error.

notation.meaning: Fixed feasible nonanticipative policy being evaluated.
Total policy cost on test trajectory i.
Number of independent test trajectories, with N at least two.
Expected total cost of the fixed policy.

children.title: Policy Upper-Bound Estimation
children.top_down_role: Statistical upper bounds derived from simulated feasible policy costs.

assumptions_latex: The problem minimizes expected total cost over nonanticipative policies.
The evaluated policy is feasible and fixed independently of the evaluation sample.
Independent policy costs have finite variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy value is an upper bound on the optimal value, and the displayed one-sided normal interval is an asymptotic confidence upper bound for that policy value.

notation.meaning: Expected cost of feasible policy pi.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention and asymptotic Monte Carlo certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimization problem, every feasible nonanticipative policy \(\pi\) satisfies
\[v^\star=\inf_{\rho}J(\rho)\le J(\pi).\]
Using \(N\) independent costs from a policy fixed before evaluation, compute \(\widehat J_N(\pi)\) and \(s_N\). Under finite, nonzero variance, the central limit theorem yields the asymptotic one-sided certificate
\[U_{N,\alpha}=\widehat J_N(\pi)+z_{1-\alpha}\frac{s_N}{\sqrt N},\qquad \lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb P\{J(\pi)\le U_{N,\alpha}\}=1-\alpha.\]
Consequently \(U_{N,\alpha}\) is also an asymptotic upper confidence bound for \(v^\star\), although it primarily certifies the fixed policy's value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any feasible policy bounds the minimum expected cost from above; independent simulation gives an asymptotic one-sided confidence upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Policy Upper-Bound Estimation

children.title: Value Lower-Bound Estimation
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound certificates obtained from value-function approximations.

assumptions_latex: The problem minimizes expected total cost.
Every approximate future-value function used in the root problem is a pointwise lower bound on the exact future value.
The root optimization is solved globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The approximate root optimum is a deterministic lower bound on the true optimal value. It becomes a statistical estimate only when conditional expectations or cuts are themselves sampled.

notation.meaning: Exact optimal value of the multistage minimization problem.
Valid lower approximation of the first future-value function.
Lower-bound value obtained from the approximate root problem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root lower bound from valid cost-to-go underestimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V_1(x)\) be the exact future cost from a root successor state and let \(\underline V_1(x)\le V_1(x)\) for every reachable \(x\). Define
\[L=\inf_{u\in U_0(x_0)}\left\{c_0(x_0,u)+\underline V_1\bigl(f_0(x_0,u)\bigr)\right\}.\]
The exact root problem replaces \(\underline V_1\) by \(V_1\); therefore \(L\le v^\star\). Thus the optimized approximate root objective is a verifiable lower-bound certificate whenever feasibility, global root optimization, and the pointwise validity of all contributing cuts are established. If sampled conditional expectations enter the cuts, additional statistical validity is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing the root problem with pointwise lower cost-to-go approximations yields a lower bound on the true minimum value.
knowledge_statements.title: Value Lower-Bound Estimation

children.title: Simulation-Certificate Bias
children.top_down_role: Bias or dependence affecting reported policy bounds.

assumptions_latex: At least two candidate policies are evaluated on the same finite sample.
The policy reported by the procedure minimizes its sample mean cost.
The reported sample is reused for certification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected in-sample mean is downward biased for the selected policy's true mean in general, so it cannot automatically serve as an unbiased upper-bound estimator. An independent evaluation sample removes this selection bias conditionally on the frozen policy.

notation.meaning: Sample mean cost for candidate policy j.
True expected cost for candidate policy j.
Index selected by minimizing the sample mean.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias caused by selecting and certifying on one simulation sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\ge2\) candidate policies have unbiased sample-mean estimates \(\widehat J_j\) of costs \(J_j\), and select \(\widehat j\in\arg\min_{1\le j\le m}\widehat J_j\). Then
\[\mathbb E[\widehat J_{\widehat j}]=\mathbb E\!\left[\min_j\widehat J_j\right]\le\min_jJ_j.\]
For example, if all \(J_j=\mu\) and the estimates are independent, nondegenerate, and identically distributed, the inequality is strict. Hence reusing the selection sample makes the reported cost optimistically biased and may invalidate an upper-bound certificate for a minimization problem. Conditional on a frozen selected policy, evaluation on a fresh independent sample restores unbiasedness for that policy's expected cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting the best policy and certifying it on the same simulations creates optimistic cost bias; independent post-selection evaluation avoids this failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulation-Certificate Bias

knowledge_statements.title: Stagewise-Independent Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagewise independence condition used by classical SDDP together with controlled-state sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite-horizon disturbance process is stagewise independent when, for every \(t=1,\ldots,T\),
\[\mathcal L(\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_t\quad\text{almost surely},\]
where \(P_t\) is a deterministic probability law. Equivalently, for every bounded measurable function \(g\),
\[\mathbb E[g(\xi_t)\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\int g(z)\,P_t(dz)\quad\text{almost surely}.\]
If, in addition, current costs, feasible decisions, and state transitions depend on the observed history only through the controlled state \(x_t\) and the current disturbance revealed before the decision, the dynamic recursion needs no additional history-dependent information-state index. Under these conditions, classical SDDP may maintain one cost-to-go function \(V_t(x)\) per stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stagewise independence means that each disturbance has a fixed conditional law given the past. One cost-to-go function per stage suffices when the controlled state also captures every history dependence in costs, feasibility, and transitions.
assumptions_latex: The disturbance sequence \((\xi_t)_{t=1}^T\) is defined on a filtered probability space with history filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\).
For each stage \(t\), the conditional law of \(\xi_t\) given \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\) is a deterministic law \(P_t\).
The controlled state \(x_t\), together with the currently observed disturbance when applicable, is sufficient for stage costs, feasible decisions, and controlled transitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The disturbance recursion carries no history-dependent information-state index, and a stage-indexed value function \(V_t(x)\) is valid when the controlled state is sufficient for the remaining model data.

notation.meaning: Information sigma-field available through stage t.
Deterministic probability law of the stage-t disturbance.
Controlled state carrying physical interstage dependence.

children.title: Markovian Information Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stagewise transitions governed by a finite or structured Markov state.

knowledge_statements.title: Markovian Information Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled Markov information regime for dynamic decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_t\in X_t\) be the controlled state, \(s_t\in S_t\) an observable information state, and \(u_t\in U_t(x_t,s_t)\) an admissible action. The regime is Markovian when a transition kernel \(K_t\) satisfies, for every measurable set \(B\subseteq X_{t+1}\times S_{t+1}\),
\[\mathbb P\bigl((x_{t+1},s_{t+1})\in B\mid\mathcal F_t,u_t\bigr)=K_t(B\mid x_t,s_t,u_t)\quad\text{almost surely},\]
and the current cost and feasible-action set depend on the observed history only through \((x_t,s_t)\). Then \((x_t,s_t)\) is a sufficient dynamic-programming state, and for a finite-horizon minimization problem the recursion is
\[V_t(x,s)=\inf_{u\in U_t(x,s)}\left\{c_t(x,s,u)+\int_{X_{t+1}\times S_{t+1}}V_{t+1}(x',s')\,K_t(d x',d s'\mid x,s,u)\right\}.\]
Thus value approximations may be indexed by the current information state rather than the complete history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Markovian information regime uses an observable information state which, together with the controlled state and action, determines conditional transitions, costs, and feasibility.
assumptions_latex: For each stage \(t\), the controlled-state space \(X_t\), information-state space \(S_t\), and action space are measurable spaces.
The feasible-action multifunction \(U_t\), stage cost \(c_t\), and controlled transition kernel \(K_t\) are well defined and measurable.
The pair \((x_t,s_t)\) captures all history dependence relevant to conditional transitions, current costs, and feasible actions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((x_t,s_t)\) is sufficient for dynamic programming, and the value recursion is indexed by the current information state rather than by the full observed history.

notation.meaning: Controlled physical or resource state at stage t.

children.title: State-Augmented Information Regimes
children.top_down_role: Expanded state representations used to recover conditional structure.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Augmented Information Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Markovization by a recursively updated sufficient statistic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H_t\) denote the observed history and define an information summary \(s_t=\phi_t(H_t)\) with recursive update
\[s_{t+1}=F_t(s_t,u_t,y_{t+1}).\]
The augmentation is exact when the conditional law of all future observations and controlled transitions, given \(H_t\) and an admissible action \(u_t\), depends on the history only through \((x_t,s_t,u_t)\), and when current costs and feasible-action sets are measurable functions of \((x_t,s_t,u_t)\). Under these sufficiency conditions, \((x_t,s_t)\) is a Markov state. The history-dependent problem and the dynamic program on the augmented state have the same optimal value, and an optimal policy may be chosen as a function of the augmented state whenever the usual dynamic-programming existence conditions hold. The augmented state may be finite- or infinite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recursively updated summary exactly Markovizes a history-dependent problem when it preserves all predictive, cost, and feasibility information needed for future decisions.
assumptions_latex: The observed history at stage \(t\) is \(H_t\), and the controlled physical state is \(x_t\).
A measurable summary \(s_t=\phi_t(H_t)\) admits a recursive update after each action and new observation.
The summary preserves the conditional laws, current costs, and feasible actions relevant to all future decisions.
The dynamic program satisfies the regularity conditions needed for its value recursion and, where claimed, existence of an optimal augmented-state policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented pair \((x_t,s_t)\) is a sufficient Markov state and yields the same optimal value as the original history-dependent formulation. Failure of predictive, cost, or feasibility sufficiency invalidates exact reduction.

notation.meaning: New observation used to update the information summary.

children.title: Markov-State Approximation
children.top_down_role: Compressed or discretized representations of the governing information state.

assumptions_latex: A history-dependent process is replaced by a measurable approximate state map.
An approximate transition kernel and stage model are specified on the reduced state space.
The induced approximate dynamic program is well posed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced model defines a computable Markov policy, but it is exact only under state sufficiency. Without a quantified model-error bound, its value is neither a certified lower nor upper bound for the original problem.

notation.meaning: Approximate transition kernel on reduced states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for reduced-state Markov approximations.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Markov Processes with Arbitrary State Space p. 101

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a reduced state \(\widetilde s_t=\psi_t(H_t)\) and replace the true history-conditioned law by a kernel \(\widetilde Q_t(\cdot\mid\widetilde s_t,u_t)\). Solving the resulting dynamic program yields a policy measurable with respect to \((x_t,\widetilde s_t)\). This replacement is exact only if histories \(h,h'\) satisfying \(\psi_t(h)=\psi_t(h')\) have identical relevant conditional future laws, costs, and feasible sets. If two such histories induce different conditional laws, no single kernel \(\widetilde Q_t\) represents both. The computed value is then an approximation and, absent a separate one-sided construction or error theorem, is neither a certified lower bound nor a certified upper bound for the original value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduced Markov state yields an approximate policy, but omitted predictive information destroys exactness and provides no value bound without an additional error theorem.

children.title: State-Sufficiency Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where the chosen state omits information needed for valid decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Sufficiency Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for strong model-based Markov-state sufficiency in multistage decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_t\) be the observed history and let \(S_t=\phi_t(H_t)\). The aggregation is model-sufficient if, whenever \(\phi_t(h)=\phi_t(h')\), the histories \(h\) and \(h'\) have the same admissible action set, the same one-stage cost for every common action, and the same conditional transition kernel for all information retained at the next stage. Under these equalities, the Bellman operator factors through \(S_t\). If an equality fails, this model-sufficiency argument no longer establishes an exact state-based recursion; state augmentation is required unless exactness is established separately through a weaker value-equivalence condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Histories may be aggregated safely when they have identical feasible actions, costs, and retained continuation laws. If this model equivalence fails, exact aggregation needs additional justification or a richer state.
assumptions_latex: The stage-\(t\) history is \(H_t\), and the proposed state is \(S_t=\phi_t(H_t)\).
Admissible actions, one-stage costs, and conditional continuation kernels are defined for every relevant history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality of the continuation model on every fiber of \(\phi_t\) is sufficient for the Bellman recursion to factor through \(S_t\); failure of that equality marks the boundary of this strong sufficiency criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: General Dependent-Process Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact history-state representation of a generally dependent exogenous information process.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_t=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\), where the disturbances take values in standard Borel spaces. A regular conditional kernel \(K_t\) may be chosen so that \(K_t(h,A)=\mathbb P((h,\xi_{t+1})\in A\mid H_t=h)\). Hence the history process is Markov with state \(H_t\). A dynamic program may use this representation when all other payoff-relevant and feasibility-relevant information is included in, or appended to, the state. A compression \(S_t=\phi_t(H_t)\) is exact only if the required conditional continuation model factors through \(S_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dependent exogenous process is Markov when its full observed history is used as its information state, provided the dynamic-programming state also retains any other relevant system information.
assumptions_latex: The disturbance process \((\xi_t)_{t=1}^T\) takes values in standard Borel spaces.
Decisions are nonanticipative with respect to \(\mathcal F_t=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\).
Any additional payoff-relevant or feasibility-relevant endogenous variables are included in the dynamic-programming state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The full disturbance history \(H_t\) is an exact Markov representation of the exogenous information process; lower-dimensional compression requires a sufficient statistic.

notation.meaning: regular conditional transition kernel for the history process

children.title: Sampling Coverage
children.top_down_role: Extent to which sampled trajectories represent relevant outcomes or transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent independent forward-sampling coverage of fixed reachable state sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a measurable state set \(B\), and let \(I_k(B)\) indicate that the forward trajectory sampled at iteration \(k\) visits \(B\). If the indicators are independent and satisfy \(\mathbb P(I_k(B)=1)=p_B>0\), then \[\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}I_k(B)=\infty\quad\text{almost surely}.\] Thus each fixed positive-probability set is visited infinitely often. The conclusion holds simultaneously for every member of any finite or countable specified family of such sets; in particular, it holds for all reachable states in a finite state space when every state has positive per-iteration visitation probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed set with positive visitation probability is visited infinitely often under independent repeated sampling. The statement applies simultaneously to any specified finite or countable family of such sets.
assumptions_latex: The measurable set \(B\) is fixed before sampling.
Forward trajectories are independent across iterations.
Each trajectory visits \(B\) with the same probability \(p_B>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The visit count \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}I_k(B)\) diverges almost surely.

notation.meaning: fixed state set whose coverage is assessed
indicator that iteration k visits B

children.title: State Reachability
children.top_down_role: States or post-decision regions attainable under admissible policies.

knowledge_statements.title: State Reachability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Policy-relative and control-model-relative probabilistic reachability at a specified stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a stage \(t\), a measurable set \(B\) in the stage-\(t\) state space, and an admissible policy \(\pi\). The set \(B\) is reachable at stage \(t\) under \(\pi\) if \(\mathbb P^{\pi}(S_t\in B)>0\). It is reachable at stage \(t\) for the control model if this inequality holds for at least one admissible policy \(\pi\). Reachability at some stage means that the model-relative condition holds for at least one \(t\) in the finite horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is reachable under a policy when that policy visits it with positive probability at the specified stage; it is model-reachable when some admissible policy does so.
assumptions_latex: A finite horizon, an initial-state law, controlled transition kernels, and a class of admissible policies are specified.
The set \(B\) is a measurable subset of the stage-\(t\) state space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model-relative reachability at stage \(t\) is equivalent to the existence of an admissible \(\pi\) satisfying \(\mathbb P^{\pi}(S_t\in B)>0\).

notation.meaning: trajectory law induced by policy pi

children.title: Rare-State Coverage
children.top_down_role: Representation of low-probability states with material policy consequences.

assumptions_latex: Independent sampled trajectories visit a specified state set \(B\) with probability \(p\in(0,1)\).
Coverage is declared after \(N\) trajectories.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The miss probability is \((1-p)^N\), so confidence \(1-\delta\) requires \(N\geq\lceil\log(\delta)/\log(1-p)\rceil\).

notation.meaning: per-trajectory visitation probability of the rare set
allowed probability of missing the set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample coverage bound for an independently sampled rare state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If each independently sampled trajectory visits \(B\) with probability \(p\), then the probability that none of \(N\) trajectories visits \(B\) is \((1-p)^N\). Hence \(\mathbb P(\text{at least one visit to }B)\geq 1-\delta\) whenever \[N\geq \left\lceil\frac{\log\delta}{\log(1-p)}\right\rceil.\] In particular, the required sample count is of order \(p^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\) as \(p\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Covering a state visited with probability p requires about p inverse times log one over delta independent trajectories.
knowledge_statements.title: Rare-State Coverage

children.title: Unvisited-State Boundary
children.top_down_role: Reliability limits for value approximations in reachable but unsampled regions.

assumptions_latex: An SDDP-type method generates cuts only from sampled trial states.
A reachable set \(B\) is never visited by any forward trajectory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cut validity may remain global, but convergence or accuracy on \(B\) does not follow from sampled-state convergence.

notation.meaning: current lower approximation of the stage value function

review_flags: missing direct SDDP source for the precise convergence boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: What forward-sampling convergence cannot establish on unvisited states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\underline V_t\leq V_t\) is updated only by cuts computed at sampled trial states, while no sampled state lies in \(B\). Although each generated cut may be globally valid, the algorithm receives no local information forcing \(\underline V_t(s)\uparrow V_t(s)\) for \(s\in B\). Therefore convergence at visited states, or convergence of the initial-state bound, does not imply pointwise or uniform convergence on \(B\) without an additional coverage, regularity, or exploration condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Never visiting a reachable region prevents sampled-state convergence arguments from guaranteeing value-function accuracy there.
knowledge_statements.title: Unvisited-State Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The limitation is plausible and appropriately classified as a failure boundary, but the record supplies no direct SDDP source establishing which sampled-state or initial-bound convergence results fail to imply pointwise or uniform convergence on an unvisited region.

assumptions_latex: At every stage, the disturbance has finite support with known positive probabilities.
Stage problems are linear programs with polyhedral feasible sets and finite optimal values on the relevant state domains.
The horizon is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every exact cost-to-go function is convex polyhedral and admits a finite maximum-of-affine representation on its domain.

notation.meaning: finite disturbance support at stage t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-horizon linear, finite-support setting for polyhedral SDDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each stage \(t\), let \(\Xi_t\) be finite and let the recourse problem, conditional on each \(\xi_t\in\Xi_t\), be a feasible finite-valued linear program whose right-hand side depends affinely on the predecessor state. Backward induction then yields a proper convex polyhedral function \(V_t\). Thus, on its effective domain, there exist finitely many affine functions \(\alpha_{tj}+\beta_{tj}^{\mathsf T}x\) such that \[V_t(x)=\max_{1\leq j\leq m_t}\{\alpha_{tj}+\beta_{tj}^{\mathsf T}x\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-support linear recourse produces convex polyhedral cost-to-go functions representable by finitely many affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Support Polyhedral Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A direct finite-support linear stochastic-programming or SDDP source is required. Finite marginal support alone does not ensure the claimed polyhedral Bellman recursion if state-dependent conditional probabilities or other nonpolyhedral dependence are allowed; a finite scenario tree or suitable fixed finite conditional distributions must be specified.

assumptions_latex: Stage objectives and constraint functions are proper, closed, and convex in decision and predecessor state.
Relevant feasible state-decision sets are nonempty and compact, with finite integrable costs.
Conditional expectations and measurable selections needed by the Bellman recursion exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cost-to-go functions are proper closed convex functions, and supporting subgradients define valid affine lower cuts.

notation.meaning: subgradient at trial state x bar

review_flags: missing direct nonlinear SDDP convergence source
hypotheses may require strengthening for a specific convergence theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex nonlinear value functions and supporting-cut validity, not a full convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated convexity, closedness, compactness, and integrability hypotheses, partial minimization and conditional expectation preserve convexity, so each Bellman cost-to-go function \(V_t\) is proper, closed, and convex on its effective domain. At any trial state \(\bar x\) where a subgradient \(g_t\in\partial V_t(\bar x)\) exists, the affine function \[x\longmapsto V_t(\bar x)+g_t^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)\] is a globally valid lower bound for \(V_t\). Unlike the polyhedral regime, finitely many such cuts need not represent \(V_t\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex nonlinear recourse preserves convex value functions, whose subgradients generate valid affine lower bounds but generally not finite exact representations.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Nonlinear Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Convexity and the subgradient inequality are standard, but the stated assumptions do not transparently guarantee properness and closedness after every partial minimization and conditional expectation. A direct nonlinear SDDP or convex dynamic-programming source is needed to identify sufficient regularity hypotheses.

children.title: Relatively Complete Multistage Recourse
children.top_down_role: Stagewise feasibility across reachable histories under admissible prior decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Relatively Complete Multistage Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure stagewise recourse feasibility from every attainable predecessor state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(t=2,\ldots,T\), let \(R_{t-1}\) be the set of predecessor states attainable through feasible nonanticipative decisions, let \(Q_t(\cdot\mid x)\) be the conditional disturbance kernel at state \(x\), and let \(X_t(x,\xi)\) be the stage-\(t\) feasible action set. Relatively complete multistage recourse holds if, for every \(t=2,\ldots,T\) and every \(x\in R_{t-1}\), \[Q_t\bigl(\{\xi:X_t(x,\xi)\neq\varnothing\}\mid x\bigr)=1.\] This condition gives almost-sure stagewise continuation feasibility; it does not by itself guarantee finite expected costs or attainment of stage optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relatively complete multistage recourse means that every attainable predecessor state admits a feasible next-stage action for almost every disturbance under its conditional law.
assumptions_latex: The horizon \(T\) is finite.
For each stage \(t\), the attainable set \(R_{t-1}\), conditional kernel \(Q_t(\cdot\mid x)\), and feasible-action multifunction \(X_t(x,\xi)\) are specified.
Attainability is defined through feasible nonanticipative decisions at prior stages.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relatively complete multistage recourse holds exactly when the stated kernel probability equals \(1\) for every \(t=2,ldots,T\) and every \(x\in R_{t-1}\).

notation.meaning: conditional disturbance kernel at predecessor state x

children.title: State-Dependent Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feasible action sets that vary with stage state or observed history.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Dependent Feasibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State domain induced by almost-sure one-stage continuation feasibility under a state-dependent disturbance kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_t(\cdot\mid x)\) be the conditional law of \(\xi_t\) given a predecessor state \(x\) that is sufficient for the stage-\(t\) feasibility model, and let \(X_t(x,\xi)\) be the feasible action set. Define \[D_{t-1}=\left\{x:Q_t\bigl(\{\xi:X_t(x,\xi)\neq\varnothing\}\mid x\bigr)=1\right\}.\] The domain \(D_{t-1}\) can be a proper subset of the predecessor-state space when feasibility or the conditional disturbance law depends on \(x\). Any policy having almost-sure stage-\(t\) recourse feasibility must keep its predecessor state in \(D_{t-1}\) almost surely. Relatively complete recourse holds at this stage when every attainable predecessor state belongs to \(D_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State-dependent recourse restricts predecessor states to those whose conditional disturbance law gives feasible next-stage actions with probability one.
assumptions_latex: The predecessor state \(x\) is sufficient for the conditional disturbance law and the stage-\(t\) feasibility model.
A conditional kernel \(Q_t(\cdot\mid x)\) is specified for every relevant state \(x\).
The feasible-action multifunction is \(X_t(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The almost-sure one-stage continuation-feasibility domain is \(D_{t-1}=\{x:Q_t(\{\xi:X_t(x,\xi)\neq\varnothing\}\mid x)=1\}\).

children.title: Feasibility-Cut Regimes
children.top_down_role: SDDP variants that explicitly represent infeasible downstream states.

assumptions_latex: For a fixed disturbance realization, recourse feasibility is \(Wy=h-Tx\), \(y\geq0\).
A trial state \(\bar x\) makes this system infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A Farkas ray yields a linear inequality satisfied by every recourse-feasible state and violated by \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-recourse feasibility certificate for a fixed scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: By Farkas' alternative, infeasibility of \(Wy=h-T\bar x\), \(y\geq0\), is certified by a vector \(r\) satisfying \(W^{\mathsf T}r\leq0\) and \(r^{\mathsf T}(h-T\bar x)>0\). Every state \(x\) for which recourse is feasible must satisfy the feasibility cut \[r^{\mathsf T}(h-Tx)\leq0.\] Indeed, the certificate is checkable using only matrix-vector products and inequalities. Adding this cut excludes \(\bar x\) while retaining every state feasible for that scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Farkas ray certifies recourse infeasibility and generates a linear cut excluding the offending state without removing scenario-feasible states.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Cut Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Farkas certificate and cut signs are mathematically consistent, and certificate is the correct content kind. However, the cited general recourse section is not an inspectable locator for Farkas' alternative or the stated feasibility-cut construction, so direct support is required.

children.title: Recourse Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Reachable histories for which no feasible continuation exists.

assumptions_latex: The predecessor decision is \(x\in[0,1]\), and \(\xi\) is Bernoulli with \(\mathbb P(\xi=1)>0\).
Second-stage feasibility requires \(y=x-\xi\) and \(y\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x<1\) has infeasible recourse with positive probability, so relatively complete recourse fails.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete positive-probability failure of relatively complete recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[0,1]\), let \(\xi\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb P(\xi=1)=p>0\), and require a second-stage variable \(y\geq0\) satisfying \(y=x-\xi\). For every \(x<1\), the realization \(\xi=1\) forces \(y=x-1<0\), so recourse is infeasible with probability \(p\). Thus the recourse value is extended-real, taking \(+\infty\) on that event, and an SDDP scheme using only finite optimality cuts is not well-defined there unless feasibility is enforced or feasibility cuts are introduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-probability scenario can make recourse infeasible, producing infinite continuation value and invalidating an optimality-cut-only scheme.
knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Failure Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\), every stagewise random vector has finite support, and every reachable subproblem is a feasible bounded linear program.
The exact backward oracle selects cuts from a finite set \(\mathcal C\) and discovers an improving cut whenever the current lower model is nonoptimal at a sampled reachable state.
Independent iteration samples assign strictly positive probability to every scenario path required by the discovery condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{K<\infty\}=1\), where after iteration \(K\) no further improving cut is generated and the first-stage lower bound equals the optimal value.

notation.meaning: finite set of cuts producible by exact backward solves

review_flags: SDDP-specific finite-convergence theorem and hypotheses require an authoritative source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support linear SDDP with an explicit finite-cut discovery assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider finite-horizon linear SDDP. Suppose every reachable subproblem is feasible and bounded, exact backward solves can produce only cuts in a finite set \(\mathcal C\), and any nonoptimal lower model encountered at a reachable trial state causes discovery of an improving member of \(\mathcal C\). If successive iterations are sampled independently and every scenario path needed for such discovery has positive probability, then with probability one there is a finite random iteration \(K\) after which no improving cut remains undiscovered. Consequently the lower models stabilize, the first-stage lower bound equals the optimal value, and every first-stage decision returned thereafter is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under finite cut generation, exact subproblems, feasibility, and positive-probability sampling, linear SDDP discovers all necessary cuts and reaches an optimal first-stage solution after finitely many iterations almost surely.
knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Finite-Convergence Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the finite-convergence leaf, but its discovery hypotheses and claim that every subsequently returned first-stage decision is optimal require a direct SDDP convergence theorem.

assumptions_latex: For each stage \(t\) and iteration \(k\), the primal and dual residual bounds \(\varepsilon_{t,k}\ge 0\) are measurable and satisfy \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon_{t,k}<\infty\) almost surely.
Every generated affine cut is globally valid as a lower bound, for example because its multiplier is dual feasible.
The exact model satisfies the usual compactness, continuity, recourse-feasibility, and infinite-sampling conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon_{t,k}\to0\) and accumulated oracle perturbations are finite, so the inexact scheme remains in a convergence-compatible regime.

notation.meaning: certified stage-subproblem error at iteration k

review_flags: Exact convergence conclusion varies with the inexact SDDP variant
Authoritative source for summable-error hypotheses is required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient summable-error regime for inexact backward and forward solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact SDDP execution is in the summable-error convergence regime when, for every stage \(t\), its certified primal and dual error sequence \((\varepsilon_{t,k})_{k\ge1}\) is nonnegative, measurable, and satisfies \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\varepsilon_{t,k}<\infty\) almost surely; every approximate dual solution still generates a globally valid lower cut; and every relevant scenario node is sampled infinitely often. Together with compact trial-state sets, continuous convex stage problems, and relatively complete recourse, these conditions make the cumulative oracle perturbation finite and force \(\varepsilon_{t,k}\to0\), which is the standard regime in which exact-SDDP convergence arguments can be transferred to inexact solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact SDDP remains convergence-compatible when certified errors are summable, all cuts stay valid lower bounds, relevant nodes recur, and the underlying convex recourse model satisfies standard regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Subproblem Convergence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and summable-error regime fit the leaf, but transfer of exact-SDDP convergence depends on the precise inexact oracle and algorithm variant.

children.title: Dependence Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Information-process dependence outside the scope of the convergence regime.

assumptions_latex: \(\xi_1\in\{-1,1\}\) is equiprobable and \(\xi_2=\xi_1\) almost surely.
The decision \(x_1\) observes \(\xi_1\), but the approximation replaces \(\mathcal L(\xi_2\mid\xi_1)\) by the marginal law of \(\xi_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V^*=0\) but \(\widehat V=1\), so an unmodeled dependence structure invalidates the decomposed recursion.

notation.meaning: decision made after observing the first-stage outcome

review_flags: Concrete standard counterexample; SDDP-specific source still required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by applying a stagewise-independent recursion to dependent uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_1\) be uniform on \(\{-1,1\}\), let \(\xi_2=\xi_1\) almost surely, and choose \(x_1\in\mathbb R\) after observing \(\xi_1\) to minimize \(\mathbb E[(x_1-\xi_2)^2]\). The correct conditional recursion chooses \(x_1=\xi_1\) and has value \(V^*=0\). A stagewise-independent SDDP recursion that substitutes the marginal law of \(\xi_2\) for \(\mathcal L(\xi_2\mid\xi_1)\) instead chooses \(x_1=0\) and reports \(\widehat V=1\). Thus convergence for the misspecified recursion does not imply optimality for the dependent process unless dependence is represented in the state or conditional sampling model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ignoring serial dependence can make SDDP converge to the wrong dynamic program; a two-stage perfectly correlated process already yields a strict value error.
knowledge_statements.title: Dependence Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally correct and fits the dependence failure boundary, but no evidence supports its SDDP interpretation.

children.title: Sampling-Coverage Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Relevant states or transitions receiving insufficient sampling exposure.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in[0,1]\), \(c>0\), and a scenario of probability \(p>0\) has recourse cost \(M(1-x)\), with \(pM>c\).
The positive-cost scenario is never sampled or otherwise included by the backward oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x=0\neq1=x^*\), so absent coverage destroys consistency despite unlimited iterations.

notation.meaning: probability and penalty of the omitted scenario

review_flags: Concrete standard counterexample; direct SDDP sampling-coverage citation required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when a positive-probability scenario is permanently absent from backward sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(x\in[0,1]\) with true objective \(F(x)=cx+pM(1-x)\), where \(c>0\), \(p>0\), and \(pM>c\). Interpret the second term as recourse in a scenario having probability \(p\), while every other scenario has zero recourse. The true minimizer is \(x^*=1\). If the positive-cost scenario is never sampled in backward passes, its cut is never generated and the maintained objective is \(\widehat F(x)=cx\), whose minimizer is \(\widehat x=0\). Hence infinite iteration count alone cannot ensure convergence: every scenario or conditional outcome capable of changing the value model must receive adequate sampling coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-probability scenario that is never sampled can hide an essential recourse cut, causing permanent convergence to a strictly suboptimal first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Coverage Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The omitted-scenario example is mathematically correct and fits the sampling-coverage boundary, but it has no cited source.

children.title: Feasibility Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Breakdown caused by infeasible reachable subproblems or missing recourse.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure without relatively complete recourse or a feasibility-cut mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[0,1]\) and define a recourse problem with \(y\ge0\) and equality \(y=\xi-x\), where \(\xi\in\{0,1\}\). For outcome \(\xi=0\), every state \(x>0\) makes the recourse problem infeasible, so \(Q(x,0)=+\infty\). Ordinary finite affine optimality cuts cannot represent this extended-valued barrier. Therefore an SDDP method assuming relatively complete recourse may visit an infeasible state, fail to obtain a dual value cut, or continue with a falsely finite lower model. Convergence requires relatively complete recourse, an exact-penalty reformulation with justified bounds, or valid feasibility cuts that exclude such states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without relatively complete recourse, some trial states have infinite downstream cost; ordinary value cuts cannot represent them, so SDDP needs feasibility cuts or a justified reformulation.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in[0,1]\), \(y\ge0\), and recourse requires \(y=\xi-x\) for \(\xi\in\{0,1\}\).
No feasibility cuts, penalties, or complete-recourse reformulation are supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(x,0)=+\infty\) for every \(x>0\), which finite affine value cuts cannot represent.

notation.meaning: recourse value for state x and outcome xi

review_flags: Concrete standard counterexample; authoritative feasibility-cut source required

children.title: Oracle Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Invalid, unreliable, or systematically inaccurate subproblem information.

assumptions_latex: The true convex value function is \(Q(x)=x^2\) on \([-1,1]\).
At \(\bar x=0\), the oracle returns the purported cut \(q(x)=\delta\) with \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(0)=\delta>Q(0)=0\), so the maintained model is not a lower bound and its bound-based convergence certificate is invalid.

notation.meaning: true value function and purported affine cut

review_flags: Concrete convex-oracle counterexample; direct inexact-SDDP citation required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by an oracle returning a cut that is not globally valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the true downstream value be \(Q(x)=x^2\) on \([-1,1]\). At \(\bar x=0\), a valid supporting cut is \(q(x)=0\). Suppose an erroneous backward oracle instead returns \(q_\delta(x)=\delta\) for some \(\delta>0\). Then \(q_\delta(0)=\delta>Q(0)=0\), so the approximate value model ceases to be a lower bound. Any reported lower bound, optimality gap, or monotone-convergence argument based on that model is consequently invalid. Approximate solves are admissible only when their residual certificates preserve global cut validity or when the convergence analysis explicitly controls possible overestimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle error that raises a cut above the true value function destroys the lower-bound invariant and invalidates SDDP bounds and stopping certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly exhibits loss of the lower-bound invariant and fits the oracle failure boundary, but the SDDP-specific claim lacks evidence.
